drafts.title: ایک نظر میں — پورا نقشہ
drafts.gloss: The whole span in one evening
drafts.summary: Opening night of «تاریخ سے سبق» runs the whole span from ۱۱ھ [verify] to ۱۹۴۷ [verify] in one evening, so that every later session has a fixed place to attach to. The room is given two objects at the door — a printed timeline («the Line», eight pegs and otherwise blank) and a base map with six anchor cities — and spends the evening writing on both: four announced pen-down moments, ending with each listener writing their own city onto the map. Three people are introduced as a deliberate preview (سیدنا عمر الفاروق ؓ, ہلاکو خان, سلطان محمد فاتح), each named as belonging to a later session that will treat them properly. Nothing sensitive is adjudicated: the fall of بغداد, the ending of the caliphate in ۱۹۲۴ [verify] and ۱۹۴۷ [verify] are marked on the line and narrated only as far as the source narrates, there is no floor Q&A slot, and the evening's single conclusion is a quotation from مولانا شمس الحق افغانیؒ shown on screen with its attribution, not the speaker's own view.
drafts.opening_scene: Both wall objects are still blank and no slide moves; the speaker stands still and describes one night in بغداد — a city that had been the centre of the Muslim world for centuries, its libraries, its translation work, a caliph whose name was read in the khutba from Central Asia to North Africa — and then the days in ۶۵۶ھ [verify] when a Mongol army under ہلاکو خان took the city, the caliph was killed, and the chroniclers recorded what became of its books [SOURCE: the volume covering the Mongols — the account of the taking of بغداد in ۶۵۶ھ, the name of the caliph, and what the chroniclers record of the libraries]. He tells it plainly, without raising his voice, and the room has no map in front of it yet — only the description. He then walks to the three-metre banner behind him, which carries eight printed pegs and nothing else, and makes one filled square at the ۶۵۶ھ [verify] peg; the room sees that the mark sits near the middle, with blank line on both sides, and everyone makes the same square on their own sheet. The question left hanging, said once and not answered: «یہ رات ہماری تاریخ کے وسط میں آتی ہے، آخر میں نہیں — اس سے پہلے کتنا وقت گزر چکا تھا، اور اس کے بعد کتنا باقی تھا؟» — and, second: how does a civilisation lose its capital and still continue for centuries afterwards?

runsheet.block: آغاز — the two objects are handed over
runsheet.content: Each person receives a single folded A3 sheet and one pen at the door; the first instruction of the course is «اپنا نام لکھ لیجیے» on the cover, and thirty seconds are given for it. The speaker points to the two blank objects — the banner behind him with eight printed pegs, and the base map with six cities marked and nothing else — and says what they are for: they will be written on tonight and every week for ten weeks. Because this is the first evening there is no «پچھلے ہفتے», so the re-anchor line is replaced by one sentence: tonight is the only evening that covers the whole line, and every other evening is one piece of it. No history is narrated in this block at all.

runsheet.block: Opening scene — بغداد, ۶۵۶ھ [verify]
runsheet.content: The scene described above is told standing still, with no map movement and no slide change. It ends with the speaker marking one filled square at the ۶۵۶ھ [verify] peg on the banner, the room copying it onto their own Line, and the two questions left hanging without answer. This is the first of four pen-down moments and the only mark made before the story begins.

runsheet.block: The story — the whole span in six moves
runsheet.content: Six moves of roughly three minutes each, each one a place on the map and a peg on the line: (1) مدینہ at ۱۱ھ [verify], one city and one generation; (2) out of Arabia to دمشق, and then west to اندلس and east to سندھ within the same decade [verify ۹۲–۹۳ھ]; (3) the capital moves east to بغداد while قرطبہ builds in the west — two capitals in the same centuries; (4) the break: the Levant, then the sweep from the east, and the ۶۵۶ھ [verify] mark from the opening now gets its context, with قاہرہ as where the scholars and books went [SOURCE: what actually survived ۶۵۶ھ, and where]; (5) recovery: a frontier state takes قسطنطنیہ in ۸۵۷ھ [verify], while in the east سندھ leads on to دہلی; (6) the long retreat to ۱۹۲۴ [verify] and the peg at ۱۹۴۷ [verify]. Three announced pen-downs fall inside this block — after moves 2, 4 and 6 — each opened with the same fixed phrase «قلم اٹھائیے» and given fifteen silent seconds.

runsheet.block: تعارف — three people, read from the card
runsheet.content: Roughly two minutes twenty each, in the four-line تراجم format: نام و نسب with the لقب the tradition gave · سنین · what they did in one sentence · ایک واقعہ. Each of the three is introduced with the explicit statement that this is a preview and not their session — «عمر الفاروق ؓ اگلے ہفتے پوری نشست میں آئیں گے», «ہلاکو خان کی نشست چھٹی ہے», «سلطان محمد فاتح ساتویں نشست میں» — so that the room understands the three marks it just made on the line are three future evenings. The incident is read aloud from the printed card in the speaker's hand, never from memory. The workbook prints the first three lines and leaves «ایک واقعہ» blank for the listener to write.

runsheet.block: کیسے پتا چلا؟ — dates are the first question
runsheet.content: The speaker asks the room to look at the line it has just drawn, and puts up one clearly-labelled hypothetical claim: suppose someone tells you that سلطان محمد فاتح sent a letter to ہلاکو خان. He points at the two marks the room made — they sit two centuries apart on the line [verify]. The claim dies with no knowledge of Arabic, of chains of narration, or of manuscripts; it dies on the sheet in their hands, and that is what a timeline is for. Then the Arabic of سفیان ثوریؒ goes on screen in Naskh with the Urdu rendering beneath it, is read aloud once, and the speaker stops [SOURCE: the Arabic wording of the saying of سفیان ثوریؒ on dates and forgery, its Urdu rendering and reference, read off the page image and supplied by the editor]. No further method is taught; the closing line is only that three minutes of this question will come every week.

runsheet.block: آج کی بات — the supplied quotation, then everyone writes
runsheet.content: One slide headed «مولانا شمس الحق افغانیؒ فرماتے ہیں», carrying the four things in Urdu script — ماضی سے ارتباط · وحدتِ فکر و عمل · فراہمیِ اسبابِ قوت · جہدِ مسلسل — with the attribution and reference printed on the slide itself [SOURCE: the exact wording of the four, and the reference the book gives for it, read by eye]. The speaker reads the four, adds one sentence of connection and no more — that the reason tonight began with the whole line rather than with the first year is that the first of the four is ماضی سے ارتباط, and the other three rest on it — and then stops. Ninety seconds of silence follow while everyone writes their own line in the printed box «آج آپ کیا لے کر جا رہے ہیں؟ ______». At most two volunteers read theirs aloud; the speaker says «شکریہ» and nothing else.

runsheet.block: اگلے ہفتے — close on a question
runsheet.content: The speaker holds up the sheet and gives one instruction: bring this back next week, it is the only thing to bring. He points at the banner: tonight was fourteen centuries; next week is twelve years — «بارہ سال», ۱۱ھ to ۲۳ھ [verify] — and he draws a small bracket around that stretch of the line so the room can see how narrow next week's ground is. Then the take-home question is said once, slowly, written on the banner, and left unanswered; the evening ends on it rather than on a summary.

people.name: سیدنا عمر الفاروق ؓ
people.did: The caliph in whose time the Persian empire was ended, Syria and Egypt passed out of Byzantine hands, and the administration of a state — its provinces, its treasury, its calendar — was actually built.
people.incident_plan: One incident of his personal conduct while holding that office, chosen so that it also lands on tonight's map: his journey to بیت المقدس and his entry into the city, and the terms given to its people. It is told as the source tells it, read from the card, with no comparison drawn to anyone. [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1, the عمر ؓ chapter — the account of the journey to and entry into بیت المقدس and the wording of the agreement given to its people. The volume slice currently held does not reach this chapter.]

people.name: ہلاکو خان
people.did: The Mongol commander whose army took بغداد in ۶۵۶ھ [verify], ending the Abbasid caliphate in that city.
people.incident_plan: One concrete incident from the taking of the city — what the chroniclers record of the fate of its libraries and its scholars — narrated flatly, with no adjectives added by the speaker and no attribution of blame to any group inside the city. He is not a Muslim figure, so no honorific is used and no لقب is given; none is invented to fill the gap. [SOURCE: the volume covering the Mongols — one authentic incident from the account of ۶۵۶ھ. Not currently held; must be obtained or the incident is not told.]

people.name: سلطان محمد فاتح
people.did: The Ottoman sultan who took قسطنطنیہ in ۸۵۷ھ [verify], turning a frontier state into the central Muslim power for the centuries that followed.
people.incident_plan: One concrete incident from the taking of the city — the kind of detail that is remembered because it is specific rather than because it is praised, such as an account of the preparation for the siege or of his conduct on entering the city. The لقب «فاتح» is not ours; it is the title already carried in the name the tradition uses. [SOURCE: the Ottoman volume — one authentic incident from the account of ۸۵۷ھ. Not currently held; must be obtained or the incident is not told.]

drafts.map: The base map is printed once and reused for ten weeks: the Mediterranean basin plus Iran and Central Asia, extended far enough east to carry سندھ and دہلی (a build requirement tonight, since the six printed anchors are all western). Six anchor cities are pre-printed and nothing else: مکہ · مدینہ · دمشق · بغداد · قرطبہ · قسطنطنیہ. Tonight adds, in this order: (1) مدینہ circled — one city; (2) an arrow مدینہ → دمشق, northwest, drawn by the speaker on the wall map only; (3) PEN-DOWN ONE — two arrows drawn simultaneously out of دمشق, one running west along North Africa through قرطبہ and on to the Pyrenees and the gates of France, one running east through Iran to سندھ, both labelled with the same decade [verify ۹۲–۹۳ھ]; (4) a short arrow دمشق → بغداد eastward as the capital moves, with قرطبہ circled at the same moment so the two capitals sit on the sheet together; (5) PEN-DOWN TWO — one broad stroke down from the northeast onto بغداد, and قاہرہ written in by hand and circled as where the books and the scholars went; (6) an arrow into قسطنطنیہ from Anatolia, and in the east an arrow سندھ → دہلی with دہلی written in by hand; (7) PEN-DOWN THREE — each person writes their own city onto the map as the seventh mark, in their own hand, and the speaker says only «آپ اس نقشے پر ہیں» and moves on. One pen each, handed out at the door; on the Line all marks are ticks except the ۶۵۶ھ [verify] mark, which is the single filled square, so it can be found again at a glance in week ten.
drafts.howweknow_plan: Three minutes, built entirely on the object the room has just made, so that no methodology is taught in the abstract. The speaker asks everyone to look at their own Line, then puts up one claim clearly labelled «فرض کیجیے» — suppose you are told that سلطان محمد فاتح sent a letter to ہلاکو خان. He asks one question of the room, «کیا یہ ممکن ہے؟», waits, then points at the two marks they made themselves: they are two centuries apart on the line [verify]. The claim collapses without any knowledge of Arabic, of chains of narration or of manuscripts — it collapses on the sheet in their hands. He then says this is not our device but the muhaddithun's, puts the Arabic of سفیان ثوریؒ on screen in Naskh with the Urdu beneath, reads it once, and stops [SOURCE: the Arabic wording of the saying of سفیان ثوریؒ on dates and forgery, with its Urdu rendering and its reference, read off the page image — the OCR text layer garbles Arabic and must not be the source of the slide]. The block closes with one sentence: three minutes on this question will come every week. Deliberately NOT used tonight: the forged Khaybar document, which is the week-3 segment and is not to be spent early.
drafts.takehome_question: «جس ہستی ﷺ کے گرد یہ سب کچھ قائم تھا، اُن کے وصال کے بعد یہ سب بکھرا کیوں نہیں؟» [When the one ﷺ around whom all of this stood had passed, why did it not fall apart?]

sensitive.what_arises: Four points of heat are touched tonight, all of them briefly. (1) The fall of بغداد in ۶۵۶ھ [verify] is the opening scene, and it is the standard entry point for a sectarian accusation of internal betrayal. (2) ہلاکو خان is one of the three تعارف figures, which puts a non-Muslim conqueror in a respectful format built for scholars and Companions. (3) The ending of the caliphate in ۱۹۲۴ [verify] carries live political charge, Turkish and Pakistani both. (4) ۱۹۴۷ [verify] is a peg on the line in a Karachi-area room, and any narration of it invites a partisan reading. A fifth risk is the classic opening-night floor question, «مسلمان زوال کا شکار کیوں ہوئے؟», which is an invitation to give a political opinion. سیدنا عمر ؓ is introduced, but nothing from the مشاجرات arises tonight; the fiqh guardrail lands in session 3 as designed, before anything disputed is narrated.
sensitive.how_handled: The fall of بغداد is narrated only as far as the source narrates it — an army came, the city was taken, the caliph was killed, this is what the chroniclers record of the books — and stops there; no internal cause is named. ہلاکو خان is given the same four factual lines as the others with no honorific, no لقب, and no adjective of the speaker's own; the format is a تراجم notice, and the plainness is the safeguard. ۱۹۲۴ and ۱۹۴۷ are marked on the line and named as dates, not narrated: the speaker says in one sentence that ۱۹۴۷ belongs to session 9 and moves on. The evening's only conclusion is the supplied quotation of مولانا شمس الحق افغانیؒ, shown on screen under its own attribution, and the listener's own takeaway box — the speaker offers no causal verdict of his own on decline. There is no floor Q&A slot in the fixed 45-minute shape and none is opened tonight.
will_not_be_said: No group, sect, community or named individual inside بغداد is identified as having betrayed the city — the ابن العلقمی narrative is not raised, and if a listener raises it the deferral line is used
No comparison or ranking between any two Companions ؓ, and no reference to the مشاجرات — the guardrail for that material is installed in session 3, not tonight
No verdict on any modern state, government, party, movement or leader — Turkish, Pakistani, Indian or Arab
No claim about who was right in ۱۹۴۷ [verify], and no narration of Partition beyond marking the peg
No statement that any present-day group is the continuation of, or the betrayer of, any past one
No causal explanation of Muslim decline offered in the speaker's own voice; the only answer given is the supplied quotation, attributed on screen
No death-date, page number, volume number or hadith number spoken from memory — every reference read from the card or not given at all
No adjective of praise or condemnation attached to ہلاکو خان beyond what the source's own wording carries
sensitive.floor_policy: No open floor is taken during the 45 minutes; the shape has no Q&A block and one is not improvised on opening night. Questions are taken at the door afterwards, one to one. Three rehearsed lines cover everything: for anything touching the Companions ؓ or the مشاجرات — «یہ سوال اہم ہے اور اس کی پوری نشست تیسری ہے، جہاں ہم فقہاء کے اصول کے ساتھ اسے دیکھیں گے۔»; for anything touching ۱۹۲۴ or ۱۹۴۷ or present-day politics — «آج کی نشست پورے نقشے کی ہے؛ اس دور کی نشست نویں ہے۔ سیاست پر میں رائے نہیں دوں گا، جو کتاب میں ہے وہی بیان کروں گا۔»; for a question of fact he cannot source — «یہ میں کتاب سے دیکھ کر اگلے ہفتے بتاؤں گا۔», said while visibly writing the question down on a sheet kept for that purpose, and actually answered the following week. If a question is asked mid-session from the floor, it is received warmly, written on that same sheet in front of the room, and not answered then.

sources_needed: The Arabic wording of the saying of سفیان ثوریؒ on dates and forgery, its Urdu rendering, and the printed page reference to appear on the slide — read off the page image, not from the OCR text layer, which garbles Arabic worst of all. The verified anchor for this is already recorded in docs/catalogue/SOURCES.md; the editor supplies the number.

The exact wording of مولانا شمس الحق افغانیؒ's four things — ماضی سے ارتباط، وحدتِ فکر و عمل، فراہمیِ اسبابِ قوت، جہدِ مسلسل — together with the statement that each depends on the one before it, and the reference the book itself gives for the quotation. Both the wording and the reference are printed on the slide, and both must be read by eye.

One authentic incident for سیدنا عمر الفاروق ؓ from the source's عمر ؓ chapter: the journey to بیت المقدس, the entry into the city, and the wording of the agreement given to its people. The volume slice currently held does not reach this chapter and it must be obtained before the night.

One authentic incident for ہلاکو خان from an account of ۶۵۶ھ, including what the chroniclers record of the city's libraries and scholars, and the name of the caliph killed. The volume covering the Mongols is not held.
One authentic incident for سلطان محمد فاتح from an account of ۸۵۷ھ. The Ottoman volume is not held.

A source-backed one-line statement of what actually happened at the two ends of the frontier in the same decade [verify ۹۲–۹۳ھ], since this is the single most memorable claim of the evening and it is asserted twice — once aloud and once as a label the audience writes on the map.

Confirmation of every one of the eight dates printed as pegs on the Line against the source before the sheet goes to the printer. A printed peg is the one artifact of the course that cannot be corrected after distribution.
A source-backed line on where the books and scholars went after ۶۵۶ھ, if قاہرہ is to be circled on the map as the refuge rather than merely mentioned.
Confirmation that the base map extends far enough east to carry سندھ and دہلی. The six printed anchor cities are all western and do not force this; tonight's final map movement does.
notes_for_speaker: Slow down at exactly one place: the two arrows out of دمشق, west to اندلس and east to سندھ in the same decade. Say the sentence, then stop talking for three seconds while the pens move. That is the line the room will carry home, and it is also the line that tells a Pakistani audience why this history is theirs. Do not decorate it — the simultaneity does the work.

The opening بغداد scene is told standing still, with no slide movement and no map. Your only movement in those five minutes is the walk to the banner at the end to make one mark. If you are nervous, this is the block to rehearse most — it is short, it is fixed, and once it lands the room is yours.

The safe ground is the banner. If you blank anywhere in the story block, walk to it, put your hand on the last mark, say «ہم یہاں ہیں», and name the next peg. The object carries you back into the narrative; you do not have to remember what came next, you can read it off the wall.

If you are running long, cut in this order: first the two volunteers reading their takeaway aloud, then move 3 (قرطبہ compressed to one sentence — «مغرب میں اسی زمانے میں دوسرا دارالحکومت قائم تھا»), then the map arrow in the third pen-down. Never cut the city-writing at the end, and never cut the pen-downs themselves — the writing is the point of the evening, the talking is not.
During a pen-down, say nothing. Count to fifteen in your head. Silence while people write reads as confidence; filling it reads as nervousness, and it also stops them writing.

Say every date once, clearly, and do not repeat it. A date said twice invites someone to test it. If a date does not come to you, describe the event instead and move on — nobody will notice, and it is safer than a number said in doubt.

Read all three تعارف incidents off the printed card in your hand. Reading a sourced incident aloud is dignified and it is what the format is for; reciting it from memory risks a wrong detail on the one night that decides whether people come back.

Do not narrate ۱۹۴۷ tonight. Mark the peg, say that its evening is the ninth, and go on. The same applies to ۱۹۲۴. This is the single easiest way for the evening to go wrong, and it is avoided by one sentence.

The hypothetical in «کیسے پتا چلا؟» must be visibly labelled «فرض کیجیے» on the slide and said as a supposition, so that nobody leaves the room believing that سلطان محمد فاتح and ہلاکو خان were contemporaries. Say «فرض کیجیے» before the claim, not after.

If a question comes from the floor mid-session, do not answer it. Thank the person, write it on the question sheet where the room can see you writing, say «اگلے ہفتے», and continue. Writing it down in public costs you nothing and buys more credibility than an improvised answer ever will.

You are not required to conclude anything tonight. The only conclusion in this evening belongs to مولانا شمس الحق افغانیؒ and it is printed on the slide with his name on it. If you feel the pull to add a moral at the end, that is the moment to stop talking and hold up the sheet instead.

drafts.title: بارہ سال
drafts.gloss: Twelve years: from a threatened city to two broken empires
drafts.summary: Session 2 covers twelve years in one evening — the caliphates of سیدنا ابوبکر ؓ and سیدنا عمر ؓ — held together by a single visible movement on the map: مدینہ begins the evening as a city that can be raided in a night, and ends it as the centre issuing orders to قادسیہ، دمشق and فسطاط. The narrative runs سقیفہ → the ردہ campaigns → the outward turn (یرموک، قادسیہ، مصر) → the دیوان and the Hijri calendar, narrated from the one named Sunni source the whole course is built on, Tareekh-e-Ummat by Maulana Muhammad Ismail Rehan, with the map moving on screen throughout. Two teaching artifacts already built for the ردہ are used inside the twenty-minute story block: a seven-stage map the speaker steps through as he narrates, and a ninety-second sorting exercise whose purpose is to stop the room from flattening every rebellion into one thing. The evening's lesson is not the speaker's — it is a quotation from the source's own numbered list of the benefits of history, put on the screen with its attribution, after which each listener writes their own takeaway in the workbook.
drafts.opening_scene: The evening opens in مدینہ, in the weeks after the Prophet ﷺ passed away, described physically rather than defined. Guards are posted at the approaches at night; the tribal delegations that had been arriving the year before have stopped arriving; the roads out of the city are unsafe, and word keeps coming in that tribes to the east and the south have stopped sending the زکات and have driven out the men who collected it. Into that, the new caliph does the thing that looks to almost everyone present like the wrong decision — he sends the army that is already mustered, the expedition under سیدنا اسامہ بن زید ؓ, north out of the city and away from the danger, because the Prophet ﷺ had ordered it before he passed; senior Companions ؓ ask him to hold it back and he does not [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1, the ابوبکر ؓ chapter — the dispatch of اسامہ ؓ's expedition and what ابوبکر ؓ said in reply, in the book's own wording]. The scene closes on the dust of that army going north while مدینہ stands with fewer men in it than it had that morning. The question is left hanging over the whole evening and is not answered yet: how does that city, twelve years later, come to be giving orders to قادسیہ and to فسطاط?

runsheet.block: آغاز — the Line and the Map go up
runsheet.content: THE LINE and THE MAP go up on the wall exactly as they do every week, and the speaker puts his hand on last week's marks: «پچھلے ہفتے ہم نے پوری لکیر ایک گھنٹے میں چلی تھی — آج ہم اس کے پہلے بارہ سال پر رکتے ہیں۔» Tonight's two pegs, ۱۱ھ and ۲۳ھ [verify], are drawn on the wall banner with a marker while every attendee marks the same two pegs in their own workbook in their own handwriting. The map goes up carrying only what session 1 left on it — the six anchor cities مکہ · مدینہ · دمشق · بغداد · قرطبہ · قسطنطنیہ and the two greyed blocks for ساسانی ایران and روم — and nothing else yet. Drop-ins are handed the single-sheet catch-up page at the door and are brought level by this physical act, not by a spoken recap.

runsheet.block: Opening scene — مدینہ under threat
runsheet.content: The اسامہ ؓ scene, delivered standing, away from the screen, with the map still dark and nothing written on the wall. No definitions, no era boundaries said aloud, no preview of what is coming — the audience is put inside one city on one set of nights and left there. It ends on the hanging question about قادسیہ and فسطاط, after which the speaker moves to the map and the story block begins.

runsheet.block: The story — from a threatened city to two broken empires
runsheet.content: Four movements, with the map moving throughout. (a) 0:08, about four minutes: سقیفہ and the بیعت, narrated as the Sunni source narrates it and then closed, followed by the decision on زکات — the hinge sentence of the evening, that the obligation would not be allowed to lapse because the man who had received it had passed. (b) 0:12, about six minutes: the ردہ, driven on screen by the seven-stage map artifact at tools/ridda-wars-map (1).html, advanced one stage at a time — the agents in place, the collapse, the muster at ذو القصہ and the division into eleven columns, خالد ؓ in نجد and یمامہ, then the east and the south — so the sequence is carried by the artifact and not by memory. (c) 0:18, ninety seconds and one round only: the sorting exercise at tools/ridda-classification.html in «Sort it yourself» mode, four columns on screen (a rival claim to prophethood · withheld زکات · political secession · never rebelled at all), the room calls out placements for three or four names, the board is revealed, and the speaker moves on. (d) 0:20, about eight minutes: the axis flips outward — خالد ؓ into عراق, the Syrian front and یرموک, then سیدنا عمر ؓ takes office and the map runs قادسیہ، مدائن، دمشق، بیت المقدس and مصر — closing on the دیوان and on the institution of the Hijri calendar, which is the very numbering used on the Line the audience is holding.

runsheet.block: تعارف — three people
runsheet.content: Three panels, two minutes twenty seconds each, in the fixed تراجم format used every week: نام و نسب with the لقب the tradition itself gave, سنین, one sentence on what they did, and one authentic incident from the source. Tonight: سیدنا ابوبکر الصدیق ؓ، سیدنا خالد بن الولید ؓ (سیف اللہ المسلول)، سیدنا ابو عبیدہ بن الجراح ؓ (امین الامۃ). The workbook prints the first three lines already; «ایک واقعہ» is left blank and the listener writes the incident by hand as it is told, which is the retention mechanism the whole course rests on. The speaker starts a timer on the first panel, because this is the block that overruns and the third person is the one that gets squeezed.

runsheet.block: کیسے پتا چلا؟ — how the Qur'ān was gathered after یمامہ
runsheet.content: Three panels on one slide — «کیا ہوا» (a large number of those who carried the Qur'ān in memory were killed at یمامہ), «کیا کیا گیا» (سیدنا عمر ؓ proposed that it be gathered in writing; سیدنا ابوبکر ؓ hesitated before doing what had not been done before; سیدنا زید بن ثابت ؓ was appointed and described the weight of the task in his own words), and «کیسے کیا گیا» (the procedure: memory alone was not accepted, written material was required alongside it; a named man answerable for the work; the gathered صحف then held in a known succession of hands). The one general statement made is the segment's point: this text was not preserved by luck, it was preserved by a procedure with names, a rule of evidence and a chain of custody — the same test session 1 taught the room to apply to any historical report. No hadith numbers and no page numbers are said aloud; the reference is printed on the slide from the source. What happened later in the time of سیدنا عثمان ؓ is named as next week's material and stopped there.

runsheet.block: آج کی بات — the supplied quotation, then everyone writes
runsheet.content: The slide is headed by the attribution, not by the speaker: this is فائدہ نمبر ۲ from the author's own numbered list of the benefits of history in the muqaddima of Tareekh-e-Ummat — a leader is superior to those he leads not in strength but in experience and judgment, and history hands a person centuries of both in an hour, so the study of history is a necessity for whoever leads a people. The author's own Urdu sentence goes on the slide beneath the heading, lifted from the page image rather than typed from memory [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1, المقدمہ, the numbered فوائد list — the wording of فائدہ ۲; confirm the sentence against the page image before it reaches the slide, because the OCR text layer garbles wording]. The speaker reads it once, says one line connecting it to what the room has just watched — that twelve years of decisions were taken by men who had been present at everything that came before — and then stops. The workbook line is «آج آپ کیا لے کر جا رہے ہیں؟ ______» and the room writes in silence; the conclusion belongs to the listener, and the speaker adds no moral of his own.

runsheet.block: اگلے ہفتے — close on a question
runsheet.content: The completed map is left up and the speaker names, in one sentence each, what is now true: the peninsula is under one authority, ساسانی ایران is finished, روم has been pushed back off شام and مصر, and there is now a salary register and a calendar. He then says what next week is: ۲۳–۴۰ھ, the caliphates of سیدنا عثمان ؓ and سیدنا علی ؓ, and — stated plainly to the room in advance — the evening in which the أصول for handling disagreement among the Companions ؓ are put on the table before anything else is said. He asks the take-home question, lets it sit without answering it, and stops; questions are taken here or after the session, never during the narrative.

people.name: سیدنا ابوبکر الصدیق ؓ
people.did: He took charge of the community when the Prophet ﷺ passed away, held the peninsula together through the ردہ, refused to let the obligation of زکات lapse, and ordered the first written gathering of the Qur'ān — inside a caliphate of a little over two years [verify].
people.incident_plan: One incident only: his exchange with سیدنا عمر ؓ over those who kept the prayer but withheld the زکات, and his refusal to separate the two — told as the source tells it, ending with عمر ؓ's own acknowledgement that the matter had been settled rightly. Delivered plainly, no raised voice, no invented dialogue; the wording comes off the page. [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1, the ابوبکر ؓ chapter — the زکات decision and the exchange with عمر ؓ, in the book's own Urdu, plus any Arabic the book carries, read off the page image]. Reserve incident if that one is not usable as printed: the dispatch of اسامہ ؓ's expedition [SOURCE: same chapter — the اسامہ ؓ dispatch].

people.name: سیدنا خالد بن الولید ؓ
people.did: He commanded the central column of the ردہ campaigns in نجد and یمامہ, opened the Iraq front against the Sasanians, crossed the desert to reinforce the armies in شام, and fought at یرموک.
people.incident_plan: One incident only: سیدنا عمر ؓ, on taking office, removed him from command of the army and placed سیدنا ابو عبیدہ ؓ over him — and he stayed in the ranks and went on fighting under his successor without withholding anything. Framed strictly as what happened, with no comment on the caliph's reason and no comparison drawn between the two men; it is told because it is the evening's clearest instance of an office outlasting the person holding it. [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1, the عمر ؓ chapter — the change of command in شام and خالد ؓ's response, in the book's own wording]. His ردہ command is narrated through بزاخہ and یمامہ; the مالک بن نویرہ affair is not narrated in this panel or anywhere else in the evening.

people.name: سیدنا ابو عبیدہ بن الجراح ؓ
people.did: He commanded the armies in شام under سیدنا عمر ؓ, received the surrender of its cities, and administered the province until he died in the طاعونِ عمواس.
people.incident_plan: One incident only: when the army in شام had to concentrate elsewhere and could no longer guarantee the protection of the people of حمص, the جزیہ that had been collected from them was returned, on the stated ground that it had been taken for a protection that could no longer be given. Told flatly, with the source's own words for the reason given at the time, and left without commentary — it lands the evening's civilizational point without the speaker having to assert one. [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1, the شام campaign — the returning of the جزیہ at حمص before یرموک, with the wording of the reason given]. The نام و نسب line notes that امین الامۃ is the title given him by the Prophet ﷺ [SOURCE: the book's own citation for the naming — no hadith number to be said aloud].

drafts.map: The base map never changes: same projection and the same six anchor cities every week — مکہ · مدینہ · دمشق · بغداد · قرطبہ · قسطنطنیہ — carrying forward the two greyed blocks placed in session 1, ساسانی ایران to the east and روم to the north-west. Tonight adds three movements, in this order. FIRST, INWARD: short arrows from نجد pointing at مدینہ, with the peninsula around it left blank, so the room sees both that the city was the target and how little of Arabia مدینہ actually held. SECOND, OUTWARD FROM ONE POINT: from the muster at ذو القصہ just outside مدینہ, arrows fan across the peninsula — to بزاخہ in نجد, یمامہ in the oasis belt, بحرین on the Gulf coast, دباء in عمان, صنعاء in یمن, and النجیر in حضرموت — and as each is reached that portion of the peninsula takes a single shade, so that by the end of the block the whole peninsula carries one colour for the first time on this map. THIRD, THE AXIS FLIPS, which is the beat the whole evening is built on: two arrows now leave Arabia and do not come back — north-east into عراق (الحیرہ، قادسیہ، مدائن) and north-west into شام (اجنادین، یرموک) — with a dashed line drawn across the desert from عراق to شام for خالد ؓ's march between the two fronts. دمشق، حمص and بیت المقدس are then ringed, and one further arrow runs south-west out of شام into مصر, ending at فسطاط. The two grey blocks are amended in front of the room at the close: the ساسانی block is struck through and gone, and the روم block is pulled back off شام and مصر toward انطاکیہ and قسطنطنیہ, where it will sit for the next several sessions. On the workbook's deliberately half-blank map each listener draws the outward fan and the two long arrows by hand; on THE LINE they mark ۱۱ھ and ۲۳ھ [verify] themselves.
drafts.howweknow_plan: Three minutes, one slide, three panels, and no page numbers or hadith numbers spoken aloud. Panel 1 «کیا ہوا»: at یمامہ a large number of those who carried the Qur'ān in memory were killed — the room has just watched یمامہ on the map ten minutes earlier, which is why this segment sits in this week rather than any other. Panel 2 «کیا کیا گیا»: سیدنا عمر ؓ came to سیدنا ابوبکر ؓ and proposed that it be gathered in writing; ابوبکر ؓ hesitated at doing what had not been done in the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime, then accepted; سیدنا زید بن ثابت ؓ was appointed to the work and described its weight in his own words [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1 — the جمعِ قرآن passage: the proposal, the hesitation, the appointment, and زید ؓ's own description, in the book's Urdu, with any Arabic read off the page image]. Panel 3 «کیسے کیا گیا» — the procedure, which is the whole point: memory alone was not treated as sufficient and written material was required alongside it; the work was given to one named man answerable for it; and the gathered صحف were then held in a known and stated succession of hands rather than left in circulation [SOURCE: same passage — the evidentiary rule and the custody of the صحف]. The segment ends on the one general sentence the speaker is permitted here: «یہ کتاب اتفاق سے محفوظ نہیں ہوئی — ایک طے شدہ طریقۂ کار سے محفوظ ہوئی» — a named committee, a rule of evidence, and a chain of custody, which is exactly the test session 1 told the room to apply to any historical report. The later stage under سیدنا عثمان ؓ is named as next week's and left there.
drafts.takehome_question: «جو ریاست بارہ سال میں دو سلطنتیں توڑ سکتی ہے، کیا وہ اپنے اندر کے امتحان میں بھی اتنی ہی مضبوط رہے گی؟» [A state that can break two empires in twelve years — will it stand as firm in the test that comes from inside it?]

sensitive.what_arises: The period narrated tonight is not where the مشاجرات fall — those belong to session 3, where the fiqh frame is installed before anything else is said. The exposure tonight comes from the floor rather than from the podium, and it is foreseeable: سقیفہ and the succession will prompt questions about whether it was contested; the word «ردہ» itself invites both a revisionist reading (that it was merely a tax revolt) and the opposite overstatement (that all of Arabia left Islam); the ردہ campaigns raise the مالک بن نویرہ affair and the disagreement between سیدنا عمر ؓ and سیدنا خالد ؓ over it; خالد ؓ's removal from command invites a question about which of the two men was right; and فدک and the events around سیدہ فاطمہ ؓ sit immediately adjacent to this material and may be raised by a drop-in. A secondary exposure is that the two ردہ teaching artifacts, built earlier, carry side panels written in a Western seminar register that treat «ردہ» as the victors' framing and cite orientalist historians by name.
sensitive.how_handled: The rule for the evening is the rule for the course: narrate what the source narrates, and stop. سقیفہ is told as the Sunni account has it, in about ninety seconds, and closed by moving to the map; no counter-position is raised in order to be knocked down. The ردہ is prevented from being flattened in either direction not by argument but by the sorting exercise, which puts four different kinds of resistance on the screen at once and includes a whole column for the tribes that never rebelled at all. On the artifacts: only the map area and the sorting board are projected, the English commentary panels are neither on screen nor read aloud, and the four column headings are relabelled in Urdu from the source's own characterisation before the night. Every foreseeable question above has a written answer in docs/catalogue/QA_BANK.md before the session, and anything not in the bank gets «مجھے معلوم نہیں — میں کتاب میں دیکھ کر اگلے ہفتے بتاؤں گا», which is also the habit the course is trying to teach.
will_not_be_said: No adjudication of any disagreement between the Companions ؓ — not between سیدنا عمر ؓ and سیدنا خالد ؓ, not between any others, whether in the narrative or from the floor.
The مالک بن نویرہ affair is not narrated; خالد ؓ's ردہ command is told through بزاخہ and یمامہ only.
Nothing on فدک or on the events surrounding سیدہ فاطمہ ؓ — not narrated, not alluded to, not used as a preview of a later session.
No claim that سقیفہ was contested by سیدنا علی ؓ, and no counter-claim rebutting that; the Sunni account is narrated and the matter is closed.
No ranking of Companions ؓ against one another beyond the settled Sunni order the source itself states, and no praise of one framed as a criticism of another.
No troop numbers and no casualty figures stated as fact — the source's own characterisation is used instead ('the heaviest fighting of the war'), which also removes a fabrication risk.
No modern political analogy: no comparison of any Companion ؓ, any campaign or either empire to a present-day state, army, leader or party.
No orientalist framing repeated from the teaching artifacts — their English commentary panels are neither projected nor read.
Nothing about the Prophet's ﷺ final illness beyond the fact of his passing, which is where the opening scene begins.
sensitive.floor_policy: Questions are taken in the final block or after the session, never mid-narrative — if one is called out during the story the speaker says «سوال نوٹ کر لیجیے، آخر میں لیتے ہیں» and continues. A question that lands on contested ground gets exactly three sentences, always in the same order and rehearsed word for word: an acknowledgement that the question is a serious one; one line of Sunni frame — that this is the history of the Muslims, and that the أدب owed to the Companions ؓ governs how it is discussed; and a named forward date — «اس کا اصولی جواب اگلے ہفتے کے موضوع کا حصہ ہے، وہیں اصول کے ساتھ عرض کروں گا» — session 3 being the evening where the fiqh of studying the مشاجرات is put on the table from the book itself. The speaker does not improvise a position, does not take a follow-up on the same question, and does not let two attendees debate each other across the room; if that begins, he closes it by returning to the map. Where a question is factual and simply unknown, the answer is that it will be looked up in the book and answered next week.

The repository currently holds only a ten-page slice of the opening of خلافتِ راشدہ, so this session cannot be written from what is on hand. Needed within it: سقیفہ and the بیعت as the book narrates them; the dispatch of اسامہ ؓ's expedition and what ابوبکر ؓ said when asked to hold it back; the زکات decision and the exchange with سیدنا عمر ؓ.

Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1 — how the book itself characterises the different kinds of resistance during the ردہ. Needed specifically to rewrite the four column headings of the sorting exercise in Urdu from the source's own categories rather than from the artifact's English ones.

Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1 — the جمعِ قرآن passage: عمر ؓ's proposal, ابوبکر ؓ's hesitation and acceptance, the appointment of زید بن ثابت ؓ and his own description of the task, the requirement that written material accompany memory, and the custody of the صحف afterwards. Needed in the book's Urdu wording; any Arabic must be read off the page image before it reaches a slide.

Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1 — the عمر ؓ chapter: the succession from ابوبکر ؓ; یرموک; قادسیہ and مدائن; the Syrian cities including دمشق، حمص and بیت المقدس; and مصر — enough of each for one map beat and one plain sentence, not a battle account.

Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1 — the administrative material of عمر ؓ's caliphate: the establishment of the دیوان, and the account of how the Hijri calendar was instituted and how its starting point was chosen. The calendar is the evening's closing beat and needs the book's own account of that decision.

Page anchors for the three تعارف incidents, one each: (a) the زکات exchange, with the اسامہ ؓ dispatch as the reserve; (b) خالد ؓ's removal from command in شام and his continuing to serve under سیدنا ابو عبیدہ ؓ; (c) the returning of the جزیہ to the people of حمص, including the wording of the reason given at the time.

The سنین line for each of the three تعارف panels, taken from the book's own dating rather than from a standard reference, and the book's own citation for the Prophet ﷺ naming سیدنا ابو عبیدہ ؓ امین الامۃ.

Verification of the wording of فائدہ ۲ in the muqaddima's numbered list of the benefits of history, read off the page image — this is the supplied «آج کی بات» and it goes on the screen as a quotation with its attribution, so the sentence must be exact.

Every ھ year that reaches a slide, the Line or the workbook must be checked against the book's own dating and entered in docs/catalogue/TIMELINE.md before use; where the book differs from a standard anchor, the book wins.
QA_BANK.md entries written before the night, one per foreseeable question: سقیفہ, فدک, the ردہ label, مالک بن نویرہ, and خالد ؓ's removal from command.
notes_for_speaker: Slow down on exactly two sentences and nowhere else. The first is the زکات decision; the second is the moment the arrows turn outward and leave Arabia. Say each slowly, then stop talking for two seconds and let the map hold the room. Everything else in the story block can be delivered at a normal pace.

The ردہ map artifact carries the sequence so that you do not have to. If you lose your place, press Next and read the stage title off the screen — the artifact was built to be the memory, and using it that way is not a failure.

If you run long, cut in this order and no other: first مصر, reduced to one sentence ('and from شام the same army turned south-west into مصر'); second the east-and-south stage of the ردہ, compressed to 'and the same pattern in the east and the south' with the map advanced silently; third the دیوان. Keep the calendar even if you cut everything else in that beat, because it lands on the Line the audience is holding.

Never cut تعارف or کیسے پتا چلا؟, and never cut them short by speeding up. The unchanging shape is what the room trusts and what lets a drop-in follow you, and it is your own safe structure — if you blank during the story, move to تعارف early and let the map catch up afterwards.

The safe ground when a question destabilises you is physical: walk to the Line, or to the map, and put your hand on it. 'What happened when' is on the wall behind you, and moving to it buys five seconds and looks deliberate.

Say no number you are not reading off the page. No troop strengths, no casualty figures. The book's own characterisation is enough, and a wrong number said with confidence is the one failure this course cannot absorb.

The sorting exercise is ninety seconds and one round. Take three or four names, show the board, move on — do not let it turn into a discussion, and keep a hand on the timer. If the room is slow to answer, place the first card yourself and ask for the second.

Both ردہ artifacts are in English and carry commentary panels written for a different audience. Project only the map and the board; do not scroll into the side notes and do not read them aloud. Relabel the four column headings in Urdu before the night from the source's own wording.

Rehearse تعارف standing, three times, with a timer. It is the block that overruns every week, and the person who gets squeezed is always the third — so start the clock on سیدنا ابوبکر ؓ and give yourself a mark at 2:20 and 4:40.

The deferral line for a hot question is memorised and said the same way every time, at the same speed. Do not extend it, do not soften it with an aside, and do not take a follow-up. Saying the identical sentence twice in one evening is fine; improvising a different one is not.

End on the question and stop. Do not add a summary and do not add a conclusion of your own — the evening's lesson already has a name and a source on the screen, and adding to it is the one thing that would put you, rather than the book, in the position of judging.

drafts.title: پہلا امتحان
drafts.summary: Session 3 covers ۲۳–۴۰ھ [verify], the caliphates of سیدنا عثمان ؓ and سیدنا علی ؓ. Roughly two-thirds of the evening is spent on what was built in these years — the unified مصحف copied and sent out to the garrison cities, the frontier moving further out, and the rise of کوفہ، بصرہ، فسطاط and دمشق as real centres of Muslim life — and only a named minimum on the مشاجرات, which are placed on the map and stated in single sentences without being narrated. The guardrail is installed in the first three minutes, before any event is told: tonight is تاریخِ مسلمین rather than the religion itself, and where the فقہاء have instructed us to stop, we stop. The evening's closing «آج کی بات» is not the speaker's conclusion but a supplied quotation — the فقہاء's own grading that studying the مشاجرات without need is مکروہ, together with ابن حجر الہیتمی رحمہ اللہ on why scholars narrate these events at all: to show the Companions' ؓ integrity, not to weigh them against one another.
drafts.opening_scene: A room in مدینہ. Sheets of the Qur'an are being copied by hand onto new leaves by a small committee working to one agreed text. When the copies are finished, riders are sent out of the city — one copy to each of the main garrison cities, and with each copy a man who could recite it aloud, because a written page in that century did not yet carry the vowels and a reader had to be sent with it. The speaker describes the riders leaving مدینہ in different directions on the same few days, and then stops and asks the room to hold one image: for the first time, the Muslims of کوفہ and the Muslims of فسطاط, a month's travel apart, are reading from one text. The question left hanging is deliberately plain — these same roads that carried the copies outward were the roads that carried men and letters back into مدینہ; and the speaker says only that we will follow both directions tonight. [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat vol. 1, the عثمان ؓ chapter — the committee, how many copies were written, which cities they were sent to, and whether a reciter accompanied each copy; the scene is told only to the extent the source carries it]

runsheet.block: آغاز — the Line and the Map
runsheet.content: The Line goes up and the speaker marks tonight's stretch on the banner in front of the room: last week closed at ۲۳ھ [verify] with the frontier held; tonight runs ۲۳ھ [verify] to ۴۰ھ [verify]. Everyone marks the same stretch in their own workbook. Then, before any event is narrated, he reads the evening's rule off a printed card in two sentences — that tonight is تاریخِ مسلمین and not the religion itself, and that where our فقہاء have instructed us to stop, we stop and do not go further. He closes the block by restating the standing format of the course: questions are not taken from the floor, slips go into the box at the door, and this is said in the same words every week so that it is plainly not a measure invented for tonight.

runsheet.block: Opening scene — the copies leave مدینہ
runsheet.content: The scene of the مصحف being copied and sent out to the garrison cities, told as described above, with no definition and no framing. The map is untouched during this block except that the four destination cities are named aloud as the riders are described. It ends on the observation that the roads ran both ways, and the speaker moves straight into the narrative without a summary sentence.

runsheet.block: The story — ۲۳ھ to ۴۰ھ, with the map moving
runsheet.content: Six movements, timed. (1) About six minutes on the شوریٰ after سیدنا عمر ؓ and the بیعت to سیدنا عثمان ؓ, then the years of building: the frontier moving further out east and west, the first ventures by sea, the mosque at مدینہ enlarged, the wealth arriving, and the مصحف unified [SOURCE: vol. 1, عثمان ؓ chapter — the شوریٰ procedure and the فتوحات of the period]. (2) About four minutes on what the امصار had become: کوفہ، بصرہ، فسطاط، دمشق, cities full of Muslims who had never seen مدینہ, a month of travel between complaint and answer, and reports moving faster than anyone could check them — the map fills in here. (3) About five minutes on the delegations arriving in مدینہ, the complaints being brought and answered, the siege of the house, and the martyrdom of سیدنا عثمان ؓ; this passage is read from a printed card in the source's own terms, kept to a few sentences, and followed by a deliberate silence [SOURCE: vol. 1 — the source's own account of the origin of the agitation, and its wording on the siege and the martyrdom; nothing is said beyond what it carries]. (4) About three minutes on سیدنا علی ؓ taking office in a city that had just seen its caliph killed, on the seat of the caliphate moving from مدینہ to کوفہ — the single most important map fact of the evening — and on the question of قصاص while the men responsible were embedded in an armed crowd; the source is followed and the matter is left where it leaves it. (5) جمل and صفین are named, placed on the map with a dot each, and given one factual sentence apiece; nothing is narrated, no letters, no speeches, no numbers, and the block moves on inside thirty seconds. (6) About two minutes to close on the خوارج and نہروان — the first group to declare other Muslims outside Islam and to act on it, and سیدنا علی ؓ standing against them — ending at ۴۰ھ [verify] in کوفہ.

runsheet.block: تعارف — three people
runsheet.content: The segment opens with one sentence that is the whole point of it: تینوں صحابی ہیں — all three men are Companions ؓ, and that is why all three are on the same page of the workbook tonight. Each of the three gets the same classical تراجم notice, roughly two minutes: نام و نسب with only the لقب the tradition itself gave, سنین read from the source, what he did in one sentence, and one authentic incident. Every incident is deliberately taken from before the events of this evening, so that the room meets each man as a Companion ؓ first and not through the disagreement. Listeners write the incident into the blank «ایک واقعہ» line themselves.

runsheet.block: کیسے پتا چلا؟ — the document that died on a date
runsheet.content: Three beats, no slide of the document. First: a parchment is produced at court, old-looking, carrying an exemption and a list of Companions ؓ as witnesses, and the room accepts it. Second: a scholar asks only for the date it claims, then reads the witness list against that date. Third: two of the names cannot stand, because one of the men had not yet accepted Islam at that date and another had already died before it, and the forgery is finished without anyone examining the ink. The speaker then makes the transfer in one sentence: this is the tool that governs tonight, which is why nothing was said about the مشاجرات whose date and chain we have not checked. [SOURCE: the name of the scholar, the document's claim, the two witnesses named and the two dating facts, in the source's own wording]

runsheet.block: آج کی بات — the supplied quotation, then everyone writes
runsheet.content: The speaker states plainly that tonight's lesson is not his, and reads it from the card: the فقہاء's own grading of this study — that going into the مشاجرات without need is مکروہ — and then ابن حجر الہیتمی رحمہ اللہ on why the scholars nevertheless narrate these events, namely to establish the Companions' ؓ integrity and not to weigh them against one another. Arabic is read first where the source carries it, with the Urdu rendering beneath [SOURCE: the Arabic wording of both passages and the Urdu rendering, read off the page image, not from an OCR text layer]. He adds nothing to it — no gloss, no second moral. The room then has about ninety seconds of silence to write its own one-line takeaway in the workbook.

runsheet.block: اگلے ہفتے — closing on a question
runsheet.content: The speaker marks the end of tonight's stretch on the banner Line, and points at کوفہ and دمشق on the map as the two places the next evening begins from. He then closes on the question, said once, slowly, and repeated once: that this disagreement was ended in the end not by a sword but by one man's decision. He does not answer it, does not hint at the answer, and closes the evening there.

people.name: سیدنا عثمان بن عفان ؓ

Deliberately not an incident from the siege. [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat vol. 1, عثمان ؓ chapter — the incident in the source's own wording, and any لقب the source itself records beyond ذو النورین]

The editor selects whichever single incident the source narrates at length rather than the plan naming one. [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat vol. 1, علی ؓ chapter — the incident in the source's own wording, and whether the source records any لقب or کنیت the tradition gave him; if it records none, the line stays blank and he is described factually]

[SOURCE: سنین, and the source's own description of his role as a scribe and the terms of his appointment]

The point being made is that he is a Companion ؓ appointed and retained by سیدنا عمر ؓ, and that fact does most of the work of the panel; nothing from صفین is used here. [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat vol. 1 — a single incident from the governorship, in the source's own wording; and confirmation of whether the source gives him any لقب, since none is assumed]

drafts.map: The base map is the standing one, same projection every week, with the six anchor cities already printed: مکہ · مدینہ · دمشق · بغداد · قرطبہ · قسطنطنیہ — بغداد stays greyed out, and the speaker says once that it does not exist yet, which is itself a useful correction. Tonight adds three new cities in the second colour: کوفہ and بصرہ on the عراق side, فسطاط in مصر. The movement is drawn in three stages, in this order. First, outward: arrows from مدینہ to کوفہ، بصرہ، فسطاط and دمشق, drawn while the opening scene is told, one arrow per copy of the مصحف. Second, inward: the same four arrows are then reversed with a marker while the delegations and complaints are described, so the room sees that the traffic ran both ways on the same roads. Third, and this is the map lesson of the evening, the centre itself moves — a single heavy line from مدینہ to کوفہ marks the seat of the caliphate leaving مدینہ for the first time, and the speaker says exactly that sentence and pauses on it. Finally the arc کوفہ–بصرہ–دمشق–فسطاط is lightly shaded as "the four new centres", the place where most Muslims now actually lived. Three small dots with names only, no battle marks and no drawings of any kind: جمل near بصرہ, صفین on the upper فرات between دمشق and کوفہ, نہروان near کوفہ. In the workbook the same three cities and the one heavy مدینہ→کوفہ line are drawn by hand by each listener.
drafts.howweknow_plan: Three minutes, told standing away from the map, with no slide and no image of the document — the point is that the room follows a piece of reasoning, not that it looks at a picture. Beat one, about forty seconds: an old-looking parchment is produced at a ruler's court, it carries an exemption and a list of Companions ؓ set down as witnesses, and everyone in the room accepts it as genuine. Beat two, about forty seconds: a scholar asks for one thing only — the year the document claims for itself — and then reads the list of witnesses against that year. Beat three, about sixty seconds: two of the names cannot stand, because one of the men had not yet accepted Islam at that date and another had already died before it, and the forgery is finished without anyone testing the parchment or the ink. The closing twenty seconds make the transfer to tonight explicitly: dates are how a false report is caught, and this is exactly why the evening named جمل and صفین and refused to narrate reports about them whose date and chain we have not checked. This segment is the strongest safety argument in the evening and management should read it as such — the method is what disciplines the narrative, not squeamishness. [SOURCE: the name of the scholar, the document's claim, the two witnesses named, and the two dating facts that void it, all in the source's own wording; the segment is not delivered until these are in hand]
drafts.takehome_question: «یہ اختلاف بالآخر تلوار سے نہیں، ایک آدمی کے فیصلے سے ختم ہوا — وہ فیصلہ کیا تھا، اور اُس نے اِس کی کیا قیمت دی؟» [This disagreement was ended in the end not by a sword but by one man's decision — what was that decision, and what did it cost him?]

sensitive.what_arises: This evening contains the مشاجرات — the disagreements among the Companions ؓ. Specifically: the complaints brought against سیدنا عثمان ؓ in his lifetime; the siege of his house and his martyrdom; the question of قصاص for it; the disagreement between سیدنا علی ؓ and سیدنا معاویہ ؓ; جمل and صفین; and the appearance of the خوارج, who declared other Muslims outside Islam and killed سیدنا علی ؓ. A Pakistani audience will also bring in things the evening does not contain: Karbala, Sunni–Shia difference as such, and modern political analogies. The venue should assume at least one listener will attempt a question in one of these directions.
sensitive.how_handled: Four mechanisms, all structural rather than improvised. (1) The guardrail is installed in the first three minutes, before any event is told, and it is stated as the فقہاء's ruling rather than as house policy or personal caution. (2) Time allocation does the work: roughly two-thirds of the narrative is on what was built in these years — the مصحف, the فتوحات, the four cities — and the disagreements are named, placed on the map, and given one sentence each. This is not evasion; it is the same proportion the فقہاء's own grading implies, and the evening says so out loud. (3) The three sensitive passages — the siege and martyrdom, the sentence on جمل and صفین, and the deferral line for the floor — are printed on a card and read verbatim. Under stage fright a speaker composes badly; reading removes that risk entirely. (4) The «کیسے پتا چلا؟» segment justifies the restraint on method rather than on nerves: an unchecked report is not repeated, which is why so little is said. Before delivery, the wording of the sensitive passages and the two card lines is to be checked with a qualified عالم, and the printed card is to carry only source-derived wording.
will_not_be_said: That any Companion ؓ was wrong, sinful, rebellious or blameworthy — no verdict of any kind is passed on any of them
Any ranking or comparison between سیدنا علی ؓ and سیدنا معاویہ ؓ, or between any two Companions ؓ
Any itemising of the specific accusations made against سیدنا عثمان ؓ in his lifetime; the evening says only that complaints were brought and that he answered them
Any speculation about the motive or inner state of any Companion ؓ
Any narration of the fighting at جمل or صفین — no manoeuvres, no letters, no speeches, no casualty figures, no naming of who killed whom
Any account of the arbitration, its terms, or who is said to have outmanoeuvred whom
Any mention of what later parties said about Companions ؓ from pulpits, in any direction
Any characterisation of Shia belief, of any other maslak, or of any sect or group living today; no 'they say / we say' at any point
Karbala, which belongs to a later evening and will not be touched tonight even if raised
Any takfir language whatsoever, other than the plain historical statement that the خوارج did this and that سیدنا علی ؓ stood against them
Any comparison, however light, between these events and current politics in Pakistan or anywhere else
Any report the source does not carry, even if a listener quotes it from the floor; and no hadith quoted from memory
The words «میری رائے» or 'in my opinion' at any point in the evening
sensitive.floor_policy: Questions are not taken from the floor during the 45 minutes. This is the standing format of all ten sessions, announced in the same words every week, so that its use tonight cannot read as a special lockdown. Written questions go on a slip into a box at the door; they are answered either in the following week's آغاز, if they fit the course, or individually afterwards from the pre-written answer bank. If a hot question is nevertheless asked aloud, the speaker uses one rehearsed sentence read from the card and then moves immediately to the next block: «یہ وہ مقام ہے جہاں ہمارے فقہاء نے رکنے کا حکم دیا ہے؛ جو کتاب میں ہے وہ میں نے پڑھ دیا، اُس سے آگے میری رائے کی کوئی حیثیت نہیں۔» [This is the point at which our فقہاء instructed us to stop; what the book carries I have read out to you, and beyond that my opinion has no standing.] If the question demands adjudication between Companions ؓ, the answer is the ابن حجر الہیتمی رحمہ اللہ passage already supplied for «آج کی بات», read out and nothing added. Questions about any living sect, party or current political matter are not answered at all — not in the room, and not afterwards; the questioner is thanked and referred to their own عالم. The speaker will not stay behind to debate, and this is stated at the close.

The scene will be told only to the extent this passage supports it

The مشاجرات guardrail passage — the فقہاء's grading that this study without need is مکروہ, and the ابن حجر الہیتمی رحمہ اللہ passage on why the scholars narrate these events at all. Needed in Arabic exactly as the source carries it, with the Urdu rendering beneath, read off the page image and not from an OCR text layer

The forged-document passage — the scholar's name, what the document claimed, the witnesses named on it, and the two dating facts that destroyed it, in the source's own wording. The «کیسے پتا چلا؟» segment is not delivered until this is in hand

سنین for all three تعارف people — birth and death years exactly as the source gives them, and any لقب the source itself records. No لقب is assumed for سیدنا علی ؓ or سیدنا معاویہ ؓ and none will be supplied from anywhere else

One authentic incident for each of the three, chosen by the editor from the source, each from before the events of this evening — an incident of expenditure from before the caliphate for سیدنا عثمان ؓ; an incident from the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime for سیدنا علی ؓ; an incident from the governorship of شام under سیدنا عمر ؓ for سیدنا معاویہ ؓ
A list of the cities and provinces the source names for this period, so the map is drawn from the source rather than from general memory
notes_for_speaker: Your safe ground is the first twelve minutes — the copies leaving مدینہ, the frontier, the four cities. None of that material can get you into trouble. If your hands are shaking at 0:08, stay in it longer and take the time back later from the فتوحات.
Read the three sensitive passages off the card. Do not paraphrase them, do not improve them while standing there. The card exists precisely so that under pressure you are reading and not composing.

Slow down markedly for the few sentences on the siege and the martyrdom, then stop and let two seconds of silence sit. The silence is correct. Do not fill it, and do not add a sentence of your own after it.

Say جمل and صفین, put the dot on the map, give the one sentence each, and be moving on inside thirty seconds. The room will go quiet at those two names; that quiet is appropriate and is not a request for more.
Say ؓ aloud after every Companion's name every single time, including the third time in one sentence. If it starts to feel laborious, that is the point — the room is hearing it.
If you blank in the narrative, go straight to تعارف. The shape never changes, the audience does not know where you were, and you can pick up the thread afterwards.

If you are running long, cut from the فتوحات — the sea ventures and the eastern frontier can go. Never cut the guardrail at the top, never cut «آج کی بات», and never shorten the silence after the martyrdom.
Do not answer anything from the floor. One card line, verbatim, then the next block. You are not being unkind; you announced the format at the top and every week before this.
If an analogy to something current occurs to you while you are speaking, discard it. Not one comparison to anything modern, tonight of all nights.

Rehearse the sensitive third aloud three times before the evening — the siege passage, the جمل and صفین sentences, and the deferral line. Rehearse them standing, at delivery volume. Confidence here comes from having said the words before, not from having read them.

drafts.title: خلافت سے بادشاہت تک
drafts.gloss: How a consultative office became a hereditary throne
drafts.summary: Session 4 covers ۴۰–۱۳۲ھ [verify] — the Umayyad century — and its subject is a single institutional question: how an office filled by consultation and بیعت became a throne passed inside one family, and what that cost. The evening runs on the same fixed 45-minute shape as every other week, opens on the handover of ۴۱ھ [verify] that ended the fighting and gave that year its name in the tradition (عام الجماعۃ), and closes on a question rather than a verdict. It contains the single most striking map movement of the whole course — three arrows drawn from دمشق in one continuous minute, reaching سندھ and الأندلس in the same decade [verify: ۹۲–۹۳ھ] — and it also contains the most sensitive material of the course: کربلا, ۶۱ھ [verify]. Karbala is handled under the guardrail installed in session 3: it is narrated from the named source, word for word from written text, at a fixed short length, with no adjudication of any kind, and the speaker's limits are announced to the room in the first two minutes and again before questions are taken.
drafts.opening_scene: The evening opens in Iraq in the summer of ۴۱ھ [verify]. Two Muslim armies are drawn up within reach of one another — many of the same men who had faced each other a few years earlier, now waiting to do it again — and the speaker describes only what the source describes: riders carrying letters between سیدنا حسن بن علی ؓ and سیدنا معاویہ ؓ, terms written and accepted, and then the two forces standing down without fighting. He then says the one sentence the whole evening hangs from: the tradition gave that year a name of its own, عام الجماعۃ — the year of the community. The question is put once, and then deliberately left unanswered for the next twenty minutes: the fighting stopped that day, so what exactly changed in the office of خلافت — and why does a Muslim living in ۱۳۲ھ [verify] live under something the book calls بادشاہت? Nothing is defined, nothing is summarised, and the speaker moves straight to the map. [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat, the بنو امیہ volume — where the two forces halted, the sequence of letters between سیدنا حسن ؓ and سیدنا معاویہ ؓ, and the wording of the terms]

runsheet.block: آغاز — the Line and the Map go up
runsheet.content: The wall banner already runs to ۴۰ھ [verify]; the speaker extends it with a marker while talking, and every attendee marks the same peg on THE LINE in their own workbook. In one sentence he says where last week ended (the centre of gravity already out of مدینہ) and where tonight ends (۱۳۲ھ [verify], دمشق fallen). He then does two things of about twenty seconds each that are never skipped: he restates the session-3 guardrail in one sentence — تاریخِ اسلام = تاریخِ مسلمین, and the فقہاء' ruling that these events are narrated for أدب and not to weigh صحابہ ؓ against one another — and he tells the room plainly that tonight touches کربلا, that it will be narrated from the book and stop there, and that all questions are taken at the very end. The base map goes up carrying nothing but the six anchor cities: مکہ · مدینہ · دمشق · بغداد · قرطبہ · قسطنطنیہ.

runsheet.block: Opening — the handover of ۴۱ھ [verify]
runsheet.content: The scene described above: two armies in Iraq, letters between سیدنا حسن بن علی ؓ and سیدنا معاویہ ؓ, terms accepted, no battle, and the year named عام الجماعۃ in the tradition. Told plainly and slowly, with no reconstructed dialogue and no detail the source does not carry. It ends on the open question — the fighting stopped, so what changed in the office itself? — which the speaker states once and does not answer.

runsheet.block: The story — ۴۱ھ to ۱۳۲ھ [verify], with the map moving
runsheet.content: Beat one (0:08–0:12): the capital moves — the speaker draws the arrow مدینہ → دمشق and shifts the دارالحکومت label onto دمشق, then states what the source states about the office itself: that succession came to be nominated within one family, and that the book records objections raised at the time by named Companions ؓ — narrated, and stopped there, with no weighing of persons. Beat two (0:12–0:14): the کربلا block, ۶۱ھ [verify], read word for word from prepared text — سیدنا حسین ؓ leaves مدینہ for مکہ and then sets out toward کوفہ; the party is intercepted at کربلا; on ۱۰ محرم [verify] he, members of his household and his companions are killed; the grief of the ummah at this has never been in dispute — then a pause, a quiet mark on the map north of کوفہ, and no analysis of any kind [SOURCE: بنو امیہ volume — the کربلا narration in the book's own words and at the book's own length]. Beat three (0:14–0:19): the state that was built anyway — the دیوان, the moving of the administration and the coinage into Arabic under عبد الملک [verify], the postal arrangements, the دمشق mosque — with the point said out loud, that a machine of government can keep growing while the office at the head of it is changing shape. Beat four (0:19–0:26) is the map movement of the whole course, three arrows drawn from دمشق in one continuous minute, described in the map section below; beat five (0:26–0:28) is ۹۹ھ [verify] and عمر بن عبد العزیز رحمہ اللہ, then ۱۳۲ھ [verify], when a movement coming west out of خراسان reverses the direction of every arrow on the board and دمشق falls.

runsheet.block: تعارف — exactly three people
runsheet.content: Three panels of about two minutes twenty each, in the fixed تراجم format: نام و نسب, سنین with the point marked on THE LINE, what the person did in one sentence, and then «ایک واقعہ» — one authentic incident from the source, which the listener writes by hand into the blank left for it in the workbook. سیدنا حسن بن علی ؓ, then عمر بن عبد العزیز رحمہ اللہ, then محمد بن قاسم. The order is deliberate: محمد بن قاسم comes last because his panel puts the audience's own geography on the map for the first time and hands the thread to session 8.

runsheet.block: کیسے پتا چلا؟ — why narrators are graded
runsheet.content: فنِ اسماء الرجال: the two-to-three-century project of recording the life of every narrator so that a name inside a chain can actually be checked, and the book's own rule that in historical reporting the chain must be investigated in three specific cases — reports touching the Prophet ﷺ and the conduct and qualities of the صحابہ ؓ; reports from which a criticism of the سلف could be drawn; and reports bearing on عقیدہ or on حلال و حرام. The worked case is محمد بن عمر الواقدی — a famous historian, a great memoriser, a man who reached the قاضی-ship of بغداد, whose material is still valued in سیر و مغازی, and who is nevertheless graded ضعیف and set aside by the محدثین exactly where the rule requires it. Delivery detail in the segment plan below.

runsheet.block: آج کی بات — the supplied quotation, then each listener writes
runsheet.content: The slide carries the attribution first, then the Arabic in Naskh — «مَا أَشْبَهَ اللَّيْلَةَ بِالْبَارِحَةِ» — with the Urdu rendering beneath it, and the source's own framing that history yields بصیرت and دوراندیشی و حزم: foresight, and vigilance. The speaker reads the quotation, gives the attribution aloud, and adds no moral of his own — the words are the source's and the reference is on the screen. Then ninety seconds of silence while every person writes their own answer to the printed workbook line «آج آپ کیا لے کر جا رہے ہیں؟ ______». [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1, المقدمہ — the فوائد of history: بصیرت and دوراندیشی و حزم, with the Arabic saying as the book prints it; wording to be read off the page image before it goes on a slide]

runsheet.block: اگلے ہفتے — close on a question
runsheet.content: The last mark of the night is a thin line from دمشق along North Africa to قرطبہ — one survivor of the fallen house — and it is left on the map as next week's opening. The speaker names next week («دو دارالحکومت» — بغداد and قرطبہ) and then puts the take-home question to the room without answering it. He repeats that questions are taken now, after the close and off the clock, and that the session itself ends here.

people.name: سیدنا حسن بن علی ؓ
people.did: In ۴۱ھ [verify] he handed over authority to سیدنا معاویہ ؓ on agreed terms and so ended the fighting between two Muslim armies; the tradition gave that year the name عام الجماعۃ.
people.incident_plan: One incident only: the handover itself as the book narrates it — the terms as they were written, and the reply he gave to those of his own side who objected to the settlement. Told plainly, with no reconstructed dialogue and nothing added for effect. [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat, بنو امیہ volume — the صلح account: the place, the terms, and his reply to the objectors] [SOURCE: his سنین in ھ and عیسوی, for the mark on THE LINE] Note for the editor: the لقب field is deliberately left empty. عام الجماعۃ is the name the tradition gave to the YEAR, not a title of the man, and it will not be printed as his لقب. [SOURCE: whether Tareekh-e-Ummat itself gives him a لقب — only a title the book carries goes on the panel]

people.name: عمر بن عبد العزیز رحمہ اللہ
people.did: In a caliphate of roughly two and a half years [verify: ۹۹–۱۰۱ھ] he returned wealth and estates held by his own family, restricted the بیت المال to lawful claims, and opened the hearing of grievances against his own governors.
people.incident_plan: One incident: his first act on taking office as the book narrates it — what was returned, and what he said to his household when they objected to it.
