drafts.map: The base map is the same one used every week — same projection, same six anchor cities: مکہ · مدینہ · دمشق · بغداد · قرطبہ · قسطنطنیہ. Tonight adds five marks, drawn live in this order. (1) At 0:08, a short arrow مدینہ → دمشق, and the label «دارالحکومت» is physically moved onto دمشق: the centre of gravity leaves the Hijaz and does not come back. (2) At 0:13, a dot at کوفہ and a small quiet mark at کربلا, north of کوفہ near the فرات — placed without emphasis, no flag, no colour, no pointing. (3) At 0:19–0:20, the map movement of the whole course: three arrows drawn from دمشق one after another inside a single continuous minute — EAST, دمشق → عراق → مکران → دیبل at the mouth of the Indus → up the river to ملتان, labelled سندھ ۹۲–۹۳ھ [verify]; NORTH-EAST, دمشق → خراسان → بخارا → سمرقند, labelled ماوراء النہر; WEST, دمشق → مصر → القیروان → across at جبل طارق → طلیطلہ and قرطبہ, labelled الأندلس ۹۲–۹۳ھ [verify]. The east and west labels carry the same years, and that repetition is the point. The speaker then stops talking, steps back, and puts one finger on ملتان and the other on قرطبہ: one authority, and the distance between his two hands is the fact the room takes home. For this audience ملتان is not a foreign place-name — it is on their own map, and the speaker says so in one sentence: the arrow that reaches سندھ is the arrow that eventually reaches this room, and session 8 picks it up there. (4) At 0:27, an arrow starting in خراسان and running WEST to دمشق, ۱۳۲ھ [verify] — the direction of movement on the board reverses for the first time in the course. (5) At 0:42, a thin line from دمشق along North Africa to قرطبہ, left standing as next week's opening. In the workbook the session-4 map page prints only the base and the six cities; the attendee draws the three arrows and writes ملتان and قرطبہ in their own handwriting. On THE LINE and on the wall banner, the pegs marked tonight are ۴۱ھ, ۶۱ھ, ۹۲–۹۳ھ, ۹۹ھ and ۱۳۲ھ [all verify].
drafts.howweknow_plan: Three minutes, delivered as one continuous piece with a single slide. It opens with a question to the room, asked and answered in fifteen seconds: «اگر آج کوئی آپ کو کوئی خبر بھیجے تو سب سے پہلے آپ کیا پوچھیں گے؟ — کس نے کہا؟» Then the fact: the ummah asked exactly that question about every man who transmitted a report, and wrote the answers down for two to three centuries, until an entire discipline existed — فنِ اسماء الرجال — whose only purpose is that a name inside a chain can be looked up. The slide carries the Arabic term in Naskh with the Urdu beneath, and the names of the great compilations as the book lists them [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1, المقدمہ — the فن اسماء الرجال section and the works it names]. Second, the book's own rule, stated in the book's own terms: historical reporting is not held to the same chain-scrutiny as hadith across the board, but the chain MUST be investigated in three cases — reports touching the Prophet ﷺ and the conduct and qualities of the صحابہ ؓ; reports from which a criticism of the سلف could be drawn; and reports bearing on عقیدہ or on حلال و حرام [SOURCE: المقدمہ — روایتِ تاریخ اور روایتِ حدیث میں فرق, the three cases where investigating the سند is obligatory]. Third, the worked case, which is the whole point of the segment: محمد بن عمر الواقدی was famous, was a great memoriser, travelled to the sites of the events he recorded, sat in the ʿAbbāsid court and became قاضی of بغداد; his material is still drawn on for the detail of سیر و مغازی — and he is nevertheless graded ضعیف, and the محدثین were cautious about taking from him, precisely because the rule was applied to him and not waived for his fame [SOURCE: المقدمہ — the notice on واقدی, and the statement that Muslim researchers do not accept even a well-known work into the list of معتبر books when the rules exclude it]. The landing line is a rule, not a moral: «مشہور ہونا سند نہیں ہے۔ سوال ہمیشہ وہی رہتا ہے — کس نے کہا؟» It is delivered as a general principle about method and is never applied on the platform to any particular report from tonight's narrative — see the sensitive section.
drafts.takehome_question: «خلافت سے بادشاہت تک کا سفر آج ہم نے دیکھا۔ سوال یہ ہے: مشورے سے خلیفہ کے انتخاب کا وہ اصول، کیا بعد کی صدیوں میں کبھی واپس آیا؟» [We have watched tonight the road from خلافت to بادشاہت. The question is: did the principle of choosing a ruler by consultation ever return in the centuries that followed?]

sensitive.what_arises: Three things, of which one is the most sensitive material in the entire course. First, کربلا, ۶۱ھ [verify] — the killing of سیدنا حسین ؓ, members of his household and his companions. Second, the nomination of a successor inside one family, and the objections the source records as having been made at the time by named Companions ؓ. Third, the standing question a room like this one always contains — whether the Umayyad rulers were legitimate, and how a Sunni gathering should speak about یزید بن معاویہ. The room is in DHA, with a regular core plus weekly drop-ins who did not hear the session-3 guardrail, and it may well contain both Sunni attendees with strong feeling on this and Shia attendees or guests. The evening is also delivered close to no particular calendar date, but the material is محرم material and will be heard as such.
sensitive.how_handled: The guardrail installed in session 3 governs the whole evening and is re-installed at 0:01 for the drop-ins, in one sentence, before anyone is inside the narrative: تاریخِ اسلام = تاریخِ مسلمین, and the فقہاء' ruling that studying the مشاجرات without need is مکروہ, while narrating them for أدب and to answer misrepresentation is permitted — the same paragraph, from the same named source, that session 3 was built on [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1, المقدمہ — the fiqh grading of historical study, and ابن حجر الہیتمیؒ on why these events are narrated at all]. The same sentence is printed at the top of the session-4 workbook page so that a person who joined tonight holds it in their hand. کربلا itself is a bounded block of about two minutes inside the twenty-minute story, written out in full in advance, approved before the night, and READ WORD FOR WORD from the page — the only part of the evening the speaker does not deliver from notes. What is said is the sequence and nothing else: سیدنا حسین ؓ left مدینہ for مکہ, then set out toward کوفہ; the party was intercepted at کربلا; on ۱۰ محرم ۶۱ھ [verify] he, members of his household and his companions were killed; the grief of the ummah at this has never been in dispute among Muslims. Then a pause, a quiet mark on the map, and the narrative moves on. The pace slows and the voice drops for that block; there is no rhetorical build into it and none out of it, and the honorific ؓ is on every single mention of every Companion, on every side of every event, throughout the evening. The «کیسے پتا چلا؟» segment that follows supplies the discipline — why narrators are graded — but is delivered purely as a general rule and is never turned on the platform into a verdict about any particular کربلا report. The evening's «آج کی بات» is the supplied quotation and nothing is added to it; no contemporary parallel of any kind is drawn.
will_not_be_said: No ruling, no verdict, no curse and no praise concerning یزید بن معاویہ — نہ لعنت، نہ تعریف، نہ فیصلہ. If pressed, the answer is that the book narrates the events and stops, and so does this gathering.
No adjudication between Companions ؓ, and no comparison of any two of them against each other, in the narrative or in answer to any question.
No claim about who bore responsibility for کربلا, who wrote or broke which undertaking, or who could have prevented it.

No reconstructed dialogue, no added detail, and no account of anyone's final hours beyond the bare sequence the source narrates — nothing said about members of the household beyond what the book carries.
No casualty numbers of any kind.
No comment, in either direction, on the محرم observances of any community — مجالس, ماتم, تعزیہ or anything else. The subject is not raised, and if raised from the floor it is not entered.
No comparison of Sunni and Shia accounts, and no naming of another community's sources in order to refute them.
No listing from the platform of the titles of واقدی's works on the internal conflicts, even though the source names them, so that the method segment cannot be heard as a ruling on the کربلا reports.
No present-day analogy — no Pakistani politics, no 'and today we see the same', no application of کربلا to any current dispute.
No claim, in either direction, about the legitimacy of Umayyad rule as such. The evening describes what changed in the office; it does not pronounce on the men who held it.
sensitive.floor_policy: Questions are taken only after the close, off the 45-minute clock, and this is announced twice — at 0:01 and again at 0:42 — specifically so that nobody interrupts during the کربلا block, which is the single most likely thing to go wrong. Three prepared tiers. (a) A factual question the book answers: answered briefly from the book, and if the answer is not in hand, «مجھے نہیں معلوم، میں کتاب سے دیکھ کر اگلے ہفتے بتاؤں گا» — written down in front of the questioner. (b) A question asking the speaker to judge a Companion ؓ, to rule on یزید, or to compare sects: one prepared sentence, said warmly and identically every time — «میں اس مجلس میں کسی صحابی ؓ یا کسی فریق پر فیصلہ نہیں دوں گا؛ ہمارا طریقہ یہ ہے کہ کتاب جو بیان کرتی ہے وہی بیان کریں اور وہیں رک جائیں» — followed by the plain statement that he is narrating a named book, not issuing a فتویٰ, and that a question of عقیدہ belongs with a qualified عالم. The question is written on the card either way. (c) A question that is really a speech: thanked, noted, and the floor moves on; the speaker does not debate and does not answer point by point. If the room becomes heated the Q&A is ended and the evening closed — that decision is pre-made, not left to the night. All of this is drafted into docs/catalogue/QA_BANK.md before the session and printed on the lectern cue card.

Every date in this plan carries [verify] and must be checked against the source before it is spoken or printed; where the book differs from the standard anchor, the book wins.
QA_BANK entries specific to this evening, written out and printed on the cue card before the night — not improvised.
notes_for_speaker: Your safe ground tonight is the map. If you lose the thread at any point, put your hand on دمشق and start describing the arrows — the room will follow you there and you will find your place again inside ten seconds.

The کربلا block is the one part of the whole course you read word for word off the page. Do not improvise there — not one sentence, not one added detail, not even a pause you had not planned. Read it, stop, mark the map, move on.
Slow down and drop your voice for that block. Do not raise it. The material carries itself; anything you add on top of it will be heard as taking a side.

Say the guardrail sentence at 0:01, before anyone is emotionally inside the story. It protects the room, and it protects you — you have told everyone in advance what you will not do, so declining later is not a retreat, it is the plan.
Announce at the start that questions come at the end. This is the single highest-value thirty seconds of the evening: it is what stops someone standing up in the middle of the کربلا block.

If you are running long, cut in this order: first the سمرقند arrow (the point survives on two arrows), then the administrative beat down to one sentence, then the second half of the عمر بن عبد العزیز رحمہ اللہ material. Never cut تعارف, never cut the guardrail, and never shorten or lengthen the کربلا block — it is fixed.
If you are running short, the عمر بن عبد العزیز رحمہ اللہ beat has the most spare material behind it in the briefing.

Keep ؓ on every single mention of every Companion, on every side of every event, all evening. That honorific tells the room your posture more clearly than any sentence you could construct, and dropping it once will be noticed.
«بادشاہت» is in the session title given by the course design — use it as the title and let it sit there. Do not build extra rhetoric on it while narrating; the title has already made the point.
Say each date once and move on. Every date is on the banner behind you and in the workbook in front of them, so you are not the one holding them.

When you do not know, say «مجھے نہیں معلوم، میں کتاب سے دیکھ کر اگلے ہفتے بتاؤں گا» and write the question down where they can see you writing it. In this room that reads as credibility, not as weakness — and it is also the honest position of someone narrating a book.

Rehearse the three tiers of the Q&A policy out loud before the night until the tier-(b) sentence comes out the same way every time. You want it to be a reflex, so that a hard question does not require a decision from you while you are standing there.

drafts.title: دو دارالحکومت
drafts.gloss: Baghdad and Córdoba — the same centuries, two capitals, two endings
drafts.summary: Session 5 covers seven and a half centuries and two continents by refusing to cover them: the evening holds on to two city names only, بغداد and قرطبہ, and tells them as a pair — two capitals of one ummah at their height in the same generations, and two very different endings. The narrative peak is the محنہ: a ruler makes a theological position a condition of office, most men give the answer demanded, and امام احمد بن حنبل رحمہ اللہ does not — narrated exactly as the source narrates it and no further, because the evening's supplied lesson (امام علی بن المدینیؒ on knowing men, علامہ سخاویؒ on wisdom that is never written down) is about scholars and books rather than about rulers. Everything else in the period is cut by prior decision, not on the night: the Fatimid caliphate at قاہرہ is named once and dropped, the Buyid and Seljuk takeovers get one sentence, the sciences and the Andalusi scholars are named and not narrated, and the مرابطین and موحدین are compressed to a single line. The source volumes for this session are not yet in hand, so every name, date, incident and quotation in this plan carries a [SOURCE: …] marker and nothing reaches a slide until it is read off the page image.
drafts.opening_scene: The evening opens on a road, not on a definition. A young man of the fallen ruling house of دمشق is escaping westward after his family has been killed in the change of power — into مصر, then years working his way along the North African coast, then across the narrow water into Spain, arriving in a province where nobody is waiting for him [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat, the اندلس volume — the flight of عبد الرحمن بن معاویہ: the route, the years on the road, and the crossing]. The speaker then says the next sentence slowly: within a few years that same man is ruling from قرطبہ, and the men who hunted him are laying out a new capital for themselves on the دجلہ which they will call بغداد. Two capitals of one ummah, produced by the same quarrel, in the same generation, at opposite ends of the Muslim world. The question is left hanging and is not answered until the last block: «ایک ہی امت کے ایک ہی زمانے میں دو دارالحکومت — دونوں اپنے عروج پر، اور دونوں کا انجام ہوا۔ پہلے کون ختم ہوا، اور کیوں؟»

runsheet.block: آغاز — the Line and the Map
runsheet.content: The Line and the Map go up. The speaker points at last week's peg — دمشق, where session 4 ended at ۱۳۲ھ [verify] — then draws tonight's peg as a long bar rather than a point, ۱۳۲–۸۹۷ھ [verify], and says the honest thing out loud: this is the longest span in the series, so the room is being asked to hold on to two city names only, بغداد and قرطبہ. Every attendee marks the bar on their own Line in their own handwriting. Drop-ins are handed the catch-up sheet at the door and told the two names before the scene begins, so nobody spends the opening five minutes lost.

runsheet.block: The opening scene — two roads out of دمشق
runsheet.content: The flight westward is told as a scene: the fall of the house at دمشق, one survivor on the road through مصر and along the North African coast, the crossing, and the arrival in a province with no one expecting him [SOURCE: اندلس volume — the flight narrative]. As it is told, the speaker draws the second arrow: the same quarrel sends the winners east, out of شام into عراق, to build a new capital on the دجلہ. Both arrows are on the board before the story block starts, and they stay there all evening. The scene ends on the hanging question and the speaker moves straight on without answering it.

runsheet.block: The story — بغداد and قرطبہ, told as a pair
runsheet.content: Five moves, timed on the cue card. (1) ~4 min: the turn of ۱۳۲ھ [verify] and the move east — a capital that was built rather than inherited, and a state that now faces خراسان, ماوراء النہر, India and China rather than the Mediterranean [SOURCE: عباسیہ volume — the transfer of power, the choice of site on the دجلہ, and the founding as the book gives it]. (2) ~4 min: what بغداد was at its height, kept to one concrete claim — it became a capital of paper, and with paper came copyists, bookshops, libraries and the translation of Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic; the great hadith and fiqh compilation of the same decades is named in one sentence [SOURCE: عباسیہ volume — what the book actually claims about paper, translation and libraries]. (3) ~5 min, the moral centre, the one block that is never cut: the محنہ — a ruler adopts a theological position and makes assent to it a condition of holding office; judges, muhaddithūn and officials are examined; most give the answer demanded; امام احمد بن حنبل رحمہ اللہ does not, and is imprisoned, brought in chains and beaten; it runs on through more than one reign until a later caliph ends it, and the position امام احمد held is the position اہلِ سنت holds today [SOURCE: عباسیہ volume, the محنہ chapter — who began it, the question put, the arrest and imprisonment, how long it ran, who ended it]. المعتزلہ are explained in exactly one sentence as a theological school of that period, and the speaker does not go one word further. (4) ~4 min: قرطبہ — from a province held by one survivor, to an امارت, to a دارالخلافہ when a later ruler takes the title [verify ۳۱۶ھ], with the جامع مسجد and the library as the two concrete things; and the plain fact, stated once and dropped, that for a stretch three men held the title at once — بغداد, قرطبہ, قاہرہ [SOURCE: اندلس volume — the taking of the title, the mosque, the library, and the year]. (5) ~3 min: the two endings, deliberately unequal. قرطبہ's ending takes four centuries and comes from inside — the caliphate breaks into ملوک الطوائف [verify ۴۲۲ھ], the little kings hire their neighbours against each other, two North African interventions postpone the end in one sentence, and the frontier moves south through طلیطلہ, قرطبہ, اشبیلیہ to غرناطہ, which ends at ۸۹۷ھ [verify]. بغداد's ending is not told: the caliph keeps the title long after others hold the power, and the speaker stops at the city gate — «ہم آج شہر کے دروازے پر رک رہے ہیں؛ اندر ہم اگلے ہفتے جائیں گے».

runsheet.block: تعارف — three people, classical تراجم notice
runsheet.content: Two minutes twenty each, four lines each on the slide and on the workbook page: نام و نسب · سنین · what they did in one sentence · ایک واقعہ. The سنین line is printed as [SOURCE: …] and stays blank on the slide until the volumes are in hand and the years are read off the page — no year is spoken from memory. The listener writes «ایک واقعہ» themselves in the workbook while the speaker tells it, which is the retention mechanism and also gives the speaker a natural, unhurried pace. The order is deliberate: the ruler at the height of بغداد, then the scholar who would not give the answer that ruler's successors required, then the man who built the other capital — so the evening's centre of gravity sits on the middle profile.

runsheet.block: کیسے پتا چلا؟ — the five mother-books, and two men with one name
runsheet.content: One slide with five spines in a row, given one clause each in the order they were written, so the row reads as a progression and not a list. Then the minute the segment exists for: two writers whose names run almost identically, ours being the Sunni imam, مفسر و محدث, and the other a writer of a different school — material was filed under the wrong man, and our الطبری has been described as something he was not [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1, المقدمہ, the موسوعات section — the five books in the book's own words, the two-name confusion, and the name of the scholar who defended him]. The speaker names that defender from the briefing, never from memory. He closes with the handover line — you establish who the man is before you accept what is attributed to him — which is the sentence امام علی بن المدینیؒ is about to be quoted saying.

runsheet.block: آج کی بات — the supplied quotation, then everyone writes
runsheet.content: Two quotations on one slide, attribution first, read off the card word for word and never paraphrased: امام علی بن المدینیؒ — «حدیث کا مطلب سمجھنا نصف علم ہے اور شخصیات کی پہچان نصف علم ہے۔» and علامہ سخاویؒ — حکمت کے دو سرچشمے ہیں، سنی ہوئی اور لکھی ہوئی؛ جو صرف سنی جائے اور لکھی نہ جائے وہ مٹ جاتی ہے [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1, المقدمہ — both lines in the book's own Urdu wording, plus the work each is footnoted to; read off the page image, not the OCR text]. The speaker adds nothing after them — no summary, no application, no sentence of his own. The workbook line is «آج آپ کیا لے کر جا رہے ہیں؟ ______», and the room gets one full minute of silence to write; two or three people may read theirs aloud if willing, and it is fine if nobody does.

runsheet.block: اگلے ہفتے — the question
runsheet.content: The speaker puts a single mark beside بغداد on the map — ۶۵۶ھ [verify] — and says that is where next week begins, along with the Levant and the صلیبی جنگیں. He notes the one fact that ties tonight to next week without drawing a moral from it: the western capital outlived the eastern one by well over two centuries. Then he says the take-home question and stops — no recap, no closing summary. The workbook page for session 6 is pointed at so people know where next week's map worksheet is.

people.name: ہارون الرشید
people.laqab: الرشید — خلافتی لقب، ماخذ میں اسی نام سے
people.did: The Abbasid caliph in whose reign بغداد stood at its height as a capital, a court and a centre of books; the honorific used on the slide will be whatever Tareekh-e-Ummat itself uses for him and nothing more [SOURCE: عباسیہ volume — the book's own form of his name and his سنین].
people.incident_plan: One attested incident from the book, told in about four sentences with nothing added — first preference the report of his alternating between حج and campaign year by year, second preference an incident of a scholar speaking plainly to him and his response. Explicitly excluded: anything from popular story-collections such as الف لیلہ, and any court anecdote not on the page. [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat, the عباسیہ volume, the ہارون الرشید chapter — which single incident the book itself narrates about him, in its own wording]

people.name: امام احمد بن حنبل رحمہ اللہ
people.did: The imam of hadith and fiqh who was examined during the محنہ and would not affirm the position the state required, and whose position on that question is the one اہلِ سنت holds.
people.incident_plan: The محنہ itself, told as one continuous incident rather than as a summary: the summons, the journey in chains, the examination, the imprisonment and the beating, and the refusal — with a hard rule that nothing is put in his mouth that is not printed on the page, since attributed speech is exactly where OCR garbling and popular retelling do their damage. If the book carries his words, they are read in Arabic first and then in Urdu; if it does not, the incident is told without any dialogue at all. [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat, the عباسیہ volume, the محنہ chapter — the arrest, the examination, and any words attributed to امام احمد رحمہ اللہ, read off the page image]

people.name: عبد الرحمن الداخل
people.did: The one survivor of the fallen دمشق house who reached Spain and established the rule at قرطبہ that became the second capital of this evening.
people.incident_plan: One incident of exile rather than one of conquest, so the profile answers the opening scene: first preference the lines he is reported to have said about a single palm tree at his estate, seeing his own condition in it — read in Arabic first and then in Urdu if the book carries the Arabic; second preference an incident from the crossing itself. [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat, the اندلس volume — whether the book carries the palm-tree lines and in exactly what wording, and its سنین for him]

drafts.map: The base map is unchanged — same projection, same six anchor cities مکہ · مدینہ · دمشق · بغداد · قرطبہ · قسطنطنیہ. Tonight adds three strokes and one erasure, in this order. (1) During the opening scene, two arrows leave دمشق in opposite directions: one east-north-east to بغداد on the دجلہ, one west along the North African coast — مصر → افریقیہ → مغرب → across the strait → قرطبہ. That single image is the whole session and it stays on the board all evening; attendees draw both arrows on their own workbook worksheet as it is told. (2) During the story, two rings of the same size, one around بغداد and one around قرطبہ, with the same centuries written beneath each — this is the pairing made visible. A third, much smaller mark goes on قاہرہ when the three simultaneous claims to the title are named, and is never returned to. (3) One short dotted line runs from بغداد east towards خراسان and ماوراء النہر and on towards the Indian and Chinese trade — a single stroke to show why the Mediterranean stops being the centre of gravity once the capital moves. (4) The erasure, in the last three minutes of the story: the shaded Iberian region is rubbed out from north to south in four strokes — طلیطلہ, then قرطبہ itself, then اشبیلیہ, then everything except a small patch at غرناطہ, which goes last at ۸۹۷ھ [verify]. The room watches a shaded area shrink for roughly ninety seconds while the speaker says only the four place names. (5) بغداد is deliberately left untouched: one mark beside it reading ۶۵۶ھ [verify], drawn in the closing block, and nothing else. The workbook worksheet for this session prints the coastline and the six cities only — the arrows and the Iberian shading are drawn by hand by each attendee, because a self-drawn map is remembered and a printed one is not.
drafts.howweknow_plan: Three minutes, one slide, two halves. First half, ninety seconds: five spines in a row — تاریخ الطبری · الکامل فی التاریخ (ابن اثیر) · تاریخ الاسلام (ذہبی) · البدایہ والنہایہ (ابن کثیر) · تاریخ ابن خلدون — each given one clause, in the order they were written, so the row reads as a progression: the first records each report together with the chain it came on and leaves the sifting to the reader; the second runs the whole world year by year, distilled; the third is the most careful sieve; the fourth weighs chains and reasoning together; the fifth opens with a مقدمہ that asks why states rise and fall at all. The point said out loud: almost everything anyone will ever tell you about this period comes, at some remove, off these five shelves. Second half, ninety seconds: two writers whose names run almost identically — ابو جعفر محمد بن جریر الطبری, ours, the Sunni imam, مفسر و محدث, and another writer of a different school whose name is nearly the same. Material was filed under the wrong man, and our الطبری has been described as something he was not; the tradition caught the confusion by the method already taught in earlier weeks — establish who the man is before you accept what is attributed to him. The scholar who defended him is named from the briefing, never from memory [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1, المقدمہ, the موسوعات section — the five books in the book's own description, the two-name confusion, and who defended our الطبری; read off the page image, because the OCR garbles both names]. The segment ends on the handover sentence, which is precisely what امام علی بن المدینیؒ is quoted saying thirty seconds later.
drafts.takehome_question: «قرطبہ کو ختم ہوتے ہوتے چار سو سال لگے، اور بغداد نے اپنا نام اپنی طاقت سے بہت زیادہ عرصے تک رکھا۔ تو ایک تہذیب اصل میں کب ختم ہوتی ہے — جس دن اس کا دارالحکومت گرتا ہے، یا اس سے بہت پہلے؟» [Córdoba took four hundred years to end, and Baghdad kept its name far longer than it kept its power. So when does a civilisation actually end — on the day its capital falls, or long before that?]

sensitive.what_arises: Three live areas. First and largest, the محنہ: a ruler examining and imprisoning a scholar is material a room will instinctively try to convert into a general position on rulers and ulama, or into a comment on present-day Pakistan, and it also opens onto عقائد — someone will ask what المعتزلہ believed and whether that belief put them outside Islam. Second, the period contains a rival caliphate at قاہرہ and three simultaneous claims to the title, which is an invitation to sectarian description that this evening will not accept. Third, the «کیسے پتا چلا؟» item about two writers sharing one name touches the Sunni–Shia question directly, and Andalus reliably produces a why-did-we-lose-Spain question that turns into modern grievance. The standing rule about the مشاجرات is not this period's own risk, but the guardrail installed in session 3 remains the answer if the floor reaches for it.
sensitive.how_handled: The محنہ is narrated exactly as the source narrates it and then stopped — what was asked, who was examined, what happened to امام احمد رحمہ اللہ, who ended it — with المعتزلہ explained in one sentence as a theological school of that period and not one word further; no attributed speech is used unless it is printed on the page. The قاہرہ claim is stated once as a fact of the period, with no account of anyone's beliefs, and dropped. The two-writers item is delivered as what it is — a name-clash that the tradition itself detected and corrected — and the wider Sunni–Shia question is not entered. Andalus is told as the source tells it, as fragmentation from within, with no modern parallel offered by the speaker and none accepted from the floor. Rulers of this period are not صحابہ and may be described by their recorded acts, but the register stays factual: no denunciation, no verdict on anyone's faith, no raised voice. Every one of these has a pre-written answer in QA_BANK.md before the night, and the speaker reads it rather than improvising.
will_not_be_said: No verdict on anyone's belief or salvation — the speaker will not say or imply that المأمون, any other caliph, or any group of that period was outside Islam, and will not use the word کفر of any of them
No modern political analogy: no present-day Pakistani ruler, party, institution or court is named, and no comparison is drawn between the محنہ and anything happening today
No comparison of any living scholar, or of 'today's ulama', to امام احمد بن حنبل رحمہ اللہ, favourably or otherwise
No account of Fatimid or Ismaili belief; the قاہرہ claim is named as a rival claim to the title and nothing more
No adjudication between Sunni and Shia positions, and no answer beyond the plain name-clash fact when the two-الطبری item is raised
No invented or half-remembered dialogue for امام احمد رحمہ اللہ under examination, and no words attributed to him that are not printed in the source
No court anecdote about ہارون الرشید drawn from popular story-collections rather than from the book
No adjudication between the Companions ؓ, and no comment on the مشاجرات from the floor — the session-3 guardrail line is used verbatim instead
No claim that Muslims 'lost' Spain because of any one named group, sect or ruler; the source's own account of internal fragmentation is given and nothing is added to it
sensitive.floor_policy: Questions are taken only in the last block, and answered in one of four ways, all decided in advance. (1) A question about tonight's facts is answered from the book, naming the book. (2) A question about عقیدہ — what المعتزلہ held, whether that belief is کفر, anything about the Fatimid caliphs' creed — gets the deferral line «یہ عقیدے کا مسئلہ ہے، تاریخ کا نہیں؛ اس کا جواب اہلِ علم سے پوچھنا چاہیے» and is not entered even one sentence deep. (3) A question inviting a modern parallel gets one warm line — «ہم آج ایک صدی میں بیٹھے ہیں؛ اسے آج پر لاگو کرنا ہر ایک کا اپنا کام ہے» — and the speaker returns to the map. (4) Anything touching the Companions ؓ gets the session-3 guardrail verbatim. Any question the speaker cannot answer is written into a notebook in front of the room with «مجھے نہیں معلوم؛ میں دیکھ کر اگلے ہفتے بتاؤں گا», and answered at the start of the next session — this is stated policy, announced as such, not treated as a failure.

QA_BANK.md entries written and rehearsed before the night for at least four questions: what المعتزلہ believed and whether it was کفر; who the Fatimids were; whether الطبری was Shia; and why Muslims lost Spain
notes_for_speaker: The evening has only two nouns. If you lose your place at any point, say «دو دارالحکومت — ایک مشرق میں، ایک مغرب میں» and put your hand on the map. You will be back on the rails in five seconds and the room will read it as a deliberate pause.

WHAT IS CUT, decided now so you are never deciding on the night: the Fatimid caliphate at قاہرہ is one clause and never returns; the Buyid and Seljuk takeovers are one sentence with no names; the sciences are a list of names with no stories; the Andalusi scholars are named and not narrated; المعتزلہ get exactly one sentence; the مرابطین and موحدین are one sentence together; no caliph other than ہارون and the ones the محنہ requires is named. None of this is a loss — it is what buys the twenty minutes for the two cities.

Slow down in exactly two places: the sentence where the two arrows leave دمشق in opposite directions, and the whole محنہ block. In the محنہ, lower your volume instead of raising it. The material carries itself, and the dignified register is far easier to hold quietly.
The محنہ is the one block that is never cut. If you reach 0:20 and you are still in the libraries of بغداد, leave them mid-sentence and go straight to it.

If you are running long, cut in this order: the two North African interventions down to a single clause, then the three-simultaneous-claims line, then the fifth mother-book to a name only. Never cut تعارف and never cut the silent writing minute — those two are the retention system, and the rest of the evening is decoration without them.
If you are running short, the paper-and-translation block and the جامع مسجد قرطبہ description each stretch safely by two minutes without adding a single new claim.

Your safe ground is the map. Any time you feel the thread going, stop talking, walk to the map, and narrate the movement — the arrows and the shading are themselves the content. Your second safe ground is تعارف: if you blank inside the story, go to the three profiles, which are four printed lines each on the cue card and can simply be read.

Never fill a gap with an anecdote you half-remember, and be especially careful of this with ہارون الرشید, where a great deal of attractive material in circulation is not in any book we are using. If it is not in the briefing, it does not get said. «یہ مجھے دیکھنا پڑے گا» is a complete and dignified answer that costs you nothing.
Say رحمہ اللہ after امام احمد every single time. You will say his name perhaps fifteen times tonight, and the room counts whether or not it means to.

The writing minute at 0:38 is a full sixty seconds of silence and it will feel three times that long from where you are standing. Do not rescue it by talking. Count to sixty on your fingers behind the lectern and let the pens do the work.

Read both quotations off the card word for word, attribution first, and then say nothing at all after them. No application, no 'so what this means for us is'. The conclusion belongs to the person writing in the workbook, and every sentence you add takes one away from them.

The ending is a stop, not a summary. Say the question, put the ۶۵۶ھ mark beside بغداد, and stop talking while the room is still thinking. Resisting the recap is the hardest thirty seconds of the evening, and it is what brings people back next week.

drafts.title: قریبِ مرگ
drafts.gloss: Two centuries in which it nearly ended
drafts.summary: Session 6 is the low point of the ten-week arc and its recovery, in the same evening. The room opens standing in بغداد in the week of its fall in ۶۵۶ھ [verify], then rewinds to ۴۹۲ھ [verify] and walks forward through two threats arriving from opposite directions — the crusading armies coming down the Levant coast from the north-west, the Mongol advance crossing ایران from the north-east — until both converge on بلادِ شام and the caliphate's capital is gone. The final four minutes of the narrative are the turn: مصر is the refuge, and the counter-move out of قاہرہ to عین جالوت in ۶۵۸ھ [verify] is the first time all evening that the map moves outward again. The evening rests entirely on the crusades-and-Mongols volume of Tareekh-e-Ummat, which is NOT yet in hand — so every factual claim below carries a [SOURCE: …] marker naming what must be obtained and read before it may be said aloud, and the sensitive material (present-day analogies, blame for بغداد's fall, sectarian accusation) is governed by a written floor policy rather than improvised at the lectern.
drafts.opening_scene: The evening opens with no slide but the map, and the speaker standing at بغداد — the city the room spent the whole of last week inside. He describes one thing and one thing only: what a person entering the city would have found in the week of its fall in ۶۵۶ھ [verify], reading the description straight from the book and saying so aloud first — «جو کچھ میں اب بیان کروں گا، وہ کتاب سے پڑھ رہا ہوں؛ اپنی طرف سے ایک لفظ نہیں بڑھاؤں گا۔» [SOURCE: the crusades-and-Mongols volume, the بغداد ۶۵۶ھ passage — the state of the city in the source's own words, one paragraph of a length that can be read aloud in ninety seconds; also what the source does NOT claim, so nothing is added]. He then draws a black ring around بغداد on the wall map: the first time in six weeks that one of the six permanent anchor cities has been struck. The question is left hanging, unanswered — «ایک قوم اپنا دارالحکومت، اپنا خلیفہ اور اپنے کتب خانے ایک ہفتے میں کھو دے، اور پھر بھی باقی رہے — یہ کیسے ہوا؟» — and instead of answering it he walks his hand back across the map to ۴۹۲ھ [verify] and starts the story from there.

runsheet.block: آغاز — the Line and the Map go up
runsheet.content: The Line is extended by hand, and tonight it does something it has not done before: last week's bracket ran ۱۳۲–۸۹۷ھ [verify], and tonight a narrower bracket, ۴۹۲–۶۵۸ھ [verify], is drawn *inside* it — the room is told plainly that we are stepping back inside last week's span, not forward past it, because these two centuries deserve their own evening. Four ticks are marked on that bracket — ۴۹۲ھ · ۵۸۳ھ · ۶۵۶ھ · ۶۵۸ھ [verify] — and everyone marks the same four in their own workbook. The one sentence a drop-in needs: «پچھلے ہفتے ہم بغداد اور قرطبہ کے اندر تھے؛ آج ہم اُنہی صدیوں میں کھڑے ہیں جن میں یہ سب ختم ہوتے ہوتے بچا۔» And the return is named out loud: «پہلی نشست میں آپ نے ہلاکو خان کا نام صرف سنا تھا اور آگے بڑھ گئے تھے؛ آج اُس سے باقاعدہ ملاقات ہے۔»

runsheet.block: opening scene — بغداد in the week of its fall
runsheet.content: The scene described above: the speaker at the map, the book open, the read-aloud paragraph on the state of the city, then the black ring drawn around بغداد. He states the source and the disclaimer before he begins, not after. Two full beats of silence after the ring is drawn — they are scripted, not accidental. Then the hanging question, and a deliberate walk back to ۴۹۲ھ [verify] without answering it.

runsheet.block: the story — ۴۹۲ھ to ۶۵۸ھ [verify], told forward, the map moving throughout
runsheet.content: 0:08–0:13, the first threat, from the north-west: armies arrive from Europe, come down the Syrian coast, and بیت المقدس is taken in ۴۹۲ھ [verify]; a thin strip is shaded along the coast for the states they set up, and the room is asked to count on their own Line how many years pass before the next tick — the arithmetic is theirs, not the speaker's. 0:13–0:18, the recovery is slow and generational: the consolidation under عماد الدین زنگی and نور الدین محمود before صلاح الدین ایوبی رحمہ اللہ ever commands, then مصر and بلادِ شام under one hand, then حطین and the return of بیت المقدس in ۵۸۳ھ [verify] [SOURCE: the volume's زنگی/نور الدین and صلاح الدین chapters — the sequence of consolidation, and the account of حطین and the entry into بیت المقدس]. 0:18–0:24, the second threat, from the opposite corner: the Mongol advance out of the east across خوارزم and ایران, and بغداد in ۶۵۶ھ [verify] — the room is now standing in the scene the evening opened on, and recognises it — then حلب and دمشق as the same arrow keeps moving west [SOURCE: the Mongol chapters — ہلاکو خان's lineage and the order of his campaign; what the source states about the causes of بغداد's fall, and what it declines to state]. 0:24–0:28, the turn: مصر is where the line holds, the مملوک institution formed in the fighting on the Nile at المنصورہ in ۶۴۸ھ [verify] is ten years later the institution that marches out, and at عین جالوت in ۶۵۸ھ [verify], under سلطان سیف الدین قطز with بیبرس in command of a wing, the north-eastern arrow is stopped for the first time [SOURCE: the مملوک chapter — المنصورہ; the command arrangement at عین جالوت between قطز and بیبرس, stated exactly as the source has it]; the gold arrow out of قاہرہ is drawn on the map while this is said.

runsheet.block: تعارف — exactly three
runsheet.content: Roughly two minutes each, in the fixed تراجم format: نام و نسب (with only such title as the source itself prints) · سنین · what they did in one sentence · ایک واقعہ, one authentic incident read from the source. The three are صلاح الدین ایوبی رحمہ اللہ · ہلاکو خان · الظاہر بیبرس, deliberately in that order so the segment itself runs loss-and-recovery in miniature. Workbooks carry the first three lines pre-printed and «ایک واقعہ» blank; the room writes while the speaker talks. ہلاکو خان's notice is delivered in exactly the same flat register as the other two — no honorific, and no denunciation either; he is narrated, not judged from the lectern.

runsheet.block: کیسے پتا چلا؟ — what actually survived
runsheet.content: The question is put to the room first: «جو کتابیں ہم پانچ ہفتوں سے پڑھ کر سنا رہے ہیں، بغداد کے گرنے والے دن وہ کہاں تھیں؟» The answer is the mechanism, not a sentiment: a chain-based tradition stores itself in many copies in many cities and in licensed transmitters who walk — دمشق، حلب، قاہرہ، نیشاپور، مکہ و مدینہ all held the same texts, and the licence to transmit lives in a person, not in a building. The speaker holds up the physical volume he has been narrating from all term and points out that its footnotes name works written before ۶۵۶ھ [verify] and works written after it, and both are in his hand tonight. He closes with the discipline itself: the famous picture of the river running black with ink will NOT be told unless this book carries it, and if it is told it will be attributed aloud — «جو کتاب میں نہیں، وہ میں نہیں کہوں گا۔»

runsheet.block: آج کی بات — the supplied quotation, then everyone writes
runsheet.content: The slide carries the attribution as its heading, the Arabic in Naskh, the Urdu rendering beneath — the supplied passage on صبر و استقامت: that communities before this one endured worse and did not leave the دین [SOURCE: the exact Arabic wording, the Urdu rendering, and the attribution as the editor supplies them, eyeballed off the page image before it reaches a slide; also the source's own framing sentence around it]. The speaker reads it and says nothing after it — no moral of his own is added, and there is no bridge sentence. Then the workbook line: «آج آپ کیا لے کر جا رہے ہیں؟ ______» and a full minute of quiet for everyone to write their own takeaway in their own hand. Two or three are read aloud only if the room offers them; nobody is called on.

runsheet.block: اگلے ہفتے — close on a question
runsheet.content: The speaker steps back to the wall map, points at the black ring on بغداد and then at the gold arrow leaving قاہرہ, and asks the closing question without answering it. He then puts a finger on Anatolia — a corner of the map that has been blank all term — and says only that next week begins there, in ۶۹۹ھ [verify], about forty years [verify] after tonight's last tick. Workbooks are collected up, the catch-up sheet is available at the door for anyone who came in tonight for the first time, and the Line stays on the wall.

people.name: صلاح الدین ایوبی رحمہ اللہ
people.did: He brought مصر and بلادِ شام under a single command and recovered بیت المقدس in ۵۸۳ھ [verify], some ninety years [verify] after it had been lost.
people.incident_plan: One incident only, on his conduct at the moment of entry into بیت المقدس — the terms he gave the people inside the city, told exactly as the book has it and with no adjectives added. It is chosen because it shows character through a decision rather than through praise, and because it is the incident the room is most likely to have heard in a garbled form elsewhere. [SOURCE: the crusades volume, صلاح الدین chapter — the terms of entry into بیت المقدس in ۵۸۳ھ [verify] as the source narrates them, one readable paragraph; plus his full نام و نسب and سنین, and only such titles as the source itself prints — no title will be used that is not on the page]

people.name: ہلاکو خان
people.did: He commanded the Mongol campaign that took بغداد in ۶۵۶ھ [verify], ending the Abbasid caliphate there, and then pushed west into حلب and دمشق.
people.incident_plan: One incident, told flat: the sequence of the demand made on the caliph and what followed — no atrocity detail beyond the source's own sentences, no numbers, no curse from the lectern. He was previewed in session 1 as a name on the Line and nothing more; tonight he is met properly, and the point made aloud is that a name on a timeline becomes a person with a sequence of decisions once you stand inside the century. [SOURCE: the Mongol chapter — his lineage as the source states it, the order of his campaign, and the account of the exchange with the caliph; also whatever the source says or declines to say about the causes of the city's fall, so that a question from the floor is answered from the book rather than improvised]

people.name: الظاہر بیبرس
people.did: A مملوک commander in the field at عین جالوت in ۶۵۸ھ [verify] who afterwards ruled مصر و شام and turned a single defensive stand into a sustained recovery.
people.incident_plan: One incident from the years immediately after عین جالوت, chosen for what it shows about rebuilding rather than about fighting — most likely a concrete administrative measure he ordered to bind قاہرہ and دمشق back together. The segment ends here on purpose: the last person the room meets tonight is the one who did the repairing. [SOURCE: the مملوک chapter — his نام و نسب and سنین, his part at عین جالوت stated exactly as the source has it (the sultan in command there was سیف الدین قطز, and this must not be blurred), and one attested incident from his reign; also the exact form of his regnal title as the source prints it — none will be used otherwise]

drafts.map: The base map is the standing one, unchanged: same projection, same six anchor cities — مکہ · مدینہ · دمشق · بغداد · قرطبہ · قسطنطنیہ. Tonight adds four labelled points to it and nothing more: بیت المقدس، حلب، قاہرہ، and عین جالوت. THREAT ONE, drawn in maroon, enters at the top-left and runs north-to-south: from Europe past قسطنطنیہ and across the sea, then straight down the Levant coast to انطاکیہ، طرابلس and بیت المقدس in ۴۹۲ھ [verify]; a thin strip is shaded along that coastline for the states established there. THREAT TWO, also maroon and drawn thicker, enters at the far right and runs east-to-west: out of the steppe across خوارزم and ایران, onto بغداد in ۶۵۶ھ [verify], then continuing west to حلب and دمشق. The teaching point is made by the geometry itself — the two arrows come from opposite ends of the map and converge on the same narrow corridor, بلادِ شام, and the room can see the squeeze without being told. بغداد, an anchor city that has been on this map since session 1, is ringed in black; it is the only anchor city ever struck in this course. THE REFUGE is drawn as a single line running south-west, out of the squeeze, from دمشق across سینا to قاہرہ, and قاہرہ is circled in gold. THE TURN is one gold arrow, and it is the only arrow on the entire map that runs the other way — out of قاہرہ, back north-east through فلسطین, to عین جالوت in ۶۵۸ھ [verify], where it meets the head of the eastern arrow and stops it. The gold arrow is drawn live, while the speaker is talking, at 0:24–0:28 — not pre-printed. Workbook version: the two maroon arrows and the coastal strip are printed; قاہرہ, عین جالوت and the gold arrow are left blank for each person to draw by hand.
drafts.howweknow_plan: Three minutes, opened with a question rather than a statement: «جو کتابیں ہم پانچ ہفتوں سے پڑھ کر سنا رہے ہیں، بغداد کے گرنے والے دن وہ کہاں تھیں؟» The answer is deliberately mechanical, not consoling — a tradition built on chains of transmission is a distributed thing by construction: the same texts sat in copies in دمشق، حلب، قاہرہ، نیشاپور and the Ḥaramayn simultaneously, and the licence to transmit a book (سماع، اجازہ) is held by a person, and a person walks out of a city. So the destruction of one building, however large, removes copies but not the text; a capital can be lost and a written tradition survive it. The demonstration is physical: the speaker holds up the actual volume of Tareekh-e-Ummat he has been narrating from all term and notes that its footnotes cite works composed before ۶۵۶ھ [verify] and works composed after it, and that both are in his hand this evening — the tradition is verifiably on the other side of the gap. This is explicitly built on weeks 1 and 5: week 1 taught that dates are the first check, week 5 introduced the great compilations, and tonight explains why those compilations reached us at all. The segment closes on the discipline rather than on the comfort: the well-known image of the river running black with ink will NOT be told unless this book carries it, and if it does carry it, it will be attributed aloud when told. [SOURCE: what the volume states about the destruction of books at بغداد and about what survived; if it treats this thinly, one named Sunni work is chosen as the openly-declared second source per the series rule, and named to the audience rather than quietly mixed in]
drafts.takehome_question: «بغداد گرا، مگر امت باقی رہی — تو وہ کیا چیز تھی جو شہر کے ساتھ نہیں گری؟ اور جب یہ امت دوبارہ اٹھی، تو کس سرزمین سے اٹھی؟» [Baghdad fell, but the ummah remained — so what was it that did not fall with the city? And when this ummah rose again, from which land did it rise?]

sensitive.what_arises: Four pressure points, all foreseeable. (1) The صلیبی جنگیں are the single easiest topic in the whole course to pull into present-day politics — a listener may connect بیت المقدس to a current conflict, or to Christians as a community, within seconds of the word being said. (2) Blame for the fall of بغداد: the accusation against a vizier, and the accusation against a named scholar, are both in wide circulation, both contested, and both sectarian in effect — this is the most dangerous thirty seconds of the evening. (3) The مملوک sultanate raises a legitimacy question (soldiers bought as boys who become the ruling institution), and so does the Abbasid line continued at قاہرہ after ۶۵۶ھ [verify]. (4) Mongol casualty figures, which circulate in wildly inflated and unsourceable forms, and which a listener may supply from the floor and expect confirmed.
sensitive.how_handled: The governing rule for the whole evening, stated aloud by the speaker in the first two minutes so the room hears the standard he is holding himself to: narrate what the book narrates, and stop. Causes of the fall of بغداد are given only as the source itself gives them, with no cause of ours added and no name supplied that the source does not supply. No number — of dead, of books, of anything — is spoken unless it is printed on the page in front of him. The مملوک and post-۶۵۶ھ caliphate questions are described factually as arrangements that existed, with no verdict on their legitimacy; that is a fiqh and history-of-institutions question, not tonight's. And nothing in this evening is extended into a statement about Christians, about any living community, or about any present-day state or conflict — the two centuries are narrated as two centuries. QA_BANK entries covering every one of these are written and rehearsed BEFORE the night, not composed at the lectern.
will_not_be_said: No individual or community will be named from the podium as the cause of بغداد's fall — the accusation against the vizier and the accusation against the scholar will not be raised by the speaker, and if raised from the floor will be neither confirmed nor denied.
No casualty figure for بغداد or for any Mongol campaign, and no atrocity detail beyond the sentences the source itself prints.
No line, explicit or implied, drawn from the صلیبی جنگیں to any present-day conflict, government, community or religion. No sentence of the form «اور آج بھی…».
No statement about Christians or Christianity as such; the armies are named as what the source names them, and the point is not extended into a claim about a faith community.
No takfir, no cursing, and no invocation against ہلاکو خان or any other named person from the lectern — he is narrated, not denounced.
No verdict on the legitimacy of the مملوک sultanate, nor on the Abbasid line continued at قاہرہ after ۶۵۶ھ [verify].
No blame assigned to any Muslim ruler of the period beyond what the source assigns.
No use of صلاح الدین ایوبی رحمہ اللہ as an analogy for any living leader, movement, party or state.
The image of the Tigris running black with ink will not be told unless the source carries it; if told, it is attributed aloud.
sensitive.floor_policy: Questions are taken at the door afterwards, not during the hour, and this is announced at 0:00 — it protects the runsheet and it removes the improvisation risk from the room's most heated moment. If a question is nonetheless called out, three prepared lines are memorised. For a present-day question: «یہ سوال آج کی سیاست کا ہے، اور یہ کورس آج کی سیاست پر بات نہیں کرتا؛ میں وہی بیان کروں گا جو کتاب بیان کرتی ہے۔» For a contested or sectarian one: «اس بارے میں مؤرخین کے بیانات مختلف ہیں؛ میں وہی سناؤں گا جو ہماری کتاب میں ہے، اور جو اُس میں نہیں، وہ میں اپنی طرف سے نہیں کہوں گا۔» And for anything he does not hold on the page: «مجھے نہیں معلوم — میں دیکھ کر اگلے ہفتے بتاؤں گا۔», which is then actually done the following week, aloud, in the آغاز block. Every deferral is warm and specific, never a brush-off; the questioner is thanked and told exactly when the answer will come.

Nothing in this plan may be spoken until that volume is obtained, extracted to page-marked text, and read. Check the same Telegram channel the two held PDFs came from, and run the text-layer test before commissioning any OCR.

The زنگی and نور الدین محمود material: the source's account of the consolidation that preceded صلاح الدین ایوبی رحمہ اللہ, needed because the whole lesson of the evening rests on the recovery being slow and generational rather than sudden.
The صلاح الدین chapter: حطین; the recovery of بیت المقدس in ۵۸۳ھ [verify]; and specifically the terms of entry into the city, as one readable paragraph, for his ایک واقعہ.

The Mongol chapters: ہلاکو خان's lineage as the source states it; the order of his campaign west; the account of بغداد in ۶۵۶ھ [verify] including one paragraph on the state of the city fit to read aloud in the opening; the advance to حلب and دمشق.

What the source states — AND what it declines to state — about the causes of the fall of بغداد. This is required specifically so the floor answer quotes the book instead of improvising into sectarian territory.

The مملوک chapters: the fighting on the Nile at المنصورہ in ۶۴۸ھ [verify]; the command arrangement at عین جالوت in ۶۵۸ھ [verify] between سلطان سیف الدین قطز and بیبرس, stated exactly (the two must not be blurred); and one attested incident from بیبرس's reign for his ایک واقعہ.
What the source says about the Abbasid caliphate after ۶۵۶ھ [verify], including the arrangement at قاہرہ — narrated, not adjudicated.

For «کیسے پتا چلا؟»: whatever the source states about the destruction of books at بغداد and about what survived it. If the volume treats this thinly, one named Sunni work is chosen as an openly-declared second source and named aloud to the audience rather than quietly mixed in.

For «آج کی بات»: the exact Arabic wording of the supplied passage on صبر و استقامت, its Urdu rendering, and its attribution — all read off the page image before they reach a slide, since the OCR text layer garbles Arabic ligatures and honorifics worst of all. No number and no chapter reference goes on the slide unless the editor supplies it verified.

Every date in this plan — ۴۹۲ھ · ۵۸۳ھ · ۶۴۸ھ · ۶۵۶ھ · ۶۵۸ھ · ۶۹۹ھ — confirmed against the source and entered into docs/catalogue/TIMELINE.md with its printed page before it goes on the Line, on a slide, or in a workbook. The [verify] markers throughout this plan come off only there.

The full نام و نسب, سنین, and any titles for all three تعارف people, taken from the source's own page and entered into docs/catalogue/PEOPLE.md. No title is used that the source does not print, and no descriptor is coined for any of the three.
notes_for_speaker: Say the disclaimer line at the very start of the opening scene — «جو کچھ میں اب بیان کروں گا، وہ کتاب سے پڑھ رہا ہوں» — and mean it. It is your protection for the entire evening, and it is also why the room will trust the next forty minutes. Never say it after a claim; always before.

SLOW DOWN in two places, both scripted: the last thirty seconds of the opening description, and the moment you draw the black ring around بغداد. Two full beats of silence after the ring — count them, do not fill them. Keep the voice level. This material does not need to be raised; a flat voice on heavy content lands harder than a loud one, and a raised voice here is the one thing that would make the evening feel theatrical.

THE TURN IS THE ONE PLACE TO LIFT. At عین جالوت, stop talking from the lectern, walk to the map, and draw the gold arrow while you speak. The room feels the recovery through the physical act before it understands it through the words. Do not pre-draw that arrow.

IF YOU BLANK, GO TO THE MAP. Put a finger on the north-west arrow and trace it down the coast, then on the north-east arrow and trace it across ایران — narrating pure geography out loud reassembles the story for you in about fifteen seconds and reads to the room as deliberate. Second safe ground: move early into تعارف; the three notices are self-contained and need nothing from the narrative.

IF RUNNING LONG, CUT IN THIS ORDER: (1) the detail on the coastal states, (2) المنصورہ ۶۴۸ھ [verify], (3) compress the زنگی and نور الدین generation into one sentence. Never cut عین جالوت, and never cut آج کی بات — the whole architecture of the evening is loss followed by the turn, and an evening that ends on the loss is a different and much worse evening than the one you planned.

DO NOT CALCULATE THE YEARS ALOUD between ۴۹۲ھ and ۵۸۳ھ. Ask the room to count it on their own Line. It lands considerably harder when they do the arithmetic themselves, and it keeps a number out of your mouth that you would then have to defend.

KEEP ہلاکو خان'S NOTICE AS FLAT AS THE OTHER TWO — no honorific, and equally no insult, no raised voice, no invocation against him. That flatness is the register of this course, and management will be watching this segment specifically.

REHEARSE THE HANDOVER INTO آج کی بات COLD. The narrative ends, and the quotation begins, with no bridge sentence of your own. You add no moral. The attributed words on the screen are the entire lesson, and anything you say after them weakens them and puts your own opinion in the room.

NUMBERS ARE THE TRAP TONIGHT. Someone will supply a casualty figure from the floor and look at you to confirm it. The prepared answer is that you only quote what is on the page in front of you. Practise saying that without apology.

LOGISTICS BEFORE THE ROOM FILLS: water, the one-page cue card, and — critically — the black marker already in your hand at 0:00, so that you are not hunting for it during the two beats of silence at بغداد.

drafts.title: آخری خلافت
drafts.gloss: Six hundred years, and how they ended
drafts.summary: Session 7 narrates the عثمانی state from a small frontier principality in north-west Anatolia to the abolition of the caliphal office in ۱۳۴۲ھ / 1924 [verify] — six centuries in 45 minutes, so the material is cut to four movements and everything else is deliberately left out. The evening's argument is carried by the map rather than by the speaker: the shaded area grows outward from one small patch of Anatolia until it holds four of the six anchor cities the audience has had on their map since week 1, then recedes along the same lines back to that patch. Three sultans are introduced with one authentic incident each from the source — سلطان محمد فاتح (previewed in session 1, met properly here), سلطان سلیمان, سلطان عبد الحمید ثانی — and the evening's «آج کی بات» is the author's own supplied passage on قومی غیرت, read aloud with no commentary. The ending is narrated soberly and the evening stops at 1924 [verify]: a boundary announced aloud at minute 7 and enforced from the floor, with no reference to any present-day state, government, party or movement. The session is gated on obtaining the عثمانیہ volume of Tareekh-e-Ummat — the three names are fixed, but the incidents and every date are not yet sourced.
drafts.opening_scene: Before dawn on a railway platform in استنبول, ۱۳۴۲ھ / 1924 [verify]. A family stands with the luggage they were able to carry; a train is waiting for them; they are leaving the city their house had held since ۸۵۷ھ [verify]. There is no siege, no army at the gates, no fighting anywhere near them — what ended had been decided in a room, on paper, and the train leaves on time. The speaker says one sentence — «یہ خاندان چھ سو سال حکومت کرتا رہا» — and then stops and says nothing for a moment. The question left hanging, which the whole evening walks back to answer: how does a state that outlasted every rival on this map end as quietly as this, and did it end on that platform, or long before it? [SOURCE: the عثمانیہ volume's account of ۱۳۴۲ھ/۱۹۲۴ — the departure, its date, and only the details the author actually gives; if the source does not carry the scene, use the fallback opening recorded in the speaker notes.]

runsheet.block: آغاز — the Line and the Map
runsheet.content: The wall banner is extended with a marker from where session 6 stopped — بغداد ۶۵۶ھ [verify], with قاہرہ as the refuge — forward to tonight's span, ۶۹۹–۱۳۴۲ھ [verify], and every attendee marks the same peg on the Line in their own workbook in their own hand. The base map goes up unchanged, with the six anchor cities that have been there every week: مکہ · مدینہ · دمشق · بغداد · قرطبہ · قسطنطنیہ. The speaker puts a finger on قسطنطنیہ and says plainly that for six weeks this city has sat on their map as a city on the other side, belonging to someone else, and that tonight it changes hands and becomes a capital. Drop-ins are handed the one-page catch-up sheet (the Line, the Map, one line per session so far) while this is happening, so nobody has to be caught up verbally.

runsheet.block: Opening scene — the platform, and the boundary
runsheet.content: The speaker describes the railway platform in استنبول in ۱۳۴۲ھ / 1924 [verify] in five or six plain sentences: the hour, the luggage, the waiting train, the absence of any battle, and the fact that the family had held that city since ۸۵۷ھ [verify]. He says «یہ خاندان چھ سو سال حکومت کرتا رہا», pauses, and puts the question that the evening exists to answer — how does something six hundred years old end this quietly, and when did it actually end? At roughly 0:07 he then says the boundary sentence once, clearly, standing still: «ہم آج ۱۹۲۴ پر رک جائیں گے۔ اس کے بعد کی سیاست ہمارا موضوع نہیں — نہ کسی ملک کی، نہ کسی جماعت کی۔» He does not explain or defend the boundary; he states it and moves straight into the story, so that the limit is set at minute 7 rather than being produced defensively at minute 42.

runsheet.block: The story — four movements, six centuries
runsheet.content: Movement 1 (~5 min): a small frontier principality in north-west Anatolia from ۶۹۹ھ [verify], one of several of the same kind whose names are now forgotten; بورصہ as the first seat; then the crossing of the water into the Balkans and ادرنہ as the capital — the point the speaker makes twice is that they had a capital in Europe before they had the city, so the state grew around قسطنطنیہ rather than out of it. Movement 2 (~5 min): ۸۵۷ھ / 1453 [verify] — the closed harbour, the chain, the ships moved overland, the entry, and then the part usually skipped: what was done the following week to refill and rebuild a half-empty city and turn a siege object into a working capital [SOURCE: the عثمانیہ volume's account of the taking of قسطنطنیہ and of the resettlement afterwards]. Movement 3 (~5 min): the century of سلیمان — دمشق, بغداد, مصر and the حرمین all inside one state, so four of the six anchor cities on the audience's own map now sit under one authority, with the قانون codified at home and the furthest point west reached at ویانا [verify] and not taken; here the speaker asks the hinge question and leaves it open — «چھ سو سال — کیا اتنی لمبی عمر خود اس بات کی دلیل ہے کہ اندر سب ٹھیک تھا؟» Movement 4 (~5 min): the long retreat — the first treaty in which land was given up rather than gained [verify — name and year from the source], the second attempt at ویانا [verify] as the turn, debt and outside control of revenue, تنظیمات, the Balkans going one after another, عبد الحمید ثانی deposed [verify], the war, and ۱۳۴۲ھ / 1924 [verify]; the causes are given strictly as the author's own list, introduced aloud as his — «مصنف اس کے یہ اسباب گناتے ہیں» — with nothing added by the speaker [SOURCE: the عثمانیہ volume — what the author himself names as the causes of the decline, in his own order and wording].

runsheet.block: تعارف — three sultans
runsheet.content: Three profiles, roughly two minutes each, in the fixed تراجم format the audience now expects: نام, سنین with the point marked on the Line, one sentence of what the man actually did, then «ایک واقعہ» — one incident from the source, which the audience writes into the blank line on their workbook page. Order is chronological — سلطان محمد فاتح, then سلطان سلیمان, then سلطان عبد الحمید ثانی — so the three profiles themselves trace the same arc the map has just drawn: the man who took the city, the man who governed the widest state, and the man who was deposed. سلطان محمد فاتح was previewed in one line in session 1; the speaker says so explicitly («پہلے ہفتے ہم نے صرف نام سنا تھا، آج تفصیل سے») so the regulars feel the payoff and the drop-ins are not lost. No epithet is used for any of the three beyond what the source itself uses, and no incident is told that is not on the page in front of the speaker.

runsheet.block: کیسے پتا چلا؟ — reading a number in a chronicle
runsheet.content: The speaker opens by pointing out something the audience will not have noticed: in twenty minutes of sieges, conquests and retreats he did not give them a single army size, a single casualty figure or a single library count — and that was deliberate. He then gives three questions to put to any number found in an old book: کس نے گنا اور کیا وہ موجود تھا؟ (an army of a given size has to eat and drink every day — ask what it would take to feed it); لکھنے والا کیا چاہتا تھا؟ (the besieger's chronicler and the besieged city's chronicler both have reasons to make the number larger); and تکرار ثبوت نہیں (a figure repeated in ten later books that all copied one earlier book is still one witness, not ten — the same logic the audience met in week 4 with أسماء الرجال). He closes on the constructive half: the numbers that survive scrutiny best are the ones nobody wrote to impress anyone — pay lists, ration and provisioning orders, tax registers — because a state had to hand over real money against them. [SOURCE: whether Tareekh-e-Ummat's مقدمہ or the عثمانیہ volume itself discusses weighing reported figures; if it does not, this is delivered purely as method with no figure quoted from anywhere.]

runsheet.block: آج کی بات — قومی غیرت
runsheet.content: The slide goes up headed with the attribution — «مولانا محمد اسماعیل ریحان صاحب لکھتے ہیں» — and the author's passage on قومی غیرت printed on it in full: a people that knows whose heirs it is will stand firm in the hardest trial, and a people in whom that sense has died begins producing traitors and small men in every household. [SOURCE: the author's exact wording and its page, supplied by the editor and read off the page image, not from the OCR text.] The speaker reads it once at normal pace, pauses, reads it a second time more slowly, and then says nothing at all — no gloss, no application, no example, and above all no attaching of the word «غدار» to any nation, group or period. Everyone then writes their own line in the workbook against «آج آپ کیا لے کر جا رہے ہیں؟ ______» while the room is silent, and the speaker deliberately lets the silence run rather than filling it. The conclusion of the evening belongs to the listener and to the author; it is not offered by the speaker.

runsheet.block: اگلے ہفتے — the question
runsheet.content: The speaker returns to the map, runs a finger once along tonight's whole movement — the small patch in Anatolia outward to ویانا and قاہرہ and بغداد, then back to the small patch — and says only that this is what the evening was. He then turns the map's attention east, well off the shaded area, to سندھ and the river, and notes that nothing tonight touched the land the audience is sitting in. He closes on the take-home question, says it twice so people can write it down, and does not answer it. The workbook page for session 8 is pointed out, and the room is told that next week runs from ۹۳ھ [verify] to the مغل, which is to say it starts six hundred years before tonight's story even began.

people.name: سلطان محمد فاتح
people.did: He took قسطنطنیہ in ۸۵۷ھ / 1453 [verify] and turned it from a besieged city into the capital of the state, having come to the throne young [verify reign years from the source] and having spent the years before the siege preparing the means to take it.
people.incident_plan: One incident from the first hours and days inside the city — where he went first, what he ordered concerning the people who were still in it, and how he dealt with those who had defended it against him. Told plainly, with no dialogue supplied by the speaker. [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat, the عثمانیہ volume — the author's narration of the entry into قسطنطنیہ, ۸۵۷ھ; one self-contained incident with the author's own wording, plus the reign years and death year as the book gives them. Also confirm the form of the name and the title as the book itself writes them.]

people.name: سلطان سلیمان
people.did: He ruled at the widest extent of the state [verify reign years from the source], in a reign in which the law of the state was codified at home while the frontier in the west reached ویانا [verify] and stopped there.
people.incident_plan: One incident in which the law bound the ruler himself — a case, a ruling, or an exchange with the شیخ الاسلام in which the sultan's own order was checked, corrected or refused on legal grounds, and he accepted it. This is the incident that carries the evening: it shows what the state's health actually rested on, without the speaker having to assert anything. [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat, the عثمانیہ volume — one such incident narrated by the author, with wording; if the author narrates no such incident, substitute an incident about the قانون نامہ itself. Also confirm whether the book uses «قانونی» — if it does not, the laqab is dropped and a plain factual descriptor is used instead.]

people.name: سلطان عبد الحمید ثانی
people.did: He ruled the state through its final decades of contraction and heavy debt [verify reign years from the source] and was deposed [verify], dying some years later as a private person.
people.incident_plan: The Hijaz railway — specifically the incident of its funding: that it was paid for substantially by subscriptions collected from ordinary Muslims across the world, including from this subcontinent, for a line to the حرمین. This is the incident that connects the evening to the room and to the author's passage on قومی غیرت, without any political claim being made. [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat, the عثمانیہ volume — the author's account of the Hijaz railway and its funding, with wording; and confirm his account of the deposition, which is narrated flatly and with no verdict. NOTE FOR THE EDITOR: the popular story of rails laid on felt near مدینہ is NOT to be told unless the source itself carries it, and the Palestine land-refusal account is excluded from this evening by the venue rule regardless of whether the source carries it.]

drafts.map: The same base map as every week — same projection, same six anchor cities already printed: مکہ · مدینہ · دمشق · بغداد · قرطبہ · قسطنطنیہ. Four things are added tonight, in this order, drawn live as the story moves. (1) A deliberately tiny shaded patch in north-west Anatolia, around سوگوت and بورصہ — small enough that people in the back row have to be told where to look; this is the state's whole extent at ۶۹۹ھ [verify]. (2) One arrow crossing the narrow water westward into the Balkans, ending at ادرنہ, which is labelled as the capital — drawn BEFORE قسطنطنیہ is touched, because the point is that the state was in Europe before it had the city. (3) قسطنطنیہ itself, already on the map for six weeks as somebody else's city, is filled in at ۸۵۷ھ [verify] and relabelled as the capital; the audience physically changes a city they have been drawing every week since session 1. (4) The shading then spreads outward along three named directions — north-west through بلغراد to ویانا [verify], which is marked as a dot the shading reaches but never covers; south-east to بغداد; and south through دمشق to مصر and on to مکہ and مدینہ — at which point the speaker stops and counts aloud: four of the six anchor cities on their own map are now inside one border, and قرطبہ, the fifth, has already gone in session 5. Then the retreat is drawn on the same sheet in a second colour, as the shading pulls back along exactly the lines it advanced: away from ویانا, back through بلغراد, out of the Balkans, and finally back to Anatolia — ending on very nearly the patch it started from. That closed loop is the evening's argument, and it is made by the drawing, not by the speaker. One non-territorial mark is added if time allows: a curved line running from the Atlantic around the southern tip of Africa and on to the east, drawn well outside the shaded area, to show world trade moving onto a route that no longer passes through the eastern Mediterranean at all [SOURCE: whether the author treats the ocean route among his causes — if he does not, this line is cut]. The workbook page for tonight prints only the tiny Anatolian patch and the six cities; the listener draws the outward arrows in one colour and the retreat in another, by hand, during the story.
drafts.howweknow_plan: Three minutes, delivered standing away from the map, as a single practical skill rather than a piece of theory. It opens by turning the preceding twenty minutes into the evidence: «آپ نے غور کیا؟ آج میں نے ایک بھی فوج کی تعداد نہیں بتائی، ایک بھی ہلاکتوں کا عدد نہیں بتایا، کتب خانے میں کتابوں کی گنتی نہیں بتائی۔ یہ جان بوجھ کر تھا۔» The speaker then gives three questions to put to any number in an old book, one sentence each, on three slide lines: کس نے گنا اور کیا وہ وہاں موجود تھا؟ — with the concrete test that an army has to eat and drink every single day, so ask what feeding a claimed number would actually require, and where the water was to come from; لکھنے والا اس عدد سے کیا کام لینا چاہتا تھا؟ — the chronicler of the besieging side and the chronicler of the besieged city both gain something by making the figure larger, in opposite directions; and تکرار ثبوت نہیں — ten later books carrying the same figure are ten copies of one witness, not ten witnesses, which is the same principle the audience already met in week 4 with أسماء الرجال, now applied to a number instead of a narrator. It closes on the constructive half, so the segment does not leave people merely sceptical: the figures that hold up best are the ones written for use and not for praise — pay registers, ration and provisioning orders, tax rolls — because a treasury had to pay real money against them, and a scribe who inflated them was stealing rather than boasting. The last line hands the audience a rule they can use outside the room: «عدد سنیں تو پہلا سوال یہ نہ کریں کہ کتنا — پہلا سوال یہ کریں کہ گنا کس نے۔» [SOURCE: whether Tareekh-e-Ummat's مقدمہ or the عثمانیہ volume discusses weighing reported figures; if it does, the segment is anchored to the author's own words. If it does not, it is delivered as method only, and — critically — no illustrative figure is quoted from any source, which is also what makes the segment safe to deliver before the volume is in hand.]
drafts.takehome_question: «آج ہم نے ایک ریاست کو چھ سو سال جیتے اور پھر خاموشی سے ختم ہوتے دیکھا۔ اب اگلا سوال: جس زمین پر ہم آج بیٹھے ہیں، یہاں اسلام کب اور کس راستے سے پہنچا؟ کیا وہ راستہ استنبول سے ہو کر آیا تھا — یا اُس سے صدیوں پہلے، بالکل دوسری طرف سے؟» [Tonight we watched a state live six hundred years and then end quietly. Now the next question: this land we are sitting on — when, and by which road, did Islam reach it? Did that road run through Istanbul, or did it come centuries earlier, from an entirely different direction?]

sensitive.what_arises: This is the most exposed evening in the series after session 3. Five pressure points are certain or near-certain. (1) The abolition of the caliphal office in ۱۳۴۲ھ / 1924 [verify] — a live subject for many listeners, and the one most likely to pull the room toward present-day politics and toward modern movements that campaign on it. (2) The deposition of سلطان عبد الحمید ثانی [verify], where listeners may want the speaker to name blame. (3) The Arab–Turk material of the final decades, which can turn into ethnic blame in either direction. (4) The supplied «آج کی بات» itself contains the word «غدار» — a listener could reasonably take it as an invitation to identify traitors by name, nation or sect, which is not what the passage is being read for. (5) Ottoman–Safavid warfare, which can pull the room into sectarian argument. In addition, the evening's whole subject is decline, and a room can convert a lecture on decline into a grievance meeting within two questions if the speaker allows it.
