sensitive.how_handled: Four mechanisms, all structural rather than improvised. First, the boundary is announced at minute 7, before any of the sensitive material — «ہم آج ۱۹۲۴ پر رک جائیں گے۔ اس کے بعد کی سیاست ہمارا موضوع نہیں» — so that when it is invoked from the floor at minute 43 it is a rule the room already accepted, not a dodge produced under pressure. Second, the ending is narrated and not judged: the speaker gives the author's account of what happened, in the author's order, attributed aloud as his («مصنف لکھتے ہیں»), and stops at the last sentence the author gives; no motive is assigned to any person and no verdict is passed on any of the men involved. Third, the evening's lesson is a quotation with a name and a reference on the screen, read twice and left entirely without commentary — the speaker adds no application of it to any people, present or past, and the workbook line asks the listener for their own takeaway rather than printing a conclusion. Fourth, the through-line of the session — that a long life is not the same as health — is delivered as an open question and by the shape of the drawing on the map, never as a pronouncement, so the speaker is never in the position of having authored a verdict about why Muslims declined. A one-page QA sheet with these answers written out is on the lectern, and venue management may read it in advance.
will_not_be_said: Nothing about any present-day state, government, party, leader, election or policy — in Turkey, in Pakistan, or anywhere else. The evening stops at 1924 [verify] and the speaker does not cross that line even to make a passing comparison.

No statement on whether the caliphal office should be restored, by whom, or by what means; and no mention, favourable or otherwise, of any modern movement, party or organisation that campaigns on the question.
No naming of individuals as responsible for the abolition and no verdict on them. The act is narrated as the source narrates it; the men are not tried from the platform.

Nothing on Palestine, on land sales, or on any modern territorial dispute — including the popular account of سلطان عبد الحمید ثانی refusing an offer for land, which is excluded from this evening entirely and will not be told even if a listener raises it by name.
No verdict on the Arab revolt of the final years and no ethnic blame in any direction — not Turks of Arabs, not Arabs of Turks.

No doctrinal verdict, comparison or polemic regarding صفوی Iran. If the Ottoman–Safavid wars are narrated at all it will be as a fact of the map and only if the source narrates them, with no theological comment attached.

No army sizes, no casualty figures, no library counts, and no plunder or treasury totals — not one number of that kind is spoken all evening, which is both a sourcing discipline and the setup for the «کیسے پتا چلا؟» segment.

The word «غدار» is spoken only inside the author's quoted passage, in his voice, and is not applied by the speaker to any nation, group, sect, dynasty or named person — before, during or after the reading.
No claim that the ummah's decline was caused by any single named group, and no comparison between the state's ending and any later event.
sensitive.floor_policy: Questions are taken only in the last minutes and are sorted into three boxes out loud. (1) In scope and sourced — answered in two sentences from tonight's material, then the speaker moves on. (2) In scope but not sourced — «یہ مجھے کتاب میں دیکھنا پڑے گا؛ میں لکھ رہا ہوں، اگلے ہفتے حوالے کے ساتھ بتاؤں گا۔» The question is physically written in a notebook in front of the room, and the answer genuinely comes back the following week, which is what makes the deferral credible rather than evasive. (3) Present-day politics, or a demand that the speaker pass judgement on a person, a country or a group — the pre-agreed line, said once, warmly, without irritation: «یہ مجلس تاریخ کی ہے، سیاست کی نہیں۔ ہم نے شروع میں طے کیا تھا کہ ۱۹۲۴ پر رک جائیں گے۔» Then the next question is taken immediately. If the same person presses a second time, the identical sentence is repeated word for word, with no addition and no argument, and the speaker moves on; the boundary is never debated, defended or renegotiated from the platform. Anything touching the مشاجرات is returned to the session-3 guardrail by name. If a question is hostile in tone rather than in content, it is answered as though it were sincere, briefly, and left there.

sources_needed: THE BLOCKING ITEM: the عثمانیہ volume of Tareekh-e-Ummat. Confirm which volume covers the Ottomans, obtain it, run the text-layer test, and extract it to page-marked text. Nothing in this plan can be built into a script, slide or handout until this is in hand — every [SOURCE] marker below resolves against it.

From that volume, the narrative spine for the four movements: the founding in north-west Anatolia and its date; the crossing into the Balkans and ادرنہ as capital; the taking of قسطنطنیہ and — separately — what was done to resettle and rebuild the city afterwards; the reign of سلیمان including the قانون and the western limit at ویانا; and the final century through تنظیمات to ۱۳۴۲ھ/۱۹۲۴.

The author's OWN list of the causes of Ottoman decline, in his order and his wording. The speaker delivers this list attributed aloud to the author and adds nothing to it, so the list must be transcribed exactly rather than summarised. Also confirm whether he treats the shift of world trade to the ocean route — if he does not, that line is cut from the map.

The author's account of ۱۳۴۲ھ / 1924 [verify]: the exact sequence, in what form the act was taken, and how the author himself narrates it. The speaker narrates this and stops at the author's last sentence. Also needed: whether the source carries the departure scene used in the opening (the platform, the train, the hour) — if it does not, the fallback opening is used instead.

The exact wording of the supplied «آج کی بات» — the author's passage on قومی غیرت — read off the page image rather than taken from the OCR text layer, together with its page, supplied by the editor. The OCR garbles ligatures and honorifics, so this passage must be eyeballed against the scan before it reaches a slide.

Three تعارف incidents, one per figure, in the author's own wording: (a) an incident from سلطان محمد فاتح's first hours and days inside قسطنطنیہ; (b) an incident in which the law bound سلطان سلیمان himself — a ruling, case or exchange with the شیخ الاسلام that checked his own order — or, failing that, an incident concerning the قانون نامہ; (c) the funding of the Hijaz railway by public subscription in سلطان عبد الحمید ثانی's reign, plus the author's flat account of the deposition.

Every date used this evening, checked against the source and entered in docs/catalogue/TIMELINE.md before any artifact is built: the founding year; ۸۵۷ھ/1453; the year مصر and the حرمین came under the state; both dates at ویانا; the first treaty of territorial loss and its name; the deposition; and ۱۳۴۲ھ/۱۹۲۴. Anything the source does not carry is either dropped from the script or spoken with no year attached.

The reign years and death years of the three sultans as the book gives them, and the exact Urdu forms of their names and titles as the book writes them. In particular, confirm whether the book uses «قانونی» for سلطان سلیمان — if it does not, that laqab is dropped and replaced with a plain factual descriptor from the text.

Whether Tareekh-e-Ummat's مقدمہ or the عثمانیہ volume discusses the weighing of reported figures in chronicles. If yes, the «کیسے پتا چلا؟» segment is anchored to the author's words; if no, it is delivered as method only, with no figure quoted from anywhere.

Whether the source narrates the Ottoman–Safavid wars, and in what terms. A decision is taken before the evening on whether to mention them at all; if mentioned, only as a fact of the map, with no doctrinal comment.

A written QA sheet for this session, added to docs/catalogue/QA_BANK.md before the night: prepared answers for the abolition, the deposition, the Arab revolt, the restoration question, and any invitation to name traitors — each with the short answer, the do-not-say, and the deferral line.
notes_for_speaker: THE SAFE GROUND IS THE MAP. If you lose the thread at any point in the twenty minutes, walk to the map and narrate the drawing — where the shading is now, which direction the next arrow goes. It is physical, it is in front of you, and it cannot be forgotten. The evening's whole argument is in that drawing, so narrating it is never filler.

IF YOU BLANK COMPLETELY, MOVE TO تعارف. The shape allows it and nobody in the room will know. Three profiles are self-contained, rehearsed, and printed in front of you; do them, then return to the map for the retreat.

SLOW DOWN IN FOUR PLACES: the last two sentences of the opening scene (say them and then stop — the silence is doing the work); the boundary sentence at minute 7 (once, standing still, no explanation); the moment قسطنطنیہ is filled in on the map (let people finish drawing before you speak); and the reading of the author's passage at 0:38 (read it twice, then say nothing at all, and let the writing minute run long rather than filling it).

YOU HAVE NO NUMBERS TO REMEMBER TONIGHT. That is deliberate and it removes an entire category of stage-fright. If a figure surfaces in your mind mid-sentence — an army size, a death toll, a book count — do not say it. Its absence is the point of the 0:35 segment.

IF RUNNING LONG, CUT IN THIS ORDER: first the ocean-trade line on the map; then تنظیمات down to a single sentence; then the second attempt at ویانا reduced to a dot on the map with no narration; then movement 1 compressed to two sentences (a small principality, then the crossing). NEVER CUT: تعارف, the quotation, or the writing minute. Those three are the retention system; the narrative is the part that can be thinner.

IF RUNNING SHORT, EXPAND HERE: the week after the city was taken — resettlement, rebuilding, and what it takes to turn a captured city into a working capital. It is the least-told part of the story, it is safe, and it is where the source will give you the most material.

FALLBACK OPENING, if the source does not carry the departure scene: open instead on the frontier at the beginning — a small principality in Anatolia, one of several of the same kind, and the plain fact that nobody now remembers the names of the others. Then the question: why did this one last six hundred years, and did lasting mean it was well? Rehearse both openings; walk in knowing which one you are using.

THE THROUGH-LINE IS A QUESTION, NOT A VERDICT. You are not to announce that length is not health. You ask it once, in the middle of the story, and then you let the map answer it by ending where it started. Do not close that loop verbally at 0:42 — point at the drawing and stop talking. If you find yourself building to a conclusion, that is the moment to stop.

REHEARSE THE LAST FOUR SENTENCES OF THE STORY OUT LOUD, WORD FOR WORD, AND SAY THEM THE SAME WAY EVERY TIME. The ending is the hardest passage in the series to deliver without editorialising, and it is exactly where nerves will push you into adding something. Write those four sentences on the cue card verbatim.

THE BOUNDARY IS NEVER DEBATED. You said it at minute 7; you repeat it word for word if pressed, once, and then take the next question. You do not justify it, you do not soften it, and you do not make an exception for a listener who seems sincere. Repeating an agreed rule calmly reads as authority in the room; arguing about it reads as weakness.

WHEN YOU READ THE PASSAGE ON قومی غیرت, ADD NOTHING. No example, no application, no 'aur aaj bhi'. The word «غدار» is the author's and stays the author's. If the room looks at you expecting the application, look back and let them write. That restraint is the most respected thing you will do all evening.

drafts.title: یہ ہم تک کیسے پہنچا
drafts.gloss: How Islam reached this land, and what was built here
drafts.era: ۹۳–۱۱۱۹ھ — سندھ، غزنوی و غوری، سلطنتِ دہلی، مغل
drafts.summary: Session 8 is the evening the course crosses from the Muslim heartlands to the ground the audience is standing on: from سندھ at ۹۳ھ [verify] to the close of the Mughal century at ۱۱۱۹ھ [verify], drawn on a map panel added east of بغداد for the first time in ten weeks. It is, after session 1, the evening this particular room will care most about — which is exactly why the plan does not pretend to more than it has. No source volume for this period is in hand: the course's named source has not yet been confirmed to cover South Asia at all, so the three تعارف people, every date and every incident below are proposals to be replaced by whatever the text actually says, and are marked as such rather than filled in with confident narration. The two blocks that are fully sourced today — «کیسے پتا چلا؟» on روایہ and درایہ, and the «آج کی بات» quotation from مولانا شمس الحق افغانیؒ — carry the evening, and the روایہ/درایہ teaching is used deliberately so that "میں یہ اُس وقت کہوں گا جب کتاب سامنے ہو" becomes a respectable answer for the whole night rather than an apology.
drafts.opening_scene: The speaker begins with one man at a writing desk in this land, setting down what he saw with his own eyes — تزکِ بابری, the memoir of the founder of the Mughal state. He tells the room that this book is not his own choice of example: the course's own source names it when it lists the four kinds of material a historian works from, and the first of those four is what the historian himself witnessed [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1, المقدمہ — the section تاریخ نگاری کے مآخذ, where تزکِ بابری is given as the example of مؤرخ کا اپنا ذاتی مشاہدہ; exact wording to be read off the page image, not the OCR]. So for the first time in this course we are in a period where a ruler's own handwriting survives, where the archives are full of فرامین and records, and where the buildings are still standing and most people in this room have walked through them. Then the speaker closes the book and asks the room a question that has no book behind it: does anyone here know when, and through whom, their own family became Muslim? Nobody is asked to answer aloud and the speaker does not fill the pause — that silence, in a room this well documented, is the subject of the evening.

runsheet.block: آغاز — the Line and the Map
runsheet.content: The wall banner and the base map go up as every week. The speaker states plainly that tonight the course does the one thing it has not done yet: it turns around. Last week ended at استنبول in ۱۹۲۴; tonight we go back to ۹۳ھ [verify] and we go east, because we have been following the thread that went west and north, and tonight we follow the thread that arrives here. Attendees mark session 8 on their own Line twice — once at ۹۳ھ [verify] and once at ۱۱۱۹ھ [verify] — because tonight is a span, not a point; the blank eastern panel is taped onto the right edge of the wall map while they do it.

runsheet.block: The opening — a scene
runsheet.content: تزکِ بابری: a ruler in this land writing down what he saw himself, named by the course's own source as its example of eyewitness material [SOURCE: as above]. The speaker draws out the contrast — an unusually well-recorded period, with memoirs, فرامین, inscriptions and standing buildings the room has visited. He then asks the room, without asking for an answer, when and through whom their own family became Muslim, and lets the silence sit. He does not resolve it; he says only that this is the question the evening walks toward.

runsheet.block: The story — سندھ to the Mughal century, with the map moving
runsheet.content: Four beats of five minutes, each ending with a mark on the map. (۱) After ۹۳ھ [verify]: what actually happened to سندھ once the campaign the room met in session 4 was over — the towns, and the plain fact that for a long stretch afterwards the frontier did not move much further east [SOURCE: the volume covering سندھ after the conquest — the extent and duration of Muslim rule there, and what the source says was and was not established]. (۲) The door shifts from the sea to the passes: غزنی, then لاہور becomes a Muslim city with scholars living in it and a major book written there; then غور, and دہلی becomes a capital [SOURCE: the Ghaznavid and Ghurid chapters — when لاہور and دہلی became capitals, and what the source records being founded in them]. (۳) دہلی as a Muslim capital for roughly six centuries: what was built — a قاضی system, madrasas, mosques, a currency; the Mongol pressure that reaches the Indus in the same decades the room watched بغداد fall in ۶۵۶ھ [verify], and whether the source records scholars and books moving east ahead of it; then the spread outward to بنگال, گجرات, دکن and کشمیر, and the source's own account of how ordinary people of this land came to Islam [SOURCE: the Sultanate chapters — institutions, the Mongol frontier, the eastward movement of scholars, and above all any passage on the means by which the population became Muslim]. (۴) The Mughal century: an empire administered from آگرہ, دہلی and لاہور, what was built and compiled here, and the scholarly current running alongside the court, closing at ۱۱۱۹ھ [verify] where session 9 will pick up [SOURCE: the Mughal chapters — administration, the works compiled, and the ʿulamā of the period].

runsheet.block: تعارف — three people (PROVISIONAL, subject to the source)
runsheet.content: Three people in the fixed تراجم format — نام و نسب with only the لقب the tradition gave, سنین and their point on the Line, one sentence on what they did, and ONE authentic incident from the source, which the room writes into the blank line in the workbook. Proposed: حضرت علی بن عثمان الہجویری رحمہ اللہ · سلطان شمس الدین التتمش · حضرت شیخ احمد سرہندی رحمہ اللہ. All three are placeholders chosen to cover the scholar, the state and the late period; every one of them, and every date and incident attached to them, is replaced by whatever the source volume carries. No profile is spoken aloud until its incident is page-cited from the text.

runsheet.block: کیسے پتا چلا؟ — روایہ اور درایہ
runsheet.content: Two columns on one slide. تاریخ بالروایہ: the narration is passed on as received, with its chain, and the historian adds nothing — the source names the classical works written this way and says the reader is left to judge, which is also its weakness, since a reader without the اصول can be misled. تاریخ بالدرایہ: the historian links a few reports and indications and reconstructs — no absurdity survives, but there is no firm floor either, since he keeps what he likes and drops what he likes. The speaker then reads the source's own example of درایہ-built history, which happens to be the ground under this room, and closes on the third and best way — روایہ and درایہ together, with the narrations as the base, each weighed by reason, and a doubtful report flagged to the reader as doubtful [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1, المقدمہ — the section تاریخ نویسی کے انداز: the three modes, the books named under each, the restraints placed on درایہ, and the ٹیکسلا/موئن جو دڑو example; all wording and every book title to be read off the page image, since OCR garbles both].

runsheet.block: آج کی بات — مولانا شمس الحق افغانیؒ
runsheet.content: The slide is headed «مولانا شمس الحق افغانیؒ فرماتے ہیں» with the reference printed beneath, and carries the four requisites in his order: ماضی سے ارتباط · وحدتِ فکر و عمل · فراہمیِ اسبابِ قوت · جہدِ مسلسل — each resting on the one before it, so the connection with the past is the first link [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1, المقدمہ — the passage quoting مولانا شمس الحق افغانیؒ's four requisites, plus the footnote reference the book itself supplies; wording read off the page image]. The speaker reads it, names it as the same quotation the course opened with in session 1, and says nothing of his own about it. Then everyone writes their own line in the workbook: «آج آپ کیا لے کر جا رہے ہیں؟ ______». Sixty seconds of silence while pens move — the speaker does not talk over it.

runsheet.block: اگلے ہفتے — closing on a question
runsheet.content: The speaker puts the marker on the Line at ۱۱۱۹ھ [verify] and says next week the course reaches ۱۸۵۷ to ۱۹۴۷ — the only stretch in the whole ten weeks that is still inside living family memory in this room. He then closes on the take-home question and stops; no summary, no moral, no recap of the evening. Catch-up sheets for drop-ins are on the back table as always.

people.name: حضرت علی بن عثمان الہجویری رحمہ اللہ
people.did: He settled in لاہور in the Ghaznavid period and wrote کشف المحجوب there — by the standard account the earliest full Persian work of its kind produced in this land, and still read [SOURCE: needed].
people.incident_plan: One incident, three sentences, from his own account of his years and travels or from the source's notice of him — chosen for what it shows about teaching and writing in لاہور, not for a karāmah. No karāmāt narrated unless the named source narrates them, and no ruling of any kind given on مزارات or on what is done at them. Reasoning for the choice: he answers the evening's question from the side the room least expects — a book, not an army — and he stands on the audience's own soil, which makes him the natural first of the three. [SOURCE: the volume's notice of علی ہجویری رحمہ اللہ — his سنین, one page-cited incident, and confirmation that the لقب داتا گنج بخش is the title the tradition gave and how it is attested; if the source does not carry the لقب, the field is left empty and he is named factually as مصنفِ کشف المحجوب]

people.name: سلطان شمس الدین التتمش
people.did: He turned the new Muslim rule at دہلی from a garrison into a state — a capital, a currency and a قاضی system — and received formal recognition from the Abbasid caliph at بغداد [SOURCE: needed].
people.incident_plan: The arrival of the caliph's investiture at دہلی told as one scene: what was sent, who carried it, what was read out and where. It is chosen because it is the single moment that joins this land to the thread the room has been following for seven weeks — the same بغداد they watched fall in ۶۵۶ھ [verify] in session 6. Reasoning: the state side of the evening needs one representative and he is the least contested candidate in the Sultanate centuries; محمد بن قاسم is deliberately not reused, having already been introduced in session 4. [SOURCE: the source's account of the Abbasid investiture — the year, the caliph's name, what was actually conferred, and the correct Urdu spelling of التتمش as the book prints it]

people.name: حضرت شیخ احمد سرہندی رحمہ اللہ
people.did: In the Mughal period he worked to hold the ʿulamā's ground at a court that had moved away from it, and his مکتوبات became the most widely circulated scholarly correspondence produced in this land [SOURCE: needed].
people.incident_plan: One incident from the مکتوبات or from the source's account of his dealings with the court, narrated exactly as the source narrates it and stopped there — no verdict passed on any ruler, no entry into the وحدت الوجود / وحدت الشہود discussion, no takfir of anyone. Reasoning: he closes the evening's arc on a scholar rather than a throne and hands directly to session 9, which already opens on شاہ ولی اللہ رحمہ اللہ. ALTERNATE if the source's coverage makes a ruler the better third: اورنگزیب عالمگیر, with the compilation of فتاویٰ عالمگیری as the institutional achievement and nothing said about the succession war — in which case شیخ احمد سرہندی رحمہ اللہ moves to the opening of session 9. [SOURCE: the volume's notice — سنین, one page-cited incident, and whether the book itself uses the لقب مجدد الف ثانی]

drafts.map: For the first time in the course the frame extends east of بغداد: a blank panel is taped onto the right edge of the wall map during آغاز, and the same panel is blank in the workbook so attendees draw it themselves. The six anchor cities (مکہ · مدینہ · دمشق · بغداد · قرطبہ · قسطنطنیہ) stay exactly where they have been for seven weeks — nothing already drawn is erased. Five movements are added, in this order. (۱) A sea arrow, west to east, from the Arabian coast to the mouth of the Indus, with dots at the delta, منصورہ and ملتان, dated ۹۳ھ [verify] and labelled "session 4 — we were here"; the shading around it is then deliberately left small, to show the frontier standing roughly still for a long stretch afterwards. (۲) An overland arrow, north-west to south-east, from خراسان through غزنی and the passes down to لاہور — لاہور is the first new dot on the eastern panel and a small book symbol is drawn beside it for کشف المحجوب. (۳) A short arrow غور ← دہلی; دہلی is drawn as a capital dot the same size as دمشق and بغداد were drawn in earlier weeks — the visual equivalence is the point and the speaker says so. (۴) The Mongol sweep line already drawn in session 6 is extended eastward and stopped at the Indus, with a second thin arrow from بخارا and سمرقند toward دہلی for scholars and books moving ahead of it [SOURCE/verify]; then shading spreads outward from دہلی toward بنگال, گجرات, دکن and کشمیر across the Sultanate centuries. (۵) An arrow کابل ← پانی پت ← آگرہ, and Mughal shading over most of the subcontinent by ۱۱۱۹ھ [verify]. Last of all, in a different colour, a single dot is placed for the venue's own city — لاہور or کراچی, set to wherever the course is actually delivered — the only mark on the whole map that is not historical. The speaker places it, says nothing, and moves on.
drafts.howweknow_plan: Three minutes, one slide, two columns, delivered off material already in hand from the muqaddima — this is the most secure block of the evening and the speaker should know it is. Column one, تاریخ بالروایہ: the report is passed on as received with its chain, the historian adding no comment, so his hands are clean and the judgement is left to the reader; the source names the classical works built this way, and names the weakness too — implausible material can travel along with the sound, and a reader who does not know the اصول can be badly misled by it. Column two, تاریخ بالدرایہ: the historian takes a few reports and physical remains and reasons his way to a connected account; nothing absurd survives, but there is no firm floor, because he keeps what suits his estimate and drops what does not. The hook that makes the room sit up: the source's own example of history built this way is the reconstruction of ancient sites — and among the sites it names are ٹیکسلا and موئن جو دڑو, which is to say the ground under this building. Then the resolution: the source's own rules for restraining درایہ — a widely transmitted report is not thrown out on reasoning alone, a weak one is set aside only if it contains something impossible or grossly unreasonable, and mere strangeness is no ground at all, since history mostly records the unusual. Best of the three is روایہ and درایہ together: narrations as the base, each weighed by reason, doubtful ones flagged to the reader as doubtful. The speaker closes by connecting it to tonight without labouring it: this is why the detailed narration of this period waits for the book, and why "میں یہ اُس وقت کہوں گا جب کتاب سامنے ہو" is not an excuse but the method. [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1, المقدمہ — the section تاریخ نویسی کے انداز covering all three modes, every book title listed under each, the restraints on درایہ, and the excavation example; and the adjacent section تاریخ نگاری کے مآخذ for the four kinds of material used in the opening scene. All wording and all book titles to be read off the page image — OCR garbles Arabic titles and honorifics badly.]
drafts.takehome_question: «آپ کے گھر میں سب سے پرانی بات کس کو یاد ہے؟ اگلے ہفتے ہم اُس زمانے میں پہنچ رہے ہیں جو آپ کے بزرگوں نے خود دیکھا تھا — اِس ہفتے ایک بار پوچھ لیجیے۔» [Who in your house remembers the oldest thing? Next week we reach the years your own elders lived through — this week, ask them, once.]

sensitive.what_arises: The planned narration is low-risk; the questions this evening invites are the highest-risk of the course after session 3. Five things sit inside it. (۱) Conquest and conversion — "was Islam spread here by the sword?", which will be asked either defensively or sceptically, and which the evening's own central question makes unavoidable. (۲) Temples and rulers — محمود غزنوی, and Mughal-era policy; live polemic in both directions and easily turned into a comment on present-day India. (۳) Shrines and تصوف — naming علی ہجویری رحمہ اللہ and the Chishti scholars touches the Barelvi–Deobandi fault line, which in a mixed DHA room is a real risk with no upside. (۴) Sect and community — the early Ismaili presence in سندھ and ملتان is part of the period's history, and the room may contain members of living communities descended from it. (۵) Ancestry — the opening question about when a family became Muslim brushes against biraderi, caste and claims of Arab or Persian descent. Separately, if تزکِ بابری is used in the opening, someone may raise بابری مسجد.
sensitive.how_handled: The governing rule is the one installed in session 3 and repeated tonight in one sentence: تاریخِ اسلام = تاریخِ مسلمین — the political and military acts of rulers are narrated as the acts of Muslims, not as the acts of the religion, and the source itself draws that line. On top of that: (۱) the evening narrates what the source narrates and stops, and where the source is silent the speaker says it is silent, which the روایہ/درایہ block has already made respectable; (۲) the ancestry question is asked rhetorically, nobody is invited to answer aloud, and the speaker moves on before anyone volunteers; (۳) the two scholars are presented strictly in the تراجم format — سنین, what they did, one incident from the source — with nothing said about practices at shrines in any direction; (۴) no living community, sect, party or country is named anywhere in the evening; (۵) the course's stated end point is ۱۹۴۷ and anything after it is out of scope by design, which is the standing answer to بابری مسجد, Kashmir and anything current. QA_BANK entries for the sword question, the temples question and the shrines question are written and rehearsed before the night, not improvised.
will_not_be_said: No general claim in either direction about how the population of this land became Muslim — not "by the sword" and not "never by the sword". The evening narrates what the source narrates about specific events and says plainly where the source is silent.
Nothing describing Hindu belief, practice or scripture. The course does not describe other religions in its own voice at any point.
No comparison of Muslim rule here with British rule, with any present-day government, or with any other period, as better or worse.
No mention of بابری مسجد, ایودھیا, Kashmir, the 1947 boundary disputes, or any post-1947 matter — out of the course's stated scope.
No ruling, opinion or aside on تصوف, بدعت, شرک, or visiting مزارات; no description of what people do at shrines.
No takfir of anyone, no verdict on any ruler's faith, and no adjudication of the Mughal succession disputes.
No naming of any present-day sect, community, party, institution, political figure, or the army.
No casualty figures, no numbers of converts, no "lakhs" or "millions" — no quantity is stated that is not on a page of the source.
No claim that any specific building standing today was or was not built on the site of something else.
sensitive.floor_policy: Three tiers, rehearsed as three fixed sentences. (۱) In the source and in scope: answer by narrating what the book says, name the book, and stop — do not extend the answer past where the page ends. (۲) Belongs to a later session: warm deferral naming the session — «یہ اگلے ہفتے کا موضوع ہے، ۱۸۵۷ کے بعد کا — تب تفصیل سے بات کریں گے» — and then genuinely return to it next week, or the room stops believing the deferral. (۳) Contemporary politics, or a request for a ruling: one prepared sentence — «یہ مسئلہ تاریخ کا نہیں، فتویٰ کا ہے — اور میں مفتی نہیں ہوں» — then move to the next hand without softening it. This week there is a fourth, and it is the important one: for any question of detail about this period, the honest answer is «کتاب ابھی میرے سامنے نہیں ہے، میں اندازے سے نہیں بولوں گا». That answer costs the speaker nothing tonight, because ten minutes earlier he taught the room the difference between a narration and an estimate. If a question is heated rather than curious, the speaker takes it after the session rather than on the floor, and says so plainly.

sources_needed: BLOCKING GATE, needed before anything else: written confirmation of whether Tareekh-e-Ummat covers Muslim South Asia at all, and in which volume(s) — taken from the publisher's own volume listing, not inferred. Every other item below branches on this answer.

IF IT DOES: the volume(s) covering the four sub-periods, with printed page ranges for each — (a) سندھ after ۹۳ھ, (b) غزنوی و غوری, (c) سلطنتِ دہلی, (d) مغل to ۱۱۱۹ھ. Extracted to page-marked text so every claim in the script is greppable to a printed page before the deck is built.

IF IT DOES NOT: a decision on ONE named Sunni second spine, announced openly on the slide rather than quietly mixed in — the course's own rule. Candidates for the editor to evaluate (named only as candidates; no claim is attached to any of them here and titles and authorship must be confirmed before use): سید ابو الحسن علی ندوی رحمہ اللہ's work on the reform and scholarly tradition of the subcontinent; شیخ محمد اکرام's trilogy on Muslim South Asia; a primary Persian chronicle of the Sultanate and Mughal periods in a reliable Urdu translation. One is chosen, named on the slide, and used for the whole of sessions 8 and 9.

The single most important passage to locate, because the evening is built on it: does the source say anything about HOW the ordinary people of this land became Muslim — traders, scholars, the Chishti and other teachers, intermarriage, settlement? If the source addresses it, the story block is rebuilt around that passage. If the source is silent, the evening must say so out loud rather than fill the space.

For the story block, specifically: (a) the extent and duration of Muslim rule in سندھ after the conquest and what the source says was established there; (b) when لاہور and دہلی became Muslim capitals and under whom; (c) what the source records the Sultanate building — قاضی system, madrasas, mosques, currency; (d) whether the source records scholars or books moving east ahead of the Mongols after ۶۵۶ھ, which is the link back to session 6 and must not be asserted without it; (e) what the Mughal chapters record being built and compiled, and which ʿulamā the source treats as significant in that century.

For تعارف, for each of the three proposed people: نام و نسب as the book prints it, سنین in ھ and عیسوی, one sentence on what they did, and ONE authentic incident with a printed page. Also: whether the book itself uses the لقب داتا گنج بخش and مجدد الف ثانی, and how each is attested — if the book does not carry a لقب, the field stays empty and the person is described factually instead.

A date list to be taken from the source rather than from general knowledge, since every date in this plan currently carries [verify]: ۹۳ھ; the Ghaznavid arrival at لاہور; the founding of the Sultanate at دہلی; the Mongol arrival at the Indus; پانی پت; and ۱۱۱۹ھ as the closing boundary. Nothing goes on a slide until it is in docs/catalogue/TIMELINE.md with its source.

For «کیسے پتا چلا؟» (already held, but must be read off the page image, not the OCR): the muqaddima section تاریخ نویسی کے انداز — the three modes, every book title listed under each, the restraints placed on درایہ, and the excavation example naming ٹیکسلا and موئن جو دڑو. OCR garbles the Arabic titles and the third mode's heading badly; the printed page image is the only acceptable source for the wording.

For the opening scene (already held, same caution): the muqaddima section تاریخ نگاری کے مآخذ — the four kinds of historical material, and the exact sentence naming تزکِ بابری as the example of a historian's own observation.

For «آج کی بات» (already held, same caution): the exact wording of مولانا شمس الحق افغانیؒ's four requisites as the book prints them, in the book's order, plus the footnote reference the book itself supplies for them — verified by eye, since this line is quoted on screen with its attribution and is the one thing in the evening that must be word-perfect.

QA_BANK entries written and rehearsed before the night for three questions in the exact words they will be asked: the sword question, the temples question, and the shrines question. Plus the standing deferral sentence for anything after ۱۹۴۷.

Correct Urdu orthography, as the chosen source prints them, for every proper name that will appear on a slide — التتمش, ہجویری, سرہندی, منصورہ, پانی پت — so that no two artifacts in the repo disagree.
notes_for_speaker: Know where the solid ground is. Two blocks are fully sourced from material already in hand: «کیسے پتا چلا؟» and «آج کی بات». If anything goes wrong tonight it will not be in those seven minutes. Rehearse them until they are automatic, and use them as the place to steady yourself.

If the source volume has not arrived by rehearsal day, deliver the fallback shape: say once, at the top, that tonight's narration is at the level of the map and that the detail waits for the book; then run the story on geography and sequence alone and let تعارف carry the human material at whatever depth the text supports. Announce it once, plainly, and do not apologise a second time — a room forgives a stated limit and distrusts a repeated one.

Slow down twice. First at the ancestors question in the opening: ask it, then stop. The pause is doing the work and filling it wastes the best thirty seconds of the evening. Second when the eastern panel goes onto the wall map — let people look at it before you start drawing on it.
If you blank during the story, go straight to تعارف. The fixed shape exists for exactly this and nobody in the room knows the running order but you.

What to cut if you are running long: the spread to بنگال, گجرات, دکن and کشمیر becomes one sentence instead of three; the second person's incident is shortened; the ٹیکسلا and موئن جو دڑو aside is dropped if the room is not with you. Never cut: the map movement, the ancestors question, the four requisites, or the minute of silence while people write.

"I don't know" is a complete sentence tonight, and it is the strongest thing you can say. Ten minutes before any hard question lands, you will have taught this room the difference between a narration and an estimate. Applying that rule to yourself in front of them is worth more than any answer you could improvise.

Nothing about present-day India or Pakistan leaves your mouth, however the question is framed and however warmly it is asked. The three prepared sentences in the QA bank cover it. Use them verbatim — that is why they were written down.

Read every proper name aloud twice in rehearsal. التتمش, ہجویری, سرہندی and منصورہ are the likeliest stumbles, and a name fumbled in the تعارف block is the one thing that will rattle you at the exact moment you need to be calm.

Do not add a lesson. The evening's one lesson is مولانا شمس الحق افغانیؒ's, it is on the screen with his name on it, and the listener writes their own line underneath. Anything you add on top of that is your opinion, and this course does not carry your opinion.

drafts.title: ۱۸۵۷ سے ۱۹۴۷ تک
drafts.gloss: Ninety years: from the end of one order to the beginning of another
drafts.summary: Session 9 covers the ninety years from 1857 [verify] to 1947 [verify] in the subcontinent — the period closest to living memory and the only evening of the ten that touches politics people in the room still argue about. It is built deliberately as a narrative of institutions and teaching rather than of parties: what ended in Delhi, what was built afterwards, and how the line of learning that runs back to شاہ ولی اللہ رحمہ اللہ carried through. The evening states its own stopping line aloud in the first three minutes — the narrative ends at 1947 [verify] and nothing after that date is discussed, from the platform or from the floor. One warning before management reads further: no source for this period is in hand yet. Every factual claim below is marked [SOURCE: ...] and the session cannot be written, let alone delivered, until the volume or the named second work listed in sources_needed is obtained; the only segment already covered by material in hand is «کیسے پتا چلا؟».
drafts.opening_scene: The evening opens in دہلی, in the weeks after the city changed hands in ۱۸۵۷ [verify]. The speaker stands still and describes one thing only, at the level of a single street: what happened there to books and to teaching — the schools attached to the mosques, the households in which Arabic and Persian were read aloud every day, the private libraries and where they went [SOURCE: a named work's description of Delhi in the months immediately after ۱۸۵۷ — what closed, what was dispersed, what was sold, and what a household of that class actually owned]. Nothing is said in this block about the fighting, and nothing is said about who won. The scene ends with two plain facts set beside each other: this city had been a centre of Muslim learning and Muslim rule in this land for centuries, and inside one lifetime it was neither. The question left hanging is the one the whole evening answers — in the ninety years that follow, who decides what the children of that street will be taught, and who writes down what happened to them?

runsheet.block: آغاز — the Line and the Map go up
runsheet.content: The banner timeline and the wall map are re-hung and the speaker says the one sentence that catches a drop-in: last week we ended with the Mughal state in this land [SOURCE: session 8's exact endpoint, as fixed by its own source]; tonight we cross ninety years, ۱۸۵۷ to ۱۹۴۷ [verify]. He marks two new pegs on the banner in front of the room and everyone marks the same two pegs in their own workbook. He then says the evening's stopping rule out loud, once, in one sentence — the narrative ends at ۱۹۴۷ [verify]; we will say what the books say and where they differ we will say that too; and we do not sit in judgment between Muslims who chose differently. Drop-ins are handed the catch-up sheet while this is said.

runsheet.block: Opening scene — دہلی after ۱۸۵۷
runsheet.content: The scene described above is delivered standing still, with no slide behind it except the word دہلی and the year [verify]. The speaker narrates only what the source carries about the city's teaching and its books, and refuses the temptation to explain causes here — causes belong to the story block. He closes on the hanging question about who taught the next generation and who wrote the record, and moves straight to the map without a pause for effect.

runsheet.block: The story — ninety years in four movements
runsheet.content: Movement one (about 5 minutes): what ended — the formal end of the Mughal name and the beginning of direct Crown rule [verify], with the map panel going to one flat colour as it is said [SOURCE: the sequence and the source's own naming of the events of ۱۸۵۷ — the name it uses must be read off the page, since books of this period use different names for the same event]. Movement two: the answers given afterwards, narrated as founding facts only — the seminary at دیوبند and the college at علی گڑھ, each with its founder's name, its year and its stated purpose, in the source's words, with two short arrows drawn out of دہلی and no comparison of the two [SOURCE: founders, years, stated purposes; also whether the source treats these institutions comparatively — if it ranks them we still report only the founding facts]. Movement three: how educational work became political work, taken up to the خلافت movement and the long arrow west across the base map to استنبول, which lands on the peg this audience drew in week 7 [SOURCE: the movement's dates, what it actually demanded, its connection to استنبول and how it ended]. Movement four: ۱۹۴۰ [verify] to ۱۹۴۷ [verify] — the resolution at لاہور, the years of negotiation, the boundary drawn, the two wings, and the movement of people across the line in both directions, stated as direction and scale of movement and nothing more [SOURCE: a fair summary or the text of the ۱۹۴۰ resolution, the sequence of ۱۹۴۷, and an atlas we can name for the boundary].

runsheet.block: تعارف — three people, four lines each
runsheet.content: Three profiles at roughly two minutes twenty each, in the fixed تراجم shape: نام و نسب with only the title the tradition gave, سنین with the point marked on the Line, one sentence on what the person did, then ایک واقعہ — a single authentic incident read from the source. The workbook prints the first three lines and leaves ایک واقعہ blank; the listener writes it while the speaker tells it, and that writing is the retention mechanism. The speaker says one rehearsed sentence explaining why شاہ ولی اللہ رحمہ اللہ appears in an evening that begins in ۱۸۵۷ [verify] — he lived before these ninety years, and the evening starts upstream of them because the teaching line that runs through the whole period runs back to his household [SOURCE: a named work that itself traces that line, so the connection is the book's and not ours].

runsheet.block: کیسے پتا چلا؟ — history read outside its own rules
runsheet.content: The speaker holds the book open in his hand for this block, because it is the one part of the evening drawn from a text already in the room. He states the source's claim — that history read against its own اصول does not merely leave a reader uninformed, it leaves him estranged from his own past and cold towards his forebears — then tells the source's own bus-stop illustration in about sixty seconds, and names the two causes the source gives for a wrong reading. He lands it on tonight's period in one sentence and closes by reading the author's own words [SOURCE: exact wording of the passage on the harms of reading history outside its rules, read off the page image rather than the text layer, which garbles it].

runsheet.block: آج کی بات — the supplied quotation, then everyone writes
runsheet.content: The slide is headed by the attribution — مولانا محمد اسماعیل ریحان — and carries his own sentences: that without the study of history we cannot know the methods of those who work against us, and that only deep study lets us answer what is put out about us in the name of history [SOURCE: the exact printed wording of these two sentences from the author's numbered list of the benefits of history, read off the page image; plus the editor's decision on which of the two sentences goes on the screen]. The speaker reads it once, adds one sentence of frame — that this is about method, about how history is written and answered — and adds nothing else; the conclusion is the author's, not his. Then ninety seconds of quiet while every person writes their own line under «آج آپ کیا لے کر جا رہے ہیں؟ ______» in the workbook. The speaker does not fill the silence.

runsheet.block: اگلے ہفتے — close on a question
runsheet.content: The speaker says what next week is: the last evening, where the whole map goes back up complete, the ten written سبق are read out together, and everyone leaves with a reading path. He asks the audience to bring their workbook, because next week they read their own handwriting aloud. Then he puts up the take-home question and stops talking — no summary of tonight, no closing statement.

people.name: شاہ ولی اللہ رحمہ اللہ
people.did: He taught hadith in دہلی in the generation before these ninety years and put the Qur'an into the language the people around him actually read, and the teaching line that runs through the whole of tonight's period runs back to his household.
people.incident_plan: One documented incident from his teaching life — an exchange with a student, a decision about what to teach or translate, or a stated reason for a piece of his work; not a summary of his thought. He is positioned as the evening's upstream figure: his mark goes on the Line inside last week's stretch, and tonight an arrow is drawn from that mark forward into ۱۸۵۷, so that a drop-in understands he is why the ninety years had a spine, not part of the ninety years. [SOURCE: his سنین in ھ and عیسوی; confirmation that محدث دہلوی is the title the adopted source itself uses for him; ONE authentic incident with a locatable place in the text; and a named work that itself states the line of transmission from him to the scholars of the post-۱۸۵۷ generation — e.g. تاریخ دعوت و عزیمت — so that the connection is the book's claim and not ours]

people.name: شیخ الہند مولانا محمود حسن رحمہ اللہ
people.did: He taught at the seminary at دیوبند, trained the generation of scholars who ran through the rest of the period, and was imprisoned overseas by the British during the First World War [verify].
people.incident_plan: The single incident is the imprisonment and the return — where he was taken, how long he was held, and what he did on his return, told plainly with no political conclusion drawn. Proposed because he is the visible link from شاہ ولی اللہ رحمہ اللہ's line to the end of the period, because شیخ الہند is a title the tradition already gave him so nothing has to be coined, and because his one incident involves no dispute between Muslims. Risk the editor must weigh: he is identified with one maslak, and this room contains several — if that is judged a problem, the alternate is a scholar of the خلافت decade named by whichever source is adopted. [SOURCE: سنین; one authentic incident with dates and place, from a named Sunni biography rather than assembled from general knowledge; and confirmation that the adopted source carries him at all]

people.name: علامہ محمد اقبال رحمہ اللہ
people.did: A lawyer and poet of لاہور whose poetry and whose address of ۱۹۳۰ [verify] gave this period much of the vocabulary in which it argued with itself.
people.incident_plan: One documented incident from his life — a specific occasion, a recorded exchange, or the circumstances in which a particular piece of work was written — not a reading of his poetry and not an interpretation of his thought. Proposed because he is honoured across every maslak likely to be in the room, which makes him the safest available third, and because he carries the evening from the scholarly line to the political outcome without requiring the speaker to narrate party politics. Alternate, if the editor wants the founder of the country in the trio rather than only in the narrative: محمد علی جناح — but note this raises the evening's political temperature and requires prepared answers about his personal practice before it is agreed. [SOURCE: سنین; ONE authentic incident with a citable location in a named biography]

drafts.map: The base map is unchanged — the same projection and the same six anchor cities the audience has been drawing since week 1 (مکہ · مدینہ · دمشق · بغداد · قرطبہ · قسطنطنیہ), with the subcontinent panel that session 8 added on the right (سندھ → لاہور → دہلی and the Mughal extent). Tonight everything happens on that right-hand panel, and it moves five times. (1) دہلی is ringed, and a short arrow is drawn میرٹھ → دہلی for the start of ۱۸۵۷ [verify], with the affected band shaded [SOURCE: an atlas or a named work for the extent of the rising — not drawn from memory]. (2) The whole panel is then washed to one flat colour as direct Crown rule is stated [verify]: one government, one colour, from the Khyber to Bengal — that single stroke is the first movement's whole point. (3) Two short arrows go outward from دہلی to two small towns, one to دیوبند and one to علی گڑھ, drawn at the same moment and in the same weight, so that neither is visually favoured. (4) The one long arrow of the evening leaves the panel and travels west across the base map, over دمشق, to استنبول, for the خلافت movement [verify] — it lands on the peg this same audience drew in week 7, and a cross is put on استنبول for ۱۹۲۴ [verify]. (5) لاہور is dotted for ۱۹۴۰ [verify]; then the boundary of ۱۹۴۷ [verify] is drawn in one continuous stroke through پنجاب and بنگال, producing a west wing and an east wing, and two arrows are drawn across that line, one in each direction, for the movement of people. The last mark of the evening is the city this course is sitting in, put on the map by the speaker and copied by everyone into their workbook. On the Line: two new pegs, ۱۸۵۷ and ۱۹۴۷ [verify], plus an arrow entering from the left out of شاہ ولی اللہ رحمہ اللہ's mark, which sits back in last week's stretch. The banner reaches its final peg tonight; session 10 adds none.
drafts.howweknow_plan: Three minutes, one line of text on the screen, and the book open in the speaker's hand — this is the only segment of the evening whose source is already in the room, and the speaker should say so, because it is the moment his sourcing discipline is visible. Sequence. First the claim, in the author's frame: a good thing used against its own rules turns harmful, and history read outside its اصول does not just leave a person uninformed — it leaves him بے زار from his own past and cold towards those who came before him [SOURCE: the exact wording of that sentence, read off the page image, not the text layer]. Second, the source's own illustration, told in about sixty seconds exactly as the book has it: a respectable-looking man is seen standing at the same bus stop at the same hour every day, and four onlookers produce four accounts of him — a plainclothes policeman watching someone, an ordinary man out walking, a man not in his right mind, and, from someone with malice, a man planning harm — while the plain fact is that he is an employee waiting for his bus to the office. Third, the source's point drawn out: history reports the event; the motive and the background are supplied by whoever is writing, and the source names two causes of a wrong reading — malice, and simply not knowing the standing of the person being written about [SOURCE: the passage listing the causes]. Fourth, one sentence connecting it to tonight, and only one: of these particular ninety years, a great deal of what is in general circulation was written by the administration of the day or by people trained in its schools, and the source specifically warns against working only from translations and against beginning one's reading with the orientalists [SOURCE: the passage on translations, on مستشرقین, and شیخ علی طنطاوی رحمہ اللہ's list of what an Islamic historian must know]. No modern writer, textbook, syllabus or television programme is named, and no living author is criticised from the platform.
drafts.takehome_question: «آج ہم اپنے ماضی کے بارے میں جو کچھ جانتے ہیں — وہ کس نے لکھا، اور اُس نے کہاں سے لیا؟» [What we know today about our own past — who wrote it, and where did he take it from?]

sensitive.what_arises: This is the evening nearest to living memory, and nearly every fault line in a Pakistani room runs through it. Specifically: what ۱۸۵۷ is to be called, since the books of the period use different names for it and each name is a position; the maslak divisions that took their present institutional shape in exactly these decades, with دیوبند, بریلی, اہلِ حدیث and ندوہ all likely represented in the audience; سر سید احمد خان, whose civil and educational record and whose religious writings are judged very differently and often by the same person; the خلافت movement and whether it was wise; the fact that respected ulama took opposite sides in the ۱۹۴۰s, some with the Muslim League and some against partition, which is still argued today; the two-nation question and its present-day political uses; the violence and the migration of ۱۹۴۷, which is family memory for people in the room, not a topic; and the standing invitation, in any Pakistani gathering, to slide from ۱۹۴۷ into current politics.
sensitive.how_handled: Three mechanisms, all structural rather than improvised. First, the evening states its own boundary aloud in the opening three minutes, before anyone has a chance to test it: the narrative ends at ۱۹۴۷ [verify]; where books differ we say that they differ and give the source's word; and we do not judge between Muslims who chose differently. Saying it at the start prevents the question rather than deflecting it later. Second, the material is chosen so that the temperature stays low by construction — the تعارف slot is spent on the line of learning rather than on party politics, the two post-۱۸۵۷ institutions are given identical treatment down to the weight of the arrows on the map, and the founder of the country is narrated in the story rather than profiled, so that no personal endorsement is implied of anyone. Third, every hot question listed above gets a written answer in QA_BANK before the evening, and the guardrail installed in session 3 — that this is تاریخِ مسلمین and not the history of the religion itself — is restated in one sentence when the ۱۹۴۰s are reached.
will_not_be_said: No verdict on whether ۱۸۵۷ was غدر or جنگِ آزادی — the differing names are reported, the source's own word is used, and neither is endorsed
No ranking or comparison of دیوبند, بریلی, اہلِ حدیث or ندوہ, and no quotation from any of the nineteenth-century polemics between them
No verdict on سر سید احمد خان's religious views in either direction; his religious writings are not discussed at all, and only the factual educational and civil record is narrated
No adjudication between the ulama who supported the Muslim League and those who opposed partition — both positions are stated as positions genuinely held by ulama, and the evening stops there
Nothing about محمد علی جناح's personal religious practice
No narration of partition violence: no casualty figures, no community named as perpetrator or victim, no photographs on any slide
Nothing whatsoever after ۱۹۴۷ — no war, no Kashmir, no ۱۹۷۱, no political party, no government, no institution of the present state
Nothing on any constitutional or sect-declaration question of the later republic
No epithet or denunciation aimed at any British figure by name; the colonial administration is described by what it enacted, not by adjective
No claim that any present-day party, group or family is the continuation of a nineteenth-century one, and no reference to any political family of this city
sensitive.floor_policy: Questions are taken only in the last block or after the session ends, never inside the story, and are answered with one of three prepared moves. If the question is inside the evening and the source covers it, the answer is what the source says, and then a full stop. If it is a difference between Muslim groups or between ulama, the answer is «اس پر کتابیں مختلف ہیں؛ میں وہی سناؤں گا جو ہماری کتاب میں ہے» — and if the book has not been consulted on that exact point, the speaker writes the question down in front of the room and brings the passage next week; this is a habit the audience has already seen, so it reads as discipline rather than evasion. If it is after ۱۹۴۷, or about a party, a government or a living figure, it is declined warmly in one sentence — «یہ ہماری حد سے آگے کی بات ہے؛ ہمارا سلسلہ ۱۹۴۷ پر ختم ہوتا ہے» — and the speaker moves on without a second sentence. Nothing on the مشاجرات or on maslak is ever improvised from the floor. A question that is really a speech is met with thanks and the offer to talk afterwards.

sources_needed: FIRST, THE BLOCKING QUESTION: whether Tareekh-e-Ummat reaches the subcontinent after ۱۸۵۷ at all. Needed: the publisher's own volume listing, the number of volumes, and the stated coverage of each. If one volume covers برصغیر into the twentieth century, that volume is the spine, the course keeps a single named source, and nothing in this list beyond the map authorities is required. Also run the text-layer test on any scan before anyone is paid to OCR it.

IF IT DOES NOT REACH: ONE named Sunni work, chosen deliberately and named aloud to the audience as the second spine rather than quietly mixed in. Two candidates already identified: تاریخ دعوت و عزیمت (سید ابو الحسن علی ندوی) for the شاہ ولی اللہ → post-۱۸۵۷ line of scholars, and تاریخ اسلام (اکبر شاہ خان نجیب آبادی) for the general narrative — needed: which volumes cover this period, and a trusted scholar's sign-off before the name is said from the platform.

شاہ ولی اللہ رحمہ اللہ: his سنین in ھ and عیسوی; whether the adopted source titles him محدث دہلوی; one sentence on what he did in the source's own framing; and ONE authentic incident with a locatable position in the text.

The line of transmission from شاہ ولی اللہ رحمہ اللہ to the scholars of the post-۱۸۵۷ generation, stated by a named work. This is load-bearing for the whole positioning of the evening's first تعارف and must be the book's claim, not a connection we assemble ourselves.

The narrative of ۱۸۵۷: what the adopted source calls the event, in its own words; the sequence; where it began and how far it spread; and what the source says happened to دہلی afterwards — specifically to its schools, its scholars and its books, which is what the opening scene is built from.

The founding of the post-۱۸۵۷ institutions: for دیوبند and for علی گڑھ, the founder's name, the year, and the stated purpose, in the source's own words. Also needed: whether the source treats them comparatively — if it does, the comparison is not used.
سر سید احمد خان: the factual educational and civil record only. Needed explicitly: whether the adopted source discusses his religious views, so that portion can be identified and left out.

The خلافت movement: dates, what it actually demanded, its connection to استنبول, and how it ended — from a source we can name aloud, since this segment carries the evening's one long map arrow back to the peg drawn in week 7.

۱۹۰۶ [verify], ۱۹۴۰ [verify], ۱۹۴۷ [verify]: the founding of the Muslim League, the text or a fair summary of the ۱۹۴۰ resolution, and the sequence of ۱۹۴۷ — each from a citable source, none from general knowledge.

تعارف people two and three: once the identities are fixed, each needs سنین, one sentence on what they did, and ONE authentic incident with a citable location — for شیخ الہند مولانا محمود حسن رحمہ اللہ, the imprisonment and return; for علامہ محمد اقبال رحمہ اللہ, a specific documented occasion rather than a reading of his verse.

Two map authorities, both to be named on the printed map: one for the extent of the ۱۸۵۷ rising, and one printed atlas for the boundary of ۱۹۴۷. Neither is to be drawn from memory or from an online image.

«کیسے پتا چلا؟» — nothing new. The muqaddima passage on the harms of reading history outside its rules, the bus-stop illustration, the two causes of a wrong reading, and شیخ علی طنطاوی رحمہ اللہ's list of the historian's qualifications are all in hand. What is needed is the eye pass: every sentence used aloud or on a slide must be read off the page image, because the text layer garbles ligatures and honorifics.

«آج کی بات» — the exact printed wording of the author's two sentences on knowing the methods of those who work against us and on answering what is published in the name of history, read off the page image; plus one decision from the editor on which of the two sentences goes on the screen, given that the fuller wording names groups and this venue has ruled out anything that could be heard as aimed at a community.

No hadith and no ayah is planned for this session. If one is wanted, it must be checked against a numbered edition before it reaches a slide — nothing is quoted with a number that has not been seen in print.
notes_for_speaker: Say the stopping rule at the start, not at the end. One sentence, in the first three minutes: our line ends at ۱۹۴۷. Said early it prevents the hard question; said late it looks like you are dodging one.

Your safe ground tonight is the map and the line of teaching. If you feel the room heating — a murmur, two people talking to each other — walk to the map and put your hand on it. The map is neutral territory and the audience follows the hand.

The most dangerous sentence you can say tonight begins «اصل میں ہوا یہ کہ…». That is the historian's interpretation, and you have just spent three minutes warning the room about exactly that. Say «کتاب یہ کہتی ہے» instead. Rehearse the substitution until it is automatic.

Slow down twice. Once when the long arrow goes from دہلی west to استنبول — stop talking for two seconds and let the room recognise the city they drew in week 7. And once when you state where the evening stops; that sentence must be said slowly enough that nobody mistakes it for a throwaway.

Rehearse the شاہ ولی اللہ sentence until it is one clean sentence. He lived before these ninety years and the evening starts upstream of them. If you fumble this, a drop-in will spend the rest of the evening thinking you have the wrong century.

Practise the bus-stop illustration aloud with a timer until it lands in sixty seconds. It is the only part of tonight that comes from a book already in your hand — hold the book while you tell it. That single gesture is worth more to your credibility than any slide.

If you run long, cut in this order: first the recap detail at the top of the story block, since session 8 already did that work; second the middle detail of the خلافت movement, keeping only the demand and the ending; third the detail of the institutions' founding, keeping both names and both years. Never cut the bus-stop illustration, never cut the ۱۹۴۷ line on the map, and never cut the ninety seconds of writing.
The writing minute is your rest. While everyone is bent over their workbook, drink water and read the first line of your next block. Do not talk into that silence — it is doing the teaching for you.
If you blank: go to تعارف. Three names, four lines each, all of it on your card. The fixed shape exists precisely so that a blank costs you a transition and nothing else.
Do not answer a political question with a joke. On any other evening a joke defuses; on this one it will be heard as a position, and it will be quoted back to you by someone who was not in the room.

When you reach ۱۹۴۷, remember that for some people in front of you this is a family, not a topic. Lower your voice, state what happened and in which direction people moved, and move on. No numbers, no adjectives.

Read the whole plan once more the morning of, then put it away and rehearse only the opening scene, the three profiles and the bus stop. Those are the four things that must come out of your mouth without notes; everything else you may read.

drafts.title: سب کچھ جوڑ کر
drafts.howweknow_plan: Three minutes, and the only three minutes of the evening where the speaker holds an object up. He holds up the physical book the whole course was narrated from — Tareekh-e-Ummat by Maulana Muhammad Ismail Rehan — and says plainly: «دس ہفتے میں نے کوئی نئی بات نہیں کہی۔ میں نے ایک کتاب سنائی ہے۔ یہ رہی وہ کتاب۔» Then the printed reading ladder card (A5, tucked in the back of the workbook, handed out tonight) goes on the screen and he reads its three rungs aloud: (۱) the book you have been listening to — start with its own مقدمہ, the section on why history matters and what it is for [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1, المقدمہ — the section «تاریخ کا مقصد اور غرض و غایت»; editor supplies the printed page range for the card]; (۲) one classical work in a named, obtainable Urdu translation — البدایہ والنہایہ [SOURCE: publisher and translator of the Urdu edition actually purchasable in Pakistan — editor to verify before the card is printed; no title or press to be named that has not been seen]; (۳) the five mother-books as a shelf you should be able to name even if you never read them cover to cover [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1, المقدمہ — the five mother-books section, the names as the book lists them]. Then the closing of the thread that ran all ten weeks, put as the three questions to ask of anything you read or are told: «کس نے کہا؟» (who narrated it, and through whom — week 1's principle, that dates were the tool by which false narrators were caught) · «کب؟» (does the chronology even permit it — week 3's forged document, killed on two dates) · «کیا یہ ممکن بھی ہے؟» (روایہ plus درایہ — week 8). Finally the one test the speaker gives them for judging any history book they pick up, taken directly from the model the source itself uses: does the book state a work's کمزوریاں as openly as its خوبیاں? He shows that our own book does exactly that for every one of the five mother-books, and says: a book that only praises its sources is not teaching you history, it is selling you a position. [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1, المقدمہ — the خوبیاں / کمزوریاں headings under two of the mother-book notices, photographed for the slide; editor supplies printed pages.]
drafts.map: The base map is the same one used for ten weeks: same projection, six anchor cities already printed — مکہ · مدینہ · دمشق · بغداد · قرطبہ · قسطنطنیہ. Tonight the speaker draws nothing. Ten numbered adhesive dots (۱ to ۱۰) come out of an envelope at the start, and during the twenty-minute wall-walk ten different attendees come up, one per stop, and place their dot on the wall map while the room says where it goes: ۱ — the whole basin framed, مکہ and مدینہ at its centre; ۲ — مدینہ held, then outward to یرموک، قادسیہ، مصر; ۳ — the new garrison centres, کوفہ · بصرہ · فسطاط · دمشق; ۴ — the widest extent, سندھ in the east and اندلس in the west inside the same decade; ۵ — the two capitals of one century, بغداد and قرطبہ; ۶ — the Levant, then the sweep from the east onto بغداد, and قاہرہ as the refuge; ۷ — اناطولیہ → قسطنطنیہ → ویانا, then the long retreat back; ۸ — سندھ → غزنی و غور → دہلی; ۹ — the subcontinent, ۱۸۵۷ [verify] and ۱۹۴۷ [verify]. Every attendee places the same ten dots on the half-blank map in their own workbook at the same moment, in their own hand. The tenth dot is the only one the speaker places himself, and it is the evening's single piece of new drawing: a dot on the city this hall stands in, joined by one straight line back to دہلی — and above the line he writes nothing, he only traces the whole route with his finger and says the direction aloud: مدینہ → شام و عراق → مغرب و اندلس → پھر واپس مشرق → دہلی → یہ شہر، یہ کمرہ. The completed map — ten dots, chronological, west-to-east then east-to-west then east again — is what they carry out of the room.
notes_for_speaker: This is the easiest of the ten evenings and the plan is built that way on purpose: the room speaks for roughly 25 of the 45 minutes. Your job for the twenty-minute wall-walk is to ask three fixed questions ten times and keep time. All thirty questions are printed on the A4 cue card in order — if you blank, you read the next line off the card.

Nothing said tonight is new. Every scene you read in the opening is read verbatim off the printed script of the week it belongs to. Hold the paper. Reading aloud from a page is dignified and is what the evening is designed around — do not re-improvise a scene from memory, because a re-improvised scene is where a wrong date gets born.
Hand the phone timer to a regular attendee before you start the wall-walk and ask him to raise a hand at two minutes per stop. You should not be watching a clock while ten people are talking.

Slow down twice. First at the آیت — read the Arabic off the printed sheet in front of you, never from memory, then pause, then the Urdu rendering beneath it. Second at the last dot on the map: say the route out loud slowly, with your finger moving, and then stop talking and let the room look at it.
Safe ground when you lose your place: put your hand physically on the banner at the last marked session and ask «اس کے بعد کیا ہوا؟» The room will carry it. The banner is your script.

If you are running long: cut the third scene fragment in the opening (it is marked optional on the script); compress stops where the room answered fast to sixty seconds; and in «آج کی بات» take two readers instead of four. Do not cut a person from «تعارف» and do not cut the reading ladder — the ladder is what the evening is for.

If you are running short, the spare material is on the cue card: one more scene fragment for recognition, and the source's own list of what a historian must be [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1, المقدمہ — the section on مؤرخ کی صفات / اسلامی مؤرخ کے اوصاف; editor supplies printed page].
Do not answer a date from memory tonight, not even one you have said nine times. Every date on your card carries [verify] and the card is the authority, not your recall.

Do not let the close turn into open Q&A. The answer to «اب آگے کیا پڑھیں؟» is the printed card in their hand, and the answer to a hot question is the deferral line at the top of the cue card. Both are printed so you never have to compose one while tired.
Say the guardrail sentence once, early, in the آغاز — one sentence, then move on. Saying it once at the start is much easier than defending it at the end.
drafts.opening_scene: The speaker picks up a printed page and reads aloud, word for word, a scene the room already heard once — the opening scene of an earlier evening, read from that week's own script, with every name and every place-name removed [SOURCE: the delivered opening-scene text of session 2, read verbatim from the session-2 script; do not re-compose it]. He reads for about two minutes and stops at the end of the scene without naming it. Then one question to the room: «یہ کون سا ہفتہ تھا؟ اور نقشے پر کہاں؟» — hands go up, the room names the session and the place, and the speaker confirms in one sentence. He then reads two shorter fragments, forty-five seconds each, from two later evenings — one from the middle of the arc and one from the last century of it [SOURCE: the delivered opening-scene texts of sessions 6 and 9, verbatim from those scripts] — and the room names both. The question left hanging is the one he does not answer: «آپ کو یہ سب یاد ہے۔ سوال یہ ہے کہ ایک سال بعد بھی یاد رہے گا؟ آج کی نشست اسی کے لیے ہے۔»

people.name: ابن جریر الطبری رحمہ اللہ
people.did: He gathered the early reports of the Muslim past, each with the chain it came down through, into one continuous chronicle that almost every later historian drew on.
people.incident_plan: One incident about how he actually worked — his own stated method of setting a report down with the chain it arrived by and leaving the reader to weigh it — told plainly, followed by one sentence of the caution the source itself attaches to reading him raw. This is also where the speaker uses the book's own answer to the objection an attendee is most likely to have heard about him, in the book's words, not his own. [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1, المقدمہ — the notice on تاریخ طبری with its خوبیاں and کمزوریاں, and the following section answering doubts raised about it; one narrated incident and his own words on method, read off the page image; editor supplies سنین and the printed pages.]

people.name: ابن کثیر رحمہ اللہ
people.did: He wrote a history running from the beginning of things down to his own age, and of these works it is the one an ordinary Urdu reader can realistically sit down with.
people.incident_plan: One incident from his working life showing the habit that makes his book usable — that he was a man of hadith before he was a chronicler, and sifted a report before he set it down. Told as a single concrete moment, not as a description of his qualities. [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1, المقدمہ — the notice on البدایہ والنہایہ with its خوبیاں and کمزوریاں; one incident from that notice, read off the page image; editor supplies سنین and the printed page.]

people.name: ابن خلدون رحمہ اللہ
people.did: He wrote a long introduction to his history in which he set out how societies gather strength and lose it, and taught readers to ask of any report whether the thing described was even possible.
people.incident_plan: One incident of him doing exactly that — a specific report he examines and rejects, with the reason he gives for rejecting it. This is the evening's closing demonstration that the three checking questions are not our invention but the tradition's own, so the incident must be one the source narrates and must be told with its reasoning intact. [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1, المقدمہ — the notice on تاریخ ابن خلدون with its خوبیاں and کمزوریاں; one worked example of a report tested against possibility, read off the page image; editor supplies سنین and the printed page.]

runsheet.block: آغاز — the completed line and the completed map
runsheet.content: The wall banner goes up as it has for ten weeks, except that tonight it is already full: every session marked in marker across the eight pegs from ۱۱ھ [verify] to ۱۹۴۷ [verify]. The speaker says one sentence only: «پچھلے ہفتے ہم یہاں رکے تھے۔ آج ہم آگے نہیں جا رہے — آج ہم پوری لکیر پر واپس چلیں گے۔» Everyone opens the workbook to the Line spread and to the collected-lessons page at the back; the envelope of ten numbered map dots and the bound «تعارف نامہ» go round. Drop-ins get the catch-up sheet and are told plainly that tonight needs no prior attendance. He also says the guardrail sentence once here, early, and moves on: this course has been تاریخِ مسلمین, the history of the Muslims, not a ruling on the religion, and tonight is a review of what was said, not a court [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1, المقدمہ — the section «تاریخ اسلام یا تاریخ مسلمین»; editor supplies the printed page for the slide].

runsheet.block: Opening — the scene they already own
runsheet.content: The speaker reads aloud, from the printed page, an opening scene the room heard in an earlier week, with names and places stripped out, and asks «یہ کون سا ہفتہ تھا؟ نقشے پر کہاں؟» The room names it. Two shorter fragments follow, from a middle evening and from the last century of the arc, and the room names those too. He closes the block on the question he leaves unanswered: you remember it tonight — will you remember it in a year? That is what tonight is for.

runsheet.block: The wall-walk — ten stops along the banner
runsheet.content: The speaker walks the banner left to right and stops ten times, roughly two minutes per stop, one stop per session, and at every stop he asks the same three questions and then stops talking: «کون سا زمانہ؟» — the room answers with the peg; «نقشے پر کہاں؟» — one attendee comes up and places that session's numbered dot on the wall map while everyone places the same dot in their own workbook; «اُس ہفتے آپ نے کیا لکھا تھا؟» — one named participant reads aloud, from their own handwriting on the back page of their workbook, the سبق they wrote that night, in their own words. The speaker adds nothing except, where the room stalls, one printed line off his cue card — the period, the place, and the one sentence of what happened, all previously delivered and previously sourced [SOURCE: the ten delivered سبق lines and ten one-line period summaries, taken verbatim from docs/catalogue/LESSONS.md and the delivered scripts]. A regular attendee holds the timer and raises a hand at two minutes so the speaker never watches the clock. By the last stop the map carries ten dots in order and every listener has heard nine other people say, in their own words, what a session meant.

runsheet.block: تعارف — three historians, to be read now by the listener
