runsheet.content: Three notices, about two minutes twenty each, in the same classical تراجم format used every week: نام و نسب as the source gives it · سنین · what the person did in one sentence · ایک واقعہ, one authentic incident read off the source page. Tonight the three are chosen for a single reason and the speaker says it out loud: these are the three whose books you can now go and open yourself. The workbook prints the first three lines of each and leaves «ایک واقعہ» blank, so the room writes the incident by hand as he tells it. The bound «تعارف نامہ» containing all thirty profiles from the ten weeks is confirmed in their hands here.

runsheet.block: کیسے پتا چلا؟ — where to go next, and how to check what you read
runsheet.content: The speaker holds up the actual book the whole course was narrated from and says he has not authored anything for ten weeks, he has narrated a book — and here it is. The printed reading ladder card goes up: start with this book's own مقدمہ, then one classical work in a named Urdu translation, then the five mother-books as a shelf you can at least name. Then the three questions that ran through all ten weeks, said together for the last time — «کس نے کہا؟» · «کب؟» · «کیا یہ ممکن بھی ہے؟» — and one test for any history book they pick up: does it state a work's کمزوریاں as openly as its خوبیاں, the way the book in his hand does for every source it uses.

runsheet.block: آج کی بات — the supplied آیت, then everyone writes
runsheet.content: The آیت on عبرت in the accounts of those who came before goes on the screen in Naskh with the Urdu rendering beneath it, and the speaker reads it off the printed sheet, not from memory, then reads the Urdu, then says nothing for a moment [SOURCE: the Arabic text of the آیت and its سورہ and آیت number, plus the Urdu rendering as the book gives it, read off the page image of Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1, المقدمہ, section «تاریخ کی اہمیت قرآن مجید کی نظر میں» — reference supplied by the editor; nothing composed by us]. He gives no lesson of his own after it. The instruction is the same as every week, and this is the tenth line: «آپ کے سامنے آپ کے اپنے ہاتھ کے لکھے دس جملے ہیں۔ ان دس ہفتوں میں سے آپ کے لیے سب سے بڑی عبرت کیا ہے — ایک جملے میں، اپنے الفاظ میں لکھیے۔» Everyone writes in silence for about ninety seconds; then three or four read theirs aloud and the speaker thanks each and does not comment on any.

runsheet.block: اگلے ہفتے — the question they take with them
runsheet.content: The block keeps its name although there is no next week from the front of the room, and the speaker says so: «اگلا ہفتہ اب میرا نہیں، آپ کا ہے۔» One concrete instruction for the coming seven days: open the مقدمہ of the book on your reading ladder and read the opening section on what history is for — that is thirty minutes, not thirty hours. He points at the map one last time, traces مدینہ → دمشق → بغداد → قرطبہ → قسطنطنیہ → دہلی → this city, then puts the marker down and closes on the question, which he does not answer; the room answers it, and the answer they call back is «کس نے کہا؟»

sensitive.what_arises: No new material is introduced, but the evening replays ten weeks in compressed form and, unusually, the audience holds the floor for about half of it. That is where the exposure sits. Three stops on the wall-walk touch periods that were handled carefully when first delivered — the مشاجرات between the Companions ؓ, the Umayyad period including Karbala, and the years from ۱۸۵۷ [verify] to ۱۹۴۷ [verify], where the subject matter shades into present-day politics. Because participants read out their own written سبق lines, a participant may phrase something more sharply than the speaker ever did, may name a Companion ؓ in a judgmental way, or may turn a lesson about the last century into a comment on current politics or on another sect. Drop-ins who attended none of the earlier evenings hear the whole arc in twenty minutes with none of the guardrails they were given in context.
sensitive.how_handled: The recall drill is deliberately closed-form: three fixed questions with short answers — which period, where on the map, what you wrote — and no open discussion at any stop. The guardrail is restated once in the first three minutes so it frames the whole evening rather than being produced defensively later, in the source's own words and not the speaker's: this has been تاریخِ مسلمین, the history of the Muslims, and the fiqh position that examining the مشاجرات without need is مکروہ [SOURCE: Tareekh-e-Ummat vol.1, المقدمہ — the sections «تاریخ اسلام یا تاریخ مسلمین» and «تاریخ کا حکم فقہاء کے نزدیک»; editor supplies printed pages]. When a participant's own written line strays, the speaker's response is fixed and gentle and is printed on his cue card: he thanks them, does not repeat the sharp phrasing back, does not comment on it, and moves to the next stop. He never adjudicates between Companions ؓ and never ranks them. Whatever was said in an earlier week is the ceiling for tonight: nothing is expanded, no new detail is added on any sensitive stop, and if a stop was narrated carefully in week 3 or week 4, tonight it gets the same sentence it got then and nothing more.
will_not_be_said: Any judgement between the Companions ؓ, any ranking of them against one another, or any verdict on who was right in the مشاجرات
Any verdict, defence or condemnation of Yazid, or any ruling of کفر, فسق or تکفیر on any named person
Any comparison, criticism or characterisation of a present-day sect, maslak, madrasa, scholar or organisation
Any comment on present-day Pakistani politics, parties, personalities, the army, the judiciary, or any current controversy; the course stops at ۱۹۴۷ [verify] and the speaker says so plainly
Any comment on India, on Hindus or on any other community as a people, in the ۱۸۵۷ [verify] and ۱۹۴۷ [verify] stops
Any page number, volume number, hadith number, chain, death-date or book reference spoken from memory rather than read off the printed card
Any claim, incident or date that was not delivered in one of the previous nine evenings from the named source — tonight introduces nothing new
Any identification or discussion of an attendee's own sect or background, and no response that begins «آپ کے مسلک میں…»
sensitive.floor_policy: There is no open Q&A tonight and the speaker announces that at the start, framed positively: tonight the room does the talking, but in a fixed shape. A hot or contested question from the floor gets one printed sentence and no improvisation: «سوال اہم ہے۔ آج کی نشست دہرانے کی ہے، نئی بات کی نہیں۔ اس کا جواب کتاب میں موجود ہے — نشست کے بعد میں آپ کو صفحہ کھول کر دکھا دوں گا۔» The question is written on a card, kept, and answered afterwards one-to-one from the page, or from the prepared answers in the QA bank; if there is no prepared answer, the honest sentence is «میں نے یہ نہیں پڑھا، میں دیکھ کر بتاؤں گا» — which is the whole course's method and costs the speaker nothing. If a question concerns the مشاجرات specifically, the answer is the restated guardrail and a full stop, with no example given. If it concerns politics after ۱۹۴۷ [verify], the answer is that the course ends there by design. The speaker never takes a second follow-up on the same question from the floor.

sources_needed: The آیت on عبرت in the accounts of those who came before: the Arabic text, its سورہ and آیت number, and the Urdu rendering exactly as Tareekh-e-Ummat gives them in the muqaddima's section on the importance of history in the Qur'an. Arabic must be read off the page image, never from the OCR text layer and never composed by us; the reference is supplied by the editor.

One authentic incident per historian, from the same notices: for ابن جریر الطبری, an incident on his own working method plus the section answering objections raised about his chronicle; for ابن کثیر, an incident showing that he sifted a report before writing it; for ابن خلدون, a worked example of a report he rejects as not possible, with his reasoning.

The خوبیاں and کمزوریاں headings under two of the mother-book notices, photographed cleanly for the slide, since the candour test in «کیسے پتا چلا؟» is demonstrated from the page rather than asserted.

The muqaddima's section on what history is for, for the آغاز framing and for the seven-day reading instruction at the close — plus the exact printed page range so the reading ladder card can point at it.
The wording of «تاریخ اسلام یا تاریخ مسلمین» and of the fiqh grading of studying the مشاجرات, for the one-sentence guardrail restatement in the آغاز.

The delivered opening-scene texts of three earlier sessions, verbatim from those weeks' scripts, printed on separate sheets for the recognition reading — the speaker must not re-compose them on the night.

The ten final سبق lines exactly as delivered, from the lessons catalogue, plus a one-line period summary per session for the cue card, so the speaker's fallback line at any stop is previously delivered text.

Publisher and translator of the Urdu edition of البدایہ والنہایہ actually purchasable in Pakistan, verified by sight before the reading ladder card goes to print — no edition, press or translator to be named that has not been seen.
The names of the five mother-books exactly as the muqaddima lists them, for the third rung of the reading ladder card.

Optional spare, if the evening runs short: the muqaddima's section on the qualities required of a historian — noting that the attribution there is garbled in the OCR text and must be verified against the page image before the name is spoken.
drafts.summary: Session 10 is a consolidation evening with no new history in it, designed so that the audience works and the speaker mostly asks questions. The completed timeline banner and the completed map go back up, and the room walks the ten weeks in ten two-minute stops: at each stop attendees name the period, one of them places a numbered dot on the wall map, and one participant reads aloud, from their own handwriting in their workbook, the lesson they wrote that week — so all ten lessons are heard in the participants' own words rather than the speaker's. The last third of the evening hands them the reading path: three historians introduced as people they can now read themselves, a printed reading ladder starting with the single book this whole course narrated, and the three checking questions that have run through all ten weeks. It closes with the supplied Qur'anic verse on عبرت, one final sentence written by every listener in their own hand, and a question the room answers rather than the speaker. Because nothing is asserted tonight that was not delivered and sourced in an earlier week, this is the lowest-risk evening of the ten for both accuracy and the speaker's nerves.

gaps: No contingency for the source. Six of the ten evenings (4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9) are explicitly blocked on volumes that are not in hand, and session 8 does not even know whether the book covers South Asia at all. There is no deadline by which a volume must arrive, no named person responsible for obtaining it, and — except for session 8 — no fallback evening if it does not. A manager will ask what is delivered on the night if the book never comes.

No named reviewer. Session 3 says the sensitive wording will be "checked with a qualified عالم" and session 4 says the کربلا text is "approved before the night", but no scholar is named, no approval date is given, and there is no sign-off route for the other eight evenings. For a venue, the question is who countersigns the کربلا page and the ۱۹۴۷ page.

Nothing about recording, photography or clips. Ten evenings on Karbala, the fall of بغداد, ۱۹۲۴ and ۱۹۴۷ will be filmed on phones. There is no stated policy on recording, on what may be posted, or on what the speaker does if a two-minute کربلا block circulates without the guardrail that preceded it.

No course calendar, and therefore no check against محرم. Session 4 says only that it falls "close to no particular calendar date" while conceding the material "will be heard as" محرم material. Management needs the ten dates and confirmation that the Karbala evening does not land in محرم or immediately beside it.

The speaker is never introduced to the room. The whole design rests on his narrating one named book rather than authoring history, but the room is not told this until session 10 («دس ہفتے میں نے کوئی نئی بات نہیں کہی»). Nothing in session 1 states aloud that he has no formal training, that he is narrating a named Sunni book, and that he will not give rulings. That sentence belongs in the first three minutes of week one.

The book and its author are never justified. A manager asked "whose book is this?" by an attendee has nothing to work from: no line on who مولانا محمد اسماعیل ریحان is, what his standing is, or why this source was chosen over another. If an attendee objects to the source itself, no evening has an answer.

Physical requirements are never listed for the venue. A three-metre banner behind the speaker, a wall map drawn on with markers every week, and both left hanging between sessions ("the Line stays on the wall") — nothing states what is fixed to the walls, how, who removes it, who repairs the surface, or where the artifacts are stored for ten weeks.

No escalation protocol. Sessions 2 and 4 anticipate two attendees arguing across the room or the room becoming heated, and session 4 pre-decides to end the evening — but no venue staff role is named, nobody is designated to intervene, and there is no agreed signal between the speaker and the venue.

The drop-in catch-up sheet is promised in seven evenings and never specified. Its content is never drafted, never sourced, and never approved — yet it is the only thing a first-time attendee holds on the کربلا evening or the ۱۹۴۷ evening.

Session 10 depends on participants who may not be there. The wall-walk needs nine attendees who each wrote a lesson on the relevant night and will read it aloud, and no plan exists for recruiting or briefing them in advance. Nor is anything read aloud pre-seen: the one moment in ten weeks where unvetted words are spoken into the room is a participant reading their own sentence, and the only mitigation offered is that the speaker will thank them and move on.

No route for an attendee who thinks something said was wrong. The plans promise repeatedly that a deferred question will be answered the following week, but there is no written record kept, no contact address, and nothing for a person who does not return.

Audience logistics are absent: expected numbers, seating, whether the gathering is mixed, whether children attend, and whether anything is provided for attendees whose Urdu is weak — in a DHA room this last is a real possibility and the entire course is delivered in Urdu.

No decision on the second spine. Sessions 6, 8 and 9 each allow a second named Sunni work to be brought in if the main source is thin, with different candidate lists and no rule about who chooses or when. If three evenings each adopt a different second book, the course's one-source premise — the speaker's whole protection — quietly disappears.

Print deadlines are never set. Session 1 warns that a printed peg is "the one artifact of the course that cannot be corrected after distribution", yet every date on it still carries [verify] and no date is given by which the Line, the base map and the workbook must be finalised and approved.
review.overall:
Read as a whole, this does read as an organised and unusually self-aware course. The fixed 45-minute shape holds in all ten evenings, the timings add up, the map is a real teaching instrument rather than decoration, and the safety thinking is structural rather than improvised: the fiqh guardrail is installed before the disputed material, the کربلا block is bounded and read from the page, ۱۹۲۴ and ۱۹۴۷ have announced boundaries, the will_not_be_said lists are specific enough to be checked against a recording, and the plans repeatedly refuse numbers, refuse verdicts and refuse modern analogies. Session 4's handling of «عام الجماعۃ» — refusing to print a year's name as a man's title — is the kind of discipline that should reassure a manager. What a manager should not be reassured by is the sourcing. Six of the ten evenings are written against volumes nobody has read, and in several places the drafting has quietly filled that vacuum: a scene composed at a railway platform in session 7, an Arabic saying set into the plan in session 4, an Urdu quotation drafted for امام علی بن المدینیؒ in session 5, a quoted phrase attributed to a book not in hand in session 2, a named forgery in session 1 that session 3 treats as unknown, a command arrangement asserted in session 6, and a count of مصحف copies built into a map artifact in session 3. Each is small; together they are the exact failure the course exists to avoid, and every one of them reaches the page under the speaker's name. Alongside these sit the mechanical rule breaches — untagged dates in every era field, a Roman Urdu phrase in session 7, a banned word in session 6, an invented symbol on session 8's map, and a maxim of the speaker's own at the close of session 10 — which are cheap to fix and should be fixed before management sees another draft.

The single weakest evening is session 7, آخری خلافت. It carries the second-highest sensitivity in the course, it depends entirely on a volume that is not held, and it is the evening where the drafting has filled that gap with the speaker's own composition: an opening scene with invented sensory detail whose source may not exist, a «کیسے پتا چلا؟» segment the plan openly concedes will be delivered as unsourced method and which ends on a coined maxim, a spoken \"six hundred years\" figure produced by arithmetic the course elsewhere forbids saying aloud, and a لقب table printing titles the plan admits may not be in the book. On top of that it is the evening that reads the word «غدار» aloud into a room the plan itself says will want to be told who the traitors were, from a passage whose fuller wording the plan concedes names groups — and the only mitigation is the speaker's silence afterwards. It is not badly conceived; the minute-7 boundary is the best single safety device in the series and should be copied into other evenings. But it currently asks the speaker to stand up on the most exposed subject after session 3 with the least of the source under his feet, and it should not be scheduled until the عثمانیہ volume is in hand and the opening scene, the method segment and the three panels have been rebuilt from it. Session 9 runs it close for the same reason — no source at all, nearest to living memory — but session 9 is candid about it, keeps the temperature down by construction, and its تعارف trio still has an unresolved question (whether محمد علی جناح joins it) that must be settled before, not on, the night.
